items.title: EASIEST Way to Catch Fish in Saltwater Marshes
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Catch more redfish, flounder, and black drum with this easy saltwater marsh fishing strategy. Learn where to cast and how to work your lure!
items.search_text: Saltwater marshes can be absolutely LOADED with redfish, flounder, and black drum. But with miles of shoreline, countless creek mouths, and plenty of places for fish to hide, where the heck do you start? On a three-day fishing trip to Louisiana, Joe and I discovered just how effective ONE simple marsh fishing strategy can be. And the best part? We caught a ridiculous number of fish without constantly changing lures, rigs, or techniques! Here’s how we did it (and how you can use the same approach in your home waters). Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Lure 1: Prawn XT Jr. (3.5″) Rigging 1: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead 1/4 oz Rod: Slam Stick Traveler (M-MH) Reel: Otis 3000 (Coming Soon) – Get the Otis 2500 here . Lure 2: Wake Mullet 1. Start With the Corners of Marsh Creek Mouths Our original plan was to target bull redfish in bigger water around Venice, Louisiana. Unfortunately, the fish didn’t get that memo. So Captain Hollywood suggested we head into the marsh and start targeting the corners where smaller creeks meet larger waterways. And that changed EVERYTHING! Instead of randomly casting along miles of shoreline, we focused on these creek intersections. The key areas were: The points and corners where smaller creeks entered larger waterways. The upcurrent shoreline leading into those intersections. Roughly 100 feet of shoreline on either side of the creek mouths. These areas gave us smaller, more manageable zones to search rather than blindly covering water. And it didn’t take long to start getting bites! We caught redfish, flounder, and black drum using this same approach across multiple sections of the marsh. One important lesson: Don’t overlook the really small creeks. One of our most productive stops was a tiny creek that didn’t look like much from the outside. Yet it produced multiple redfish, including some really nice ones! Sometimes the smallest openings can hold a surprising number of fish. 2. Let the Current Do Some of the Work Finding the right location is only half the battle. HOW you present your lure can make just as much of a difference. Throughout most of this trip, I used a Prawn XT Jr. rigged on a 1/4 oz Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead . My retrieve was incredibly simple: Cast upcurrent toward the structure or shoreline you’re targeting. Allow the shrimp lure to sink toward the bottom. Use slow twitches and hops to bounce the lure along the bottom. Maintain contact with your lure and pay attention for those subtle thumps! That was pretty much it! We were often fishing unfamiliar bottom structure, including areas where I could feel what seemed like rocks or shell. The weedless jighead allowed me to work those areas with less risk of getting snagged. And here’s an important detail… You don’t have to use the exact same retrieve speed in every depth. In deeper water, I could let the lure sink and bounce it along the bottom. When we moved into shallower sections, I sped up the retrieve slightly to keep the lure from constantly dragging bottom. The goal was to keep the shrimp moving naturally through the strike zone. This simple adjustment helped us catch fish in water ranging from very shallow sight-fishing areas to deeper marsh channels. 3. Don’t Ignore the Shorelines BETWEEN Creek Mouths Creek intersections were our primary targets, but they weren’t the only places we found fish. As we worked from one creek mouth to the next, we continued casting along the shoreline. And that produced some excellent action, too! One particularly productive approach was casting tight against the reeds, letting the lure reach bottom, and slowly twitching it away from the shoreline. We also paid close attention to signs of fish activity. On day two, we noticed large wakes moving along a marsh bank. Some were mullet, but others were redfish! Once we got into position, the action was incredible. Joe sight-fished a nice redfish, and we continued catching fish along that same stretch of shoreline. I even switched briefly to a Wake Mullet to gain some extra casting distance and reach those aggressive fish. The takeaway? Start with the high-percentage areas, like creek mouths and points, but keep your eyes open as you move between them. Nervous baitfish, wakes, and other signs of activity can help you locate fish that aren’t holding directly on the obvious structure. 4. When You Catch ONE Fish, Don’t Leave Just Yet! This might be one of the most important lessons from the entire trip. Catching a fish doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve finished fishing that spot! In fact, we repeatedly caught multiple fish from the same small areas. At one creek mouth, I landed a redfish, cast right back into the same general zone, and hooked another one almost immediately. Joe then hooked an even bigger fish nearby! At another location, we caught roughly half a dozen fish before the bite finally slowed down. We even returned to a productive shoreline later in the day and caught more fish. Here’s the simple approach I’d recommend: When you catch a fish, make another cast to that same area. Work the surrounding water before assuming the action is over. If the bite slows down, move to the next similar piece of structure. When you discover a productive pattern, look for other locations that share those features. It’s easy to get excited after landing a nice redfish and immediately start looking for the next spot. But sometimes the next fish is sitting just a few feet away! And there’s no need to make this more complicated than it has to be. We used essentially the same strategy across three different days and multiple marsh locations, catching everything from flounder to an 18-pound black drum. Even more impressive, the individual Prawn XT Jr. I relied on throughout the trip was still in great shape afterward. That durability meant more time fishing and less time digging around in the tackle box. Final Thoughts This trip was a great reminder that successful marsh fishing doesn’t have to be complicated. We explored unfamiliar water, targeted similar types of structure, and used one basic presentation to catch a TON of fish. Redfish, flounder, black drum… the same strategy produced all three! And while having the right tackle certainly helps, knowing WHERE to cast and HOW to work your lure is what makes this approach so valuable. So the next time you’re exploring a saltwater marsh, start with the creek intersections, pay attention to the current, and don’t overlook the shoreline between your spots. You might be surprised how many fish you can catch without ever changing your setup! Have you had more success fishing marsh creek mouths or the shorelines between them? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Where should you start fishing in a saltwater marsh? Creek mouths, points, and intersections where smaller waterways enter larger channels are great starting points. During our Louisiana trip, we focused on the corners of these intersections and approximately 100 feet of shoreline on either side. What’s the best lure for catching redfish, flounder, and black drum in marshes? A soft plastic shrimp imitation is an excellent option for targeting all three species. We had tremendous success using the Prawn XT Jr. on a weedless jighead, bouncing it along the bottom near creek mouths and marsh shorelines. What size jighead should you use for marsh fishing? I used a 1/4 oz Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead throughout this trip. It gave me a versatile setup for fishing several depths by adjusting my retrieve. The ideal weight for your situation will depend on water depth, current, and how you want to present your lure. Should you move after catching a redfish in a marsh creek? Not immediately! We caught multiple redfish from the same small areas throughout this trip. After landing a fish, make several more casts to that location and nearby water before moving on.

items.title: You’re Probably Fishing the Tides WRONG (4 Common Mistakes)
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Making these 4 common tide fishing mistakes? Learn how to fish incoming, outgoing, and slack tides to find more redfish, trout, and snook.
items.search_text: Most inshore anglers know when high tide and low tide are going to happen. But knowing WHEN the tide changes and knowing HOW to actually fish the tide are two completely different things! As the water moves, bait moves, fish reposition, and the spot you’re fishing right now might be completely wrong an hour from now. I’ve seen anglers make the same mistakes over and over again when fishing changing tides. So in this video, I’m breaking down 4 common tide fishing mistakes that could be costing you fish and, more importantly, what you should be doing instead! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Plan Smarter. Catch More Fish! Having a game plan BEFORE you hit the water already puts you one step ahead! Use Smart Fishing Spots to check tides, explore promising areas, and plan your next trip with confidence. Then, once you’re on the water, combine that game plan with these 4 tips to adapt to changing conditions and give yourself a HUGE advantage! EXPLORE SMART FISHING SPOTS → Mistake #1: Fishing the Tide Chart Instead of the Water I use tide charts all the time. They’re great tools for planning a fishing trip. They give me an idea of when the water should be rising, falling, and reaching high or low tide. But here’s the important part: A tide chart is a prediction, NOT a guarantee of what’s actually happening on the water! Wind, offshore storms, rainfall, and freshwater runoff can all influence water levels and conditions. If my tide chart says the water should be falling, but I get to my fishing spot and the water isn’t moving yet, I’m going to fish what I actually see. There are a few simple things I look for: Oyster bars and shoreline grass: Is the water covering or exposing them? Floating grass and debris: Which direction is the water carrying them? Points, docks, and creek mouths: How is the current moving around the structure? I’m really trying to answer three questions: Is the water rising or falling? How much is it moving? What is that movement doing to the area I’m fishing? The takeaway: Use tide charts to PLAN your trip, but let your observations on the water determine WHERE and HOW you fish. Mistake #2: Not Moving With the Water This is probably the BIGGEST mistake on my list! I see anglers find a productive fishing spot, catch a few fish, and continue fishing that same exact spot as the tide changes. Eventually, the bite stops, and they assume the fish are done feeding. But that’s not necessarily what’s happening. Those fish might not have stopped feeding. They might have just MOVED! Let’s say you’re fishing a grass shoreline near high tide. There are redfish feeding tight against the grass, and you’re getting bites. As the tide begins falling, those fish might stay along that shoreline for a while. But eventually, the water gets too shallow, and they have to reposition. They might move toward: The outer edge of a flat A nearby trough or depth change A creek mouth or drain pulling bait out Another area with enough water to continue feeding That’s why I like breaking incoming and outgoing tides into early, middle, and late stages. An early outgoing tide might leave plenty of water along a shoreline, while a late outgoing tide could leave that same shoreline almost completely exposed. Both are technically outgoing tides, but they’re very different fishing situations. So when the bite stops, don’t immediately assume you need to find an entirely new fishing spot. Instead, ask yourself: Where would these fish logically move as the water level changes? Sometimes you don’t need to find new fish. You just need to FOLLOW the fish you’ve already found! Mistake #3: Assuming Stronger Current Is Always Better We’ve all heard that moving water is good for fishing. And generally speaking, I agree! But that doesn’t mean I want to find the strongest current possible and cast my lure right into the middle of it. What I’m really looking for is somewhere that moving water creates an easy feeding opportunity. Think about an oyster bar with current flowing around it. The structure interrupts that current, creating faster-moving water on one side and a slower pocket behind it. Predator fish can use that slower water to conserve energy while the current delivers food nearby. That’s exactly the type of feeding opportunity I want to find! Different species can also position differently around current. For example: Snook, trout, and flounder often take advantage of faster-moving current. Redfish may position in slower, calmer areas where they can feed without fighting strong current. I look for these opportunities around oyster bars, points, islands, grass lines, creek mouths, docks, and depth changes. Instead of asking where I can find the strongest current, I ask: Where is this current creating the EASIEST feeding opportunity? Because fish are predators. If they can conserve energy while food is being delivered right to them, that’s a pretty good place to start fishing! The takeaway: Don’t assume stronger current automatically means better fishing. Look for productive current and pay attention to how it interacts with structure. Mistake #4: Giving Up When the Tide Goes Slack You’ve probably experienced this before. The water is moving, you’re catching fish, and everything seems to be going great. Then the current starts slowing down. Eventually, it almost completely stops. And so do the bites! It’s easy to assume the feeding window is over. But here’s something I want you to remember: Slack tide isn’t necessarily the END of the bite. It’s a TRANSITION! There are still situations where fish will feed even without much current. For example, during high slack tide, redfish might continue feeding across a flooded grass flat. During low slack tide, those same fish might become concentrated in deeper pools after the surrounding water drains away. But here’s another important thing to consider. When the tide goes slack, the water is getting ready to move in the opposite direction. That’s going to create an entirely new fishing situation. Instead of sitting in the same spot waiting for the bite to return, I start thinking about what’s coming next. Where will the water move when the tide turns? What areas will become available? Where will the bait likely reposition? Which areas will create the next feeding opportunity? Maybe I’m fishing a point during an outgoing tide, and the bite suddenly slows. Instead of continuing to cast to the same place, I’ll think about how that point is going to fish when the current reverses. Maybe the productive side of the structure changes. Or maybe there’s another nearby spot that sets up much better on the incoming tide. The key is to get into position BEFORE that next feeding opportunity develops! So don’t automatically interpret slack tide as the end of your fishing trip. Use it as an opportunity to prepare for what’s coming next. Final Thoughts All four of these mistakes come back to one important idea: Fishing the tides isn’t just about knowing WHEN the water moves. It’s about understanding WHAT that movement does to the fish! Use tide charts to plan your trips, but pay attention to what’s actually happening once you’re on the water. Follow the fish as water levels change, look for productive current around structure, and use slack tide to anticipate the next feeding opportunity. Instead of just asking yourself when high or low tide will occur, ask: What is the water doing to the fish RIGHT NOW? Once you start thinking that way, you’ll have a much better idea of where you should be fishing. I hope these tips help you make better decisions and catch more fish on your next trip! What’s your favorite stage of the tide to fish? Incoming, outgoing, high, or low? Let me know in the comments below! Frequently Asked Questions Is incoming or outgoing tide better for inshore fishing? Both can be productive. I focus more on how the moving water affects bait and fish positioning than whether the tide is simply incoming or outgoing. The specific stage of the tide and the surrounding habitat can make a big difference. Can you catch fish during slack tide? Absolutely! Fish don’t necessarily stop feeding when the current slows. Redfish, for example, may continue feeding on flooded grass flats during high slack tide or concentrate in deeper pools during low slack tide. Is stronger current always better for fishing? Not necessarily. I look for areas where current creates an easy feeding opportunity, especially where moving water interacts with structure. The strongest current isn’t always where the fish will be holding. Why do fish stop biting when the tide changes? Sometimes they haven’t stopped feeding at all. They’ve simply repositioned as water levels change. Before leaving an area, check nearby depth changes, troughs, drains, and other places those fish could have moved. How accurate are fishing tide charts? Tide charts are useful planning tools, but conditions like wind, offshore storms, rainfall, and freshwater runoff can affect actual water levels. I always compare tide predictions with what I’m seeing on the water.

items.title: Why It’s Important To Match The Hatch In The Fall
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Learn why matching the hatch matters for fall fishing and how the right lure presentation can help you catch more redfish, trout, and snook.
items.search_text: Fall is one of the BEST times of year to catch redfish, trout, and snook! As water temperatures begin to cool, baitfish become a major food source for inshore predators. And if you can figure out what those fish are feeding on, you’re already one step closer to getting more strikes! That’s where matching the hatch can make a HUGE difference. In this video, I’m breaking down how I match the hatch during the fall, why lure profile and presentation matter, and how I adjust my approach as conditions change. And to put this strategy to the test, I managed to catch a complete inshore slam! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Lure 1: Skinny Lipper Lure 2: 4″ Mulligan Paddletail Line: 10 lb J-Braid Leader: 20-30lb Ande Mono Salt Strong Insiders save 20% on tackle at Fish Strong! MATCH THE HATCH & SAVE BIG! Want more options for matching the baitfish this fall? We’ve put together 9 proven mullet-inspired lures to help you cover different baitfish sizes, profiles, and presentations! Get all 9 lures and SAVE 20%! SALT STRONG INSIDERS SAVE 40%! 👉 SHOP THE MATCH THE HATCH COLLECTION → Why Matching the Hatch Matters in the Fall During the fall, there’s often an abundance of baitfish throughout the inshore shallows. And redfish, trout, and snook are taking full advantage! When predators are dialed in on a particular food source, using a lure that resembles what they’re feeding on can help you get more bites. But matching the hatch isn’t JUST about choosing the right color. It’s about matching the size, profile, and presentation of the baitfish in the area. For example, during this trip, there were plenty of large mullet swimming around and creating big boils on the surface. Those larger mullet were stirring up the bottom and disturbing smaller baitfish. And those smaller baitfish presented an easy feeding opportunity for nearby predators! That’s why paying attention to the baitfish around you is so important. You don’t necessarily need to imitate the biggest baitfish you see. Sometimes it’s the smaller baitfish getting disturbed that predators are actually targeting. Choosing the Right Lure to Match the Hatch For this trip, I brought along two different lures with similar baitfish profiles: The Skinny Lipper hardbait The Mulligan paddletail Both featured a natural mullet color pattern, but the real advantage was having two different presentations to match the changing conditions. Starting With the Skinny Lipper Early in the morning, I started throwing the Skinny Lipper. The water was murky, and we were fishing around submerged grass, oysters, and other shallow structure. The Skinny Lipper was a great choice because it creates plenty of wobble, vibration, and noise to help fish locate the lure. It also swims just beneath the surface and floats back up when paused. This allowed me to keep the lure above the structure while staying in the strike zone. And it didn’t take long to start getting results! I caught a speckled trout followed by a nice snook, both on the Skinny Lipper. Two species down. One more to go! Adjusting Your Presentation as Conditions Change One of the biggest mistakes anglers can make is sticking with the same presentation when conditions change and the bite slows down. As the morning progressed, the sun got higher, the wind picked up, and the Skinny Lipper bite started slowing down. Rather than continuing to throw the same lure, I switched to the Mulligan paddletail. The important thing? I was still matching the same general baitfish profile, just presenting it differently! This allowed me to adjust to the conditions without completely changing my approach. And that switch paid off! I hooked into a beautiful redfish sitting along a shoreline cut where wind-driven water was flowing through. That redfish completed my inshore slam for the morning! It’s a great reminder that sometimes you don’t need an entirely different lure color or baitfish imitation. You just need to change HOW you’re presenting it. Finding Feeding Fish Is MORE Important Than Lure Color Now, there’s one important point I want to make. You can have the perfect baitfish imitation tied on, but if you’re fishing where there aren’t any actively feeding fish, you’re going to struggle. Finding the right fish in the right conditions is ALWAYS a priority. Take the redfish from this trip, for example. I was fishing a spot marked in our Smart Fishing Spots app, but the fish wasn’t just sitting anywhere along that shoreline. It was positioned near a point, right beside a cut where water was flowing through. That’s what we mean when we talk about finding the spot within the spot. You can’t just pull up to a promising shoreline and expect fish to be everywhere. Look for the smaller details that concentrate baitfish and create feeding opportunities, such as: Points with current wrapping around them Shoreline cuts with moving water Baitfish activity near structure Areas where wind and current create feeding opportunities Those little details can make all the difference! And once you find those feeding fish, matching the hatch with the right lure profile and presentation can help you capitalize on the opportunity. Final Thoughts Matching the hatch is one of my favorite strategies for fall inshore fishing. But remember, there’s no single magic lure color that’s going to catch fish everywhere! If you already have a lure color that’s producing fish, there’s no reason to change it. However, if you’re struggling to get bites or aren’t sure where to start, choosing a natural baitfish imitation is a great option. Pay attention to what the fish are feeding on, match the general size and profile of those baitfish, and adjust your presentation as conditions change. Most importantly, focus on finding actively feeding fish! If you’re struggling to locate productive fishing spots, be sure to check out the Salt Strong Insider Club for access to Smart Fishing Spots, fishing courses, and a community of anglers sharing what’s working on the water. What’s your favorite lure or strategy for matching the hatch during fall fishing? Let me know in the comments below! Frequently Asked Questions What does matching the hatch mean in fishing? Matching the hatch means selecting a lure or bait that resembles what fish are naturally feeding on. For inshore fishing, this typically involves matching the size, profile, color, and movement of local baitfish or other prey. Why is matching the hatch important during fall fishing? During the fall, many inshore predators focus heavily on baitfish as water temperatures begin to cool. Using lures that imitate those baitfish can help you present something familiar to actively feeding redfish, trout, and snook. Does lure color matter when matching the hatch? Lure color can play a role, but it’s just one part of the equation. Lure size, profile, action, presentation, and finding feeding fish are all important considerations. If a particular color is already working for you, there’s no reason to change it simply to match a different pattern. Should I use a hardbait or paddletail in the fall? Both can be effective! A shallow-running hardbait like the Skinny Lipper is a great option for covering water and creating vibration near the surface. A paddletail offers a different presentation that can be especially useful as lighting, wind, and water conditions change. What’s the best way to find feeding fish in the fall? Look for baitfish activity, moving water, shoreline points, cuts, and structure that create feeding opportunities. Pay attention to the specific areas where predators can position themselves to ambush baitfish rather than fishing an entire shoreline without a plan.

items.title: Is Fluorocarbon a SCAM? Here’s What My Tests Show
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Is fluorocarbon better than mono? See what years of fishing line tests reveal about abrasion resistance, knot strength, visibility, and cost.
items.search_text:
Is fluorocarbon fishing line really better than monofilament, or have anglers been paying MORE for LESS? After years of fluorocarbon vs. mono testing , I’ve uncovered some pretty surprising results when it comes to abrasion resistance, knot strength, and even catching fish! Check out the video below to see why. ﻿
Featured Gear Monofilament Leader Fluorocarbon Leader Abrasion Resistance: Mono Keeps Winning One of fluorocarbon’s biggest selling points is its supposed superior abrasion resistance. But my testing has consistently shown something different. I’ve tested: 20 lb mono vs. 25 lb fluorocarbon: Mono won. 15 lb mono vs. 20 lb fluorocarbon: Mono won again. Across the abrasion tests I’ve performed, monofilament has consistently come out ahead. And even when testing knot strength, I’ve found that 15 lb mono can hold its own against 20 lb fluorocarbon. Can Fish Really See the Difference? Fluorocarbon is also marketed as being less visible underwater. But does that actually translate into more strikes? I haven’t noticed a meaningful difference when comparing lines of similar diameter. I’ve successfully caught bonefish, permit, mutton snapper, and mangrove snapper using monofilament leaders in crystal-clear water. These include species known for being particularly line-shy! Fewer Breakoffs AND a Lower Price? Here’s where things get really interesting. When targeting larger fish like redfish, snook, cobia, and tripletail, I’ve experienced far fewer breakoffs with mono compared to fluorocarbon. And the price difference is HUGE. Fishing Line Cost Per Yard Fluorocarbon 79¢ Mono Leader Spool 9¢ Bulk Monofilament 3¢ That’s more than 26 TIMES the price when comparing fluorocarbon to the bulk mono I typically use! These are the prices of the specific lines I compared, but they illustrate just how significant the difference can be. Final Thoughts After years of testing fluorocarbon against monofilament, I’m more convinced than ever that mono is the better choice for my fishing. It’s performed better in my abrasion tests, I’ve experienced fewer breakoffs, and it costs significantly less. And for full transparency, we sell both types of line at Fish Strong. Fluorocarbon actually has higher profit margins for us! But I’d rather recommend what I’ve found works best. Now I’m curious: Have YOU tested fluorocarbon against mono? What were your results? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Is fluorocarbon more abrasion-resistant than mono? Not in my testing! I’ve consistently found that monofilament outperforms fluorocarbon in the abrasion comparisons I’ve conducted. Can fish see monofilament leaders underwater? Mono is generally more visible underwater than fluorocarbon, but I haven’t noticed a difference in strikes when comparing similar line diameters, even in clear water. Is fluorocarbon worth the extra money? Based on my testing and fishing experience, I don’t believe the added cost is justified for the applications I’ve tested.

items.title: Advanced Inshore Fishing: Success Is In These 3 Details
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Discover 3 small inshore fishing adjustments that can make a BIG difference when targeting redfish, snook, and trout.
items.search_text: You can be fishing the RIGHT spot, throwing the RIGHT lure, at the RIGHT time… And STILL struggle to catch fish! That’s because once you get past the basics of inshore fishing, it’s often the smallest details that separate a frustrating trip from an incredible day on the water. In the video below, I’m breaking down three important details that can make a HUGE difference in your fishing success. And I’ve got some nice redfish and snook catches to prove it! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: Rod: Slot Machine Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Lure : The Mulligan 5″ Bomber Hook: Hoss Helix Hook 4/0 1/8oz Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 15lb Mono Leader w/ 30lb Tippet 1. Find the BEST Spot Within a Good Fishing Spot Just because you’ve found a productive shoreline doesn’t mean fish are feeding along the entire stretch. You need to find the 90/10 zone WITHIN the 90/10 zone! When I’m working a shoreline, I’m looking for anything that stands out: Small islands, cuts, or points Isolated trees or submerged structure Culvert pipes with moving water Areas where baitfish might concentrate During this trip, I caught redfish near unique shoreline features and a nice snook near a culvert pipe with flowing water. The lesson? Don’t just find a good fishing spot. Find the BEST areas within that spot! 2. Pay Attention to Boat Positioning and Casting Angles You can have the perfect lure tied on and still get ignored if you’re approaching fish incorrectly. First, give yourself enough distance from the fish to avoid spooking them. During this trip, I stayed roughly 20 to 25 yards away from the structure I was targeting. Next, pay attention to the current. Ideally, you want to cast into the current and retrieve your lure naturally with the flow of the water. If the wind isn’t cooperating, try casting across the current instead. Avoid retrieving directly against strong current when it’s pulling your lure out of the strike zone. Small adjustments to your casting angle can help keep your lure in front of feeding fish longer. 3. Make SMALL Presentation Adjustments Before Switching Lures When fish aren’t biting, it’s tempting to start changing lures. But sometimes you already have the right lure tied on! Before switching, try adjusting: Retrieve speed: Slow down or speed up depending on how fish are responding. Pauses: Give fish an opportunity to strike during your retrieve. Rod tip position: Keep it lower to help your lure stay deeper in the water column. Lure action: Experiment with subtle movements instead of constantly working your lure aggressively. During this trip, I was using a larger 5-inch Mulligan Bomber paddletail. With bigger lures, sometimes less action is MORE effective! The key is figuring out what the fish want before completely changing your approach. Final Thoughts Catching more inshore fish isn’t always about finding a secret spot or buying another lure. Sometimes it’s about paying attention to the little details. The next time you’re fishing a promising area without getting bites, take a closer look at your positioning, casting angles, and lure presentation before moving on. And if you want help putting together a better fishing game plan, check out the Salt Strong Insider Club . What’s one SMALL adjustment that’s made a BIG difference in your fishing? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Why am I not catching fish in good inshore fishing spots? Fish often concentrate around specific features rather than spreading evenly throughout an area. Look for unique structure, moving water, and places where baitfish gather. Should you cast with or against the current when fishing artificial lures? Casting into the current and retrieving with the flow often creates a more natural presentation. Casting across the current can also help keep your lure in the strike zone. Should I change lures when fish aren’t biting? Not always! Before switching lures, experiment with your retrieve speed, rod tip position, casting angle, and lure action. Small adjustments can sometimes make a BIG difference.

items.title: How to Make Your Popping Cork Rig MORE Versatile
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Make your popping cork rig more versatile with one simple trick! Learn how to quickly change leader lengths and spend more time fishing.
items.search_text: Popping corks are one of the most effective rigs for catching redfish, trout, snook, and flounder. But there’s one limitation with traditional popping cork setups that you might not think about until you’re out on the water. The good news? A little preparation before your trip can make your popping cork rig WAY more versatile! I’ll show you how to get set up in the video below so you can spend less time re-rigging and more time catching fish. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: Dr. Popper XT – Our extra-tough popping cork featuring a flexible steel cable that resists kinking and holds up to tough fishing conditions. Salt Strong Insiders save 20% on tackle at Fish Strong! The Biggest Problem With Traditional Popping Cork Rigs There’s a reason popping corks are so popular among inshore anglers. They create noise and surface disturbance that help attract fish, and they’re incredibly effective when paired with the right lure or bait. But traditional popping cork setups have one major limitation: Your leader length is fixed once you tie everything together. Let’s say you’re fishing with an 18-inch leader beneath your popping cork. If you move into shallower water and need a shorter leader, you’ll have to cut your line and retie your lure. And if you move into deeper water and need a longer leader? You’ll have to replace the entire leader, tying new knots at both ends. That’s valuable fishing time spent re-rigging instead of casting. Fortunately, there’s a much easier way to handle changing conditions. How to Make Your Popping Cork Rig More Versatile Here’s a simple adjustment I recommend making to your popping cork setup. Instead of tying your leader directly to the bottom of your popping cork, tie it to a small fishing snap. A small snap rated around 45 pounds works well, although you generally want to keep it as small as practical. Then attach your leader and jighead as usual. Now, rather than having one fixed leader permanently tied to your cork, you have a setup that allows you to swap leaders in seconds. For example: You’re fishing with an 18-inch leader and decide you need to switch to a shorter 8-inch leader. Instead of cutting and retying knots, simply: Open the snap. Remove your existing leader. Attach your shorter, pre-tied leader. Close the snap and get back to fishing! That’s it! You’ve adjusted your popping cork rig to match the conditions in seconds instead of minutes. And the best part? You can make these adjustments throughout the day as you move between different water depths. Prepare Your Popping Cork Leaders Before Your Next Trip Here’s another tip that makes this system even more effective. Prepare several different leader lengths before you hit the water. I recommend having a few options ready to go, such as: 8-inch leaders: For extremely shallow water. 12-inch leaders: For fishing shallow flats and shorelines. 18-inch leaders: A versatile option for slightly deeper water. 24-inch leaders: For situations where you need your lure farther beneath the cork. These are just starting points. Your ideal leader length will depend on the water depth, structure, and where the fish are feeding. Make several of each length so you have backups ready. Then store your pre-tied leaders in a small, organized bag inside your tackle box. When conditions change, you’ll already have the right setup waiting. No cutting. No retying. No wasted time. Just swap your leader and keep fishing! Final Thoughts Popping corks are already one of the most productive rigs in inshore fishing. But making this one simple adjustment gives you a much more versatile setup that can adapt to changing conditions throughout your fishing trip. And when you spend less time messing with your tackle, you have more time to catch fish! Give this trick a try on your next trip and let me know how it works for you. Do you typically stick with one popping cork leader length, or do you adjust it throughout the day? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions How long should a popping cork leader be? Popping cork leader length depends on the water depth and where fish are feeding. Common lengths include 12, 18, and 24 inches, but shorter or longer leaders may work better depending on the conditions. The goal is to keep your lure in the strike zone without dragging the bottom. Can you adjust the leader length on a popping cork? Yes! While traditional popping cork setups use a fixed leader, adding a small fishing snap allows you to quickly swap between pre-tied leaders of different lengths without cutting and retying knots. What is the best popping cork setup for redfish and trout? A popping cork paired with a fluorocarbon leader and an appropriately weighted jighead or hook is a popular setup for redfish and speckled trout. The ideal leader length and lure depend on water depth, current, and feeding conditions. Why should you change your popping cork leader length? Changing your leader length allows you to adjust how deep your lure sits beneath the cork. This helps keep your presentation in the strike zone as water depth and fishing conditions change. What makes the Dr. Popper XT different? The Dr. Popper XT features a flexible steel cable designed to resist kinking while providing extra durability. It’s built to withstand demanding inshore fishing conditions while delivering the noise and surface disturbance anglers expect from a popping cork.

items.title: When To Switch From Plugs To Soft Plastic Jerk Lures
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Learn when to switch from topwater plugs to soft plastic jerk lures and how to adjust your retrieve to catch more redfish, trout, and snook.
items.search_text: I was fishing a GREAT-looking spot loaded with baitfish during prime feeding hours. The problem? ZERO fish. Instead of finding another spot, I changed my approach and fished the exact same water again. The result? A quick inshore slam, including some NICE redfish and snook! Watch below to see how I turned a tough bite around and how you can use this same strategy before giving up on a promising fishing spot. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine – Medium 7’6″ Reel: Otis 2500 Line: J-Braid 8 Grand – 8lb Leader: Ande Mono – 12lb Bite Tippet: Ande Mono – 20lb Lure: Polk County Tweaker (Black Ice) Rigging: – 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/16oz Location & Vessel: Launch City: Sebastian, FL Vessel: 22 ft Micro Draft Why My Topwater Plugs Weren’t Working I started fishing before sunrise, targeting a shallow grass flat loaded with mullet. Everything looked right. There were plenty of fish around, and I was fishing during the twilight hours when topwater plugs typically produce some of their best action. I started with the Moonwalker and even tried a smaller prop bait. I had a few follows and strikes, but the fish just weren’t committing. The fish were there. They just weren’t interested in what I was throwing. That’s when I decided to try something different. Instead of leaving to find another spot, I went right back through the same area with a soft plastic jerk lure. And that’s when things got interesting. When to Switch From Plugs to Soft Plastics Here’s the biggest lesson from this trip: The amount of vibration your lure produces can make or break your results. During nighttime and twilight hours, fish are usually more aggressive, making louder plugs an excellent choice. But as the sun came up, the conditions changed. The water was extremely calm, there was very little current, and the fish were getting spooky. Those same aggressive presentations that can work so well in low light were now working against me. So I switched to a Polk County Tweaker in Black Ice . It’s a soft plastic jerk lure that allows me to fish with significantly less vibration. That one change turned the entire trip around. I started catching redfish almost immediately, including a beautiful 29-inch fish! And the action didn’t stop there. Straight Retrieve vs. Twitch Retrieve Choosing the right lure was only half the equation. HOW I retrieved that lure was just as important. When the water was calm and the fish were spooky, I kept my rod tip relatively still and used a slow, steady retrieve. No aggressive jerks. No unnecessary movement. Just a subtle presentation that allowed the lure to move naturally through the water. I’ve found that this straight-retrieve approach can be incredibly effective when fish are finicky. But later in the morning, something changed. The wind picked up, the water started moving, and visibility decreased. So I started adding more action to the lure. First, I introduced a little rod movement. Then, as the water became more churned up, I switched to quicker twitches. And that’s when I hooked into the biggest fish of the day… a beautiful snook! The takeaway? Calm water + spooky fish: Start with a slow, straight retrieve and minimal vibration. More wind + moving water: Experiment with adding twitches and additional lure movement. You don’t always need a different lure. Sometimes you just need to change how you’re working it. Don’t Give Up on a Good Fishing Spot Too Soon One of the most important decisions I made that morning had nothing to do with tackle. It was deciding to stay in an area where I knew fish were present. I made multiple passes through the same zone. The first pass produced nothing. The second pass, with a different lure, produced some excellent redfish. And after adjusting my retrieve as conditions changed, I eventually landed some really nice snook, too. I even had a monster trout swipe at my lure right beside the boat! Although I never landed the big trout I was targeting, the trip turned into an incredible morning. Same fishing spot. Different presentation. Completely different results. That’s why I always encourage anglers to pay attention to the conditions and how fish respond before abandoning an otherwise promising area. Final Thoughts Hard plugs can be incredibly effective during twilight hours. But they’re never a guarantee. This trip was a perfect example of why choosing the right lure for the conditions matters more than simply fishing during the “perfect” time of day. I started with zero catches during what should have been prime feeding conditions. Then I switched to a low-vibration soft plastic jerk lure, returned to the exact same spot, and ended up catching some beautiful redfish and snook. And as conditions changed, adjusting my retrieve helped keep the bites coming. For a deeper breakdown of when each lure style performs best, check out my Advanced Lures Lesson inside the Salt Strong Fishing School . Have you ever switched lures and immediately started catching fish in an area you thought was dead? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions When should I switch from topwater plugs to soft plastic lures? Consider switching when fish are following or striking your plugs without committing, especially as the sun rises and the water becomes calm. A soft plastic jerk lure can provide a more subtle presentation that helps trigger strikes from spooky fish. Should I twitch a soft plastic jerk lure or use a straight retrieve? It depends on the conditions. In calm water with finicky fish, I prefer starting with a slow, straight retrieve. As wind and water movement increase, adding twitches can help attract more attention. Can soft plastic jerk lures catch redfish, trout, and snook? Absolutely! During this trip, I caught redfish and snook using the Polk County Tweaker and even had a monster trout strike near the boat. It’s one of my favorite lure styles for targeting multiple inshore species. What color soft plastic works best on sunny days? I’ve had excellent results with Black Ice, especially during clear, sunny conditions. Its dark profile has become one of my favorite options when targeting redfish, snook, and trout.

items.title: How to Find Inshore Fish During High Water
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: High water can completely change where inshore fish feed. Learn where to find redfish and trout when water levels rise.
items.search_text: Water levels are HIGH across a lot of the Southeast right now. And when all that extra water floods shorelines, grass, trees, and creeks, the fish suddenly have a whole lot more territory to explore. That can make them tougher to find. But there’s one simple rule I use to adjust. Here’s what that looked like on my latest trip. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Lure: 2.0 Hook: Hoss Helix Hook 3/0 1/8oz Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 15lb Mono Leader w/30lb Tippet High Water Opens Up New Feeding Areas When water levels rise, fish can reach areas that normally aren’t available to them. That includes flooded grass, mangroves, trees, shoreline cover, and areas farther back inside creeks. So if I’m fishing water that’s noticeably higher than normal, one of the first things I’ll do is move tighter to the shoreline. On this trip, that paid off with a solid redfish sitting right along a flooded treeline. The important part is not simply fishing “shallow.” It’s recognizing that the productive edge has moved. Look for Shorelines That Keep Fish Within Reach Not every flooded shoreline is equally easy to fish. If high water extends 20, 30, or 50 feet back into heavy cover, fish may push so far back that you can’t effectively reach them. I prefer shorelines where the water has risen into cover but there is still a defined edge I can target. That concentrates the fish into a smaller area and gives me a much better chance of putting my lure in front of them. The same idea applies to flooded grass and creeks. If the water gives fish access to a new feeding zone, expect at least some fish to take advantage of it. Follow The Water This is the simplest way I think about changing water levels: Water comes up, I move up. Water goes down, I move out. When water levels are low, many of those fish are forced away from the shoreline and into slightly deeper water. When the water comes back up, those same fish can move right back into areas they couldn’t previously access. Instead of fishing the exact same spots regardless of the conditions, adjust with the water. Don’t Get Tunnel Vision High water doesn’t mean EVERY fish will be buried against the shoreline. That’s something this trip reminded me of pretty quickly. While I was focused on the flooded cover, I spotted a speckled trout cruising through floating grass roughly 20 feet away from the bank. A quick cast in front of him produced another quality fish. So even when you have a strong pattern going, keep scanning the water around you. Look for wakes, nervous bait, movement through floating grass, and anything else that might give away a cruising fish. Sometimes the best opportunity is sitting right next to the spot you’re focused on. Find The Productive Water Faster One of the challenges with unusually high water is simple: There’s more water for the fish to use. And if you haven’t been on the water recently, figuring out where the fish have moved can take a lot of time. That’s where current fishing reports, recent community intel, and Smart Fishing Spots can help narrow down the search before you ever launch the boat. Instead of blindly covering miles of shoreline, you can start by identifying the areas that give fish the right combination of structure, depth, current, and feeding opportunities for the conditions you’re dealing with. Final Thoughts High water doesn’t necessarily make the fishing worse. It just changes where you should be looking. If water is flooding new shoreline, grass, or creek habitat, start by following it and looking for fish that have moved into those new feeding zones. But keep your eyes open. As that trout proved, they’re not all going to be against the bank. Are you seeing unusually high water where you’re fishing right now? And where have you been finding the fish? Frequently Asked Questions Where do redfish go when water levels are high? Redfish will often move into newly flooded shoreline habitat, including grass, mangroves, flooded trees, creeks, and other shallow feeding areas that aren’t accessible during lower water. Should you fish closer to shore during high water? Often, yes. Rising water can allow baitfish and predators to move closer to shore and farther into flooded cover. Focus on areas where fish can access the new habitat without moving so far back that they’re impossible to reach. Is high water good for inshore fishing? It can be. High water creates new feeding opportunities for redfish, speckled trout, snook, and other inshore species. The challenge is that fish also have more available habitat, so locating them can take more effort. What lures work well during high water? Paddletails are a great option because they allow you to cover water efficiently and can be worked around flooded shorelines, grass, and other shallow structure. I used the Slam Shady 2.0 paddletail successfully on this trip. Should I only fish flooded shorelines during high water? No. Flooded shorelines can be productive, but fish may still cruise farther away from shore. Keep watching for bait activity, wakes, floating grass movement, and visible fish while you’re working the shoreline.

items.title: Is This the Most Overlooked Lure Color for Inshore Fishing?
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Are you overlooking black lures for redfish and trout? Watch Coach Pat test Black Ice across multiple lure profiles on a kayak fishing trip.
items.search_text: Only 8% of the Insiders we surveyed picked dark colors as their most trusted soft plastics. That got me wondering… are we overlooking something? So I took the kayak out with one rule: every lure I threw would be BLACK ICE. Watch to see how the fish responded as I switched through different profiles, and why a dark lure might deserve a spot beside your favorite color. Plus, I’ll share the four color categories I recommend carrying so you don’t need every shade in the tackle shop. Watch Below To See How Black Ice Held Up. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Insiders: Put Black Ice to the test and claim ONE plug of your choice with this month’s Tackle Tester! 👉 [CLAIM YOUR BLACK ICE PLUG HERE] Featured Gear Here’s what I brought along in Black Ice: 2.0 Paddletail Polk County Tweaker The Mulligan 4-Inch Paddletail Moonwalker Topwater Lure Wake Mullet Skinny Lipper The Flea Flicker was supposed to come along, too. Unfortunately, that one never made it into the kayak! The Redfish Had My Attention The trip started with a follow and a swipe at the Wake Mullet on my second cast. Of course, I didn’t have the camera rolling yet. Then I found a school of nice redfish, hooked one on the Tweaker, and lost it. That one hurt. But shortly afterward, I spotted fish swimming right beside the kayak and hooked up again, this time on the 2.0. That’s when things got REALLY interesting. While I was fighting that redfish, its buddies stayed with it, competing for the lure. They were close enough that I seriously considered throwing another bait out while I still had the first fish hooked. Tempting? Absolutely. But trying to manage two hooked redfish by myself in a kayak sounded like a good way to lose a rod. I decided to land the one I already had. Getting a bite was encouraging. Seeing other redfish trying to get in on it was something else. One Color, Several Different Profiles I wanted to see how many different Black Ice profiles I could get action on before the trip ended. And the bites kept coming as I worked through the lineup. A solid trout ate the Moonwalker. Later, I spotted another redfish and put the 4-inch Mulligan in front of it. That fish took the lure, but I missed the hookset. Then it turned around and came looking for it AGAIN. That second chance turned into the last fish of the trip, a beautiful redfish I called overslot in the video. Lightning in the area cut the outing short, so I headed in after roughly three hours on the water. Here’s how everything shook out: Lure What happened Wake Mullet Follow and swipe before the camera was rolling Polk County Tweaker Hooked a redfish, but lost it 2.0 Paddletail Landed a redfish Moonwalker Landed a trout 4-inch Mulligan Landed a redfish Skinny Lipper No action recorded Flea Flicker Left behind, so it never got tested That’s action on five of the six profiles I actually brought. Three produced landed fish. The other two drew a strike or hookup, so I’m counting those as action, not catches. For a short trip, that gave me plenty of confidence in putting Black Ice to work. You Don’t Need Every Color of the Rainbow Now, am I saying those fish wouldn’t have eaten a different color? No. I didn’t compare Black Ice against light or natural colors on this trip. What I did see was redfish and trout responding to it across several different lure profiles. And that’s why I like having a dark option available. When we asked our Insiders which soft plastic colors they trusted most, light and natural colors dominated. Those are useful options, but I wouldn’t let them crowd every dark lure out of the tackle box. My recommendation is to cover four basic color categories: Light: Something like white. Dark: Something like black. Natural: Something that resembles the bait in your area. Bright: Something that stands out. You don’t need every shade in every lure. Cover those four categories, and you’ve got a simple starting point without carrying the whole tackle shop. If all your confidence is tied to one color, give yourself a chance to build confidence in another. A trip like this is a pretty good way to do it. Final Thoughts Black Ice earned its place in my kayak on this trip. Redfish competing for the 2.0, a trout on the Moonwalker, and a redfish coming back for the Mulligan gave me plenty of reasons to keep throwing it. You can still love your light and natural colors. Just leave some room for a dark option, too. What soft plastic color do YOU have the most confidence in, no matter the conditions? Let me know in the comments! Want to try the lures from this trip? Check out the featured gear above and choose your next Black Ice profile. If you’re an Insider, remember to use your member pricing. Frequently Asked Questions Do black lures work for redfish and trout? Yes. On this trip, I landed redfish on the Black Ice 2.0 and 4-inch Mulligan, plus a trout on the Black Ice Moonwalker. Did Black Ice outperform lighter colors? This trip didn’t establish that. I rotated through different profiles in Black Ice rather than comparing colors. It showed that the dark color got bites, but it doesn’t mean another color wouldn’t have worked. What lure colors should I keep in my tackle box? I recommend having a light, dark, natural, and bright option. That covers four useful categories without needing every color available. How many Black Ice lures caught fish? Three profiles produced landed fish: the 2.0, Moonwalker, and 4-inch Mulligan. Including the Wake Mullet swipe and the redfish I lost on the Tweaker, I got action on five of the six profiles I brought. Did you test the Flea Flicker? No. I planned to, but accidentally left it out of the kayak. It wasn’t part of the on-water test.

Honestly, I probably would’ve passed right by it too… But one thing gave me enough confidence to stop, grab my travel rod, and make a few casts. Don’t Automatically Skip Dirty Backwaters In Summer When I first got to this spot, conditions honestly didn’t look all that promising. There were culvert pipes nearby, and this time of year I’d normally expect rainfall to create some water movement through them. But there was basically no flow. The water was also shallow, dirty, and HOT. Still, the spot was highlighted in the app, so I decided to give it a chance. Almost immediately, I hooked a trout right near the shoreline. Then, after covering a little more water and moving to another pocket, I hooked into a solid snook. That was a good reminder that summer fish don’t always behave exactly how we expect them to. Sometimes an overlooked backwater can still hold quality fish, especially if it gives them the right combination of cover, shade, and protection. Look Closer To The Shoreline Once The Sun Gets High One mistake I caught myself making was trying to cast as far as possible. When you get to a new spot, it’s easy to think longer casts automatically mean you’re covering more productive water. But during the heat of the day, that isn’t always where the fish are. In shallow summer backwaters, fish are often looking for: Shade Cover Cooler water Protection And a lot of that is going to be right along the shoreline. Once the sun gets high, I’d rather pay close attention to shaded pockets, vegetation, structure, and any little irregularities along the bank than blindly bomb casts into the middle of open water. That’s exactly where the fish showed themselves on this trip. Adjust Your Lure To The Water Clarity The water in this spot was extremely dirty, so I went with the Black Silver Slam Shady 2.0. The darker profile helps the lure stand out better when visibility is poor. I paired it with a 1/8 oz. Hoss Round Eye Jighead with a chartreuse eye to add another little visual target. My retrieve was simple. I’d cast the paddletail out and use a steady retrieve, but every so often I’d give the rod tip a couple of small pops. In dirty water, that extra movement can help draw attention to the lure. If the water were clean, I’d simplify things even more and mostly stick with a slow, steady retrieve. The dirtier the water gets, the more willing I am to add a little extra action. Use Smart Fishing Spots To Find Areas Other Anglers Overlook One of my biggest takeaways from this trip had nothing to do with the fish themselves. It was the spot. I probably wouldn’t have had high expectations for this area based on how it looked when I arrived. But when I pulled up the Smart Fishing Spots app, I was sitting right in the middle of a spot marked as productive. And it produced. That’s one of the biggest advantages of using the app. It can help point you toward areas you might otherwise drive right past. That becomes even more valuable when you’re fishing heavily pressured areas. Instead of going back to the same obvious spots everybody else knows about, try somewhere different. Try a backwater. Try an area you’d normally save for another season. Try the spot that looks a little ugly. You never know what might be tucked back there. Final Thoughts This trip went a lot better than I expected. I left the boat at home, walked into a shallow dirty backwater in the summer heat, and ended up finding both trout and snook. The biggest lesson? Don’t automatically skip a spot just because it doesn’t look perfect. Pay attention to where fish can find shade and cover, adjust your lure presentation to the water clarity, and use every tool you have available to find areas other anglers may be overlooking. Would you have stopped to fish a backwater spot like this, or would you have kept looking for cleaner water? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Can you catch snook in dirty backwater areas during summer? Yes. Snook can use shallow backwaters during summer, especially when those areas provide shade, structure, cover, or other protection. Focus on the highest-percentage areas rather than fishing featureless open water. Where should I cast in shallow backwaters during the heat of the day? Start close to shoreline cover, shaded pockets, vegetation, structure, and other areas where fish can escape direct sunlight. Fish may be much closer to the bank than expected. What lure color works best in dirty water? Darker lure colors can create a stronger silhouette in dirty water. In this trip, I used a Black Silver Slam Shady 2.0 paired with a jighead featuring a chartreuse eye. How should I retrieve a paddletail in dirty water? A steady retrieve is a great starting point. In dirty water, occasionally adding a couple of small pops with the rod tip can create extra movement and help fish locate the lure. Are backwater fishing spots worth trying during summer? Absolutely. While some shallow backwaters can become extremely hot, areas with shade, cover, structure, or other favorable conditions can still hold fish. Don’t rule them out without giving the best-looking sections a chance.

items.title: Will A Spot Produce The Same Results 3 Years Later?
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Can you really catch fish in the exact same spot three years later? Today, we’re putting that to the test. I’m heading back to a spot that produced years ago, during the same season, under nearly identical conditions, to see if history repeats itself
items.search_text: Can you really catch fish in the exact same spot three years later? Today, we’re putting that to the test. I’m heading back to a spot that produced years ago, during the same season, under nearly identical conditions, to see if history repeats itself… or if everything has changed. This isn’t just about one fishing spot. It’s about understanding why fish were there in the first place and whether those patterns still hold up over time. Let’s hit the water and find out if this spot still has what it takes. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Artificial Lure Setup: Rod: Slam Stick 7’6 Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Lure 1: Moonwalker Topwater Lure 2: Prawn XT Jr. (3.5″) Lure 3: The Mulligan 4″ Paddletail Hook: Hoss Helix Hook 3/0 1/8oz Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 15lb Mono Leader Bridge Fishing Setup: Rod: Slam Stick 7’6 Medium Heavy Reel: Diawa BG MQ 3000 Hook: Hoss Football Jighead 4/0 1/8oz Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 20lb Leader: Ande 30lb Mono Leader The Original Summer Game Plan This trip started around 6:00 in the morning with glass-calm conditions. The air temperature was approximately 77 degrees and expected to climb into the 90s. Water temperature was already around 86 degrees. That made the timing important. During the summer, fish can move onto shallow flats and shorelines to feed early. As the sun rises and the water gets hotter, many of those fish slide toward deeper, more comfortable water. The causeway I planned to fish had both options close together: Shallow shoreline habitat Nearby deep water Shade Current Bridge structure I could start shallow and then adjust without having to run across the entire bay. Plenty Of Bait, But Not Many Bites The shallow causeway had nearly everything I wanted to see. There was plenty of bait along the shoreline, larger fish were pushing wakes, and there wasn’t much floating grass to interfere with a topwater lure. I started with three artificial lures: Slam Shady Moonwalker Prawn Jr XT The Mulligan in the Slam Shady color The Moonwalker produced a nice trout along the shallow shoreline, even with a dolphin cruising through the deeper water nearby. That fish was likely using the shallows to feed while also staying away from the dolphin. But aside from that trout, the fish weren’t very aggressive. There was life everywhere, but very little feeding activity. One possibility is that the causeway lights created a productive feeding zone overnight. If those fish had already eaten heavily before sunrise, they may not have been interested in chasing lures once I arrived. Either way, forcing the shallow-water bite wasn’t the answer. It was time for Plan B. Returning To A Productive Spot Three Years Later Before this trip, I reviewed my previous catches in Smart Fishing Spots. That’s when I noticed the bridge had produced some quality fish almost exactly three years earlier during the same time of year. Would those fish still be using it? There was only one way to find out. I moved over to the bridge, watched the fish finder while circling the channel, and focused on the fender system and submerged pilings. It didn’t take long to find fish. My first shrimp was immediately crushed by something strong enough to break me off. Another drop produced a healthy mangrove snapper, followed by another large fish that buried itself in the structure. The old spot was still holding fish. Now I needed to adjust my setup so I could actually land them. The Adjustments That Changed The Trip I started with 20 lb leader, which wasn’t enough for the size of the fish or the amount of structure below the boat. So I made three important changes: Increased my leader to 30 lb monofilament. Tightened the drag so the fish couldn’t immediately reach the pilings. Switched from shrimp to a large piece of blue crab. The shrimp proved that fish were there, but it was also attracting smaller snapper and bait stealers. A half blue crab created a much larger offering. That helped discourage the smaller fish while specifically targeting the heavy fish holding around the pilings. The result was immediate. I hooked a big fish, put pressure on it, and used the trolling motor to pull away from the bridge. This time, the fish didn’t make it into the structure. Plan B officially paid off. How To Fish Bridge Fender Systems From above the water, a bridge fender can look like one solid wall. But underwater, many of these structures are supported by rows of individual pilings. Those pilings create shade, current breaks, vertical structure, and reef-like habitat that attracts baitfish and larger predators. My presentation was simple. I dropped the crab vertically along the outside of the fender and allowed it to fall beside the submerged pilings. The important part was being prepared before the strike happened. I kept the trolling motor pointed away from the bridge. As soon as a fish ate, I could apply heavy pressure and use the motor to create distance from the structure. When fishing this way: Keep the bait close to the structure. Use a leader heavy enough to handle abrasion. Tighten the drag before dropping. Be ready to move the boat immediately. Don’t give the fish time to wrap around a piling. Once I made those adjustments, the bridge produced multiple quality fish, including the biggest one of the trip. Why Fishing Catch Logs Matter It would have been easy to forget about this bridge. Three years is a long time between visits, and there are countless other spots that could have distracted me. But a fishing catch log doesn’t forget. Logging catches allows you to look back at: The exact location Time of year Tide Weather conditions Wind Water temperature Lure or bait Species caught The goal isn’t simply to save a waypoint. A waypoint only tells you where something happened. A detailed catch log helps explain when and why it happened. That’s what makes the information useful. When similar seasonal conditions return, you can revisit spots that have already proven themselves instead of starting from scratch. The fish may not be sitting in the exact same place every year, but seasonal patterns often repeat. In this case, a productive bridge from three years ago became the best spot of the entire trip. Final Thoughts The original plan was to catch fish in the shallows before the summer heat took over. There was plenty of bait and activity, but the bite never developed the way I expected. Instead of spending the entire morning waiting for those fish to cooperate, I adjusted. An old fishing catch log pointed me toward a bridge that had produced during the same time of year three years earlier. The fish were still there. I simply had to locate them, adjust my tackle, change baits, and keep them away from the structure. That’s why every trip should include more than one plan, and why every productive trip should be saved in your catch log. The information you record today could put you on the best fish of your trip three years from now. Do you regularly look back at old fishing reports before planning a trip? Let me know in the comments! Tight lines!

items.title: Why You Should Start Throwing Bigger Lures This Fall
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Thinking about throwing bigger lures this fall? Learn when to upsize, when to stay small, and how to fish bigger paddletails with confidence.
items.search_text: Still throwing the same small lures you used all summer? They might deserve another trip… but it could be time to give them some BIGGER competition. As we head into fall, I start paying closer attention to lure size. And there are situations where switching things up can help get your bait noticed. But bigger isn’t ALWAYS better. In this video, I’ll show you what makes me reach for a larger paddletail, when I stick with a smaller lure, and one common mistake to avoid once you make the switch. You’ll have a better idea of what to throw on your next trip, and how to put it to work with confidence. Watch below to see when it pays to go BIGGER. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Ready to go BIGGER this fall? Grab the Fall Bundle, featuring the 5-inch Mulligan Bomber used in this video, plus more proven lures for your next trip. Click Here To Get Your Fall Bundle Featured Lures Lure 1: Mulligan 5-Inch Bomber Rigging 1: 4/0 Weedless Hoss Helix Lure 2: 2.0 Paddletail Rigging 2: 3/0 Weedless Hoss Helix Why I Start Reaching for Bigger Lures During spring and much of summer, I like throwing 3.5- to 4-inch lures. But as late summer turns to fall, mullet and other baitfish are often larger and more abundant. Redfish, trout, and snook are also feeding aggressively as seasonal patterns change. That’s when I like to bump up to a 5-inch paddletail. I’m trying to match the larger forage, give the fish a meal worth chasing, and help my lure stand out when there’s plenty of bait around. The Mulligan Bomber is one of my go-to options. Along with that larger profile, it casts well and lets me cover water while fish are on the move. The goal is to match what’s happening around you, rather than keep throwing the same thing out of habit. When I DON’T Upsize Before you start throwing bigger lures this fall, take a look at the bait and the water you’re fishing. There are a few situations where I’ll stick with a smaller presentation: Smaller lures are catching fish. If you’re consistently getting bites, keep doing what’s working. The bait is tiny. Far back in a creek, you might find small baitfish, glass minnows, or little shrimp. A larger lure may not be the best match. The water is very clear. Bigger profiles can spook fish in those conditions, so I try to avoid them. But if the smaller lures you’ve been throwing aren’t getting attention, it might be time to give a larger profile a shot. Let the conditions help you make that decision. Stop Overworking Your Paddletail One of the biggest mistakes anglers make with larger lures is doing TOO MUCH with the rod tip. Constant twitching, popping, and jerking can overwork the presentation. With a paddletail like the Mulligan Bomber, I usually keep it simple with a straight, steady retrieve . Another option is a smooth sweep: Point the rod toward your lure and reel until the line is tight. Stop reeling and pull the rod to move the lure through the water. Reel up the slack, then repeat. You’re smoothly pulling the lure, rather than snapping it around. I’ll give it a couple of pops if I feel grass on the line or lure. Otherwise, I let the paddletail do its job. A bigger profile already has plenty of presence in the water. You don’t need to go crazy to get it noticed. Rig for the Water You’re Fishing Most of the shallow water I’m fishing is around 1 to 3 feet deep, so I keep this lure on a weedless hook and don’t need much weight. If you’re fishing deeper, a heavier weighted hook or a jighead may be a better choice. The key is choosing a rig that puts the lure where you need it. A bigger lure doesn’t automatically call for a bunch of extra weight. Match your setup to the depth and conditions. Lure Choice Is Only Part of the Puzzle On this trip, I caught a redfish around 3 p.m. on the 5-inch Mulligan Bomber in Slam Shady. The water was a little dirty, which can be a good situation for a larger profile. But the location mattered, too. That fish was holding right off a point where wind-driven current was wrapping around the shoreline. I show the area in Smart Fishing Spots so you can see exactly how that point was positioned. Choosing the right lure helps. Putting it in front of fish is still the biggest part of the puzzle. Final Thoughts Fall is a good time to have larger lures ready. If bigger baitfish are around and your smaller lures aren’t producing, upsizing can give you another way to get noticed. Keep your retrieve simple, rig for the depth, and let the conditions guide your choice. And if the smaller lure is still catching fish? Keep throwing it! Do you switch to bigger lures in the fall, or stick with the same size all year? Let me know in the comments! Ready to go BIGGER this fall? Grab the Fall Bundle, featuring the 5-inch Mulligan Bomber used in this video, plus more proven lures for your next trip. Click Here To Get Your Fall Bundle Frequently Asked Questions Why should I consider throwing bigger lures this fall? Larger baitfish can become more abundant during late summer and fall. Upsizing can help you match that forage and make your lure stand out among the bait. When should I keep using smaller lures? Keep using smaller lures when they’re consistently catching fish, when the available bait is tiny, or when very clear water calls for a less imposing presentation. What retrieve do you use with a bigger paddletail? I usually use a straight, steady retrieve. A smooth rod sweep followed by reeling up the slack is another option. Avoid constantly twitching and popping the lure. What lure are you using in the video? I’m fishing the 5-inch Mulligan Bomber in Slam Shady, rigged weedless. Should I use a jighead or a weedless hook? I use a weedless hook for the shallow water I’m fishing in this video. A jighead or heavier weighted hook can help when you need to fish deeper.
