items.title: Why Fishing Rods With Similar Specs Feel Completely Different
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Have you ever picked up two fishing rods with almost identical specs… but one just felt WAY better? Lighter. Crisper. More responsive. There’s actually something happening during every cast that helps explain why. And you probably can’t see it with y
items.search_text: Have you ever picked up two fishing rods with almost identical specs… but one just felt WAY better? Lighter. Crisper. More responsive. There’s actually something happening during every cast that helps explain why. And you probably can’t see it with your naked eye. In the video below, I slowed several rods down so you can actually see what’s happening after the cast and why rod recovery can make such a big difference in how a fishing rod feels AND performs. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine Medium The Slot Machine was designed to be lightweight, crisp, responsive, and consistent through the cast. In the slow-motion testing for this video, it also had the quickest recovery time of every rod tested. And during Fish Strong Week, you can save BIG on the Slot Machine , plus find major savings on the Slam Stick, Slam Stick Traveler, combos, bundles, and more. But don’t wait on these insane deals; Fish Strong Week ends September 8th, 2026! [CHECK OUT THE SLOT MACHINE + FISH STRONG WEEK DEALS] What Is Fishing Rod Recovery? Watch a fishing rod immediately after you make a cast. The rod blank doesn’t simply straighten out and stop moving. It continues to oscillate up and down before eventually settling back into its neutral position. That settling process is what we’re talking about when we refer to rod recovery . And different rods can behave VERY differently. Some blanks settle almost immediately. Others continue bouncing back and forth noticeably longer. You may also see a difference in the amplitude of those oscillations, or how far the rod tip continues moving up and down. At normal speed, this happens so quickly that you probably won’t notice it. Slow it down, though, and the difference becomes pretty obvious. Why Two Fishing Rods With The Same Specs Feel Different This is where things get interesting. You can pick up two rods with the same listed length, power, and action, yet they can feel completely different in your hand. One might feel light, crisp, and responsive. The other might feel softer, heavier, or almost “mushy.” That’s because the specifications printed on a fishing rod mostly tell you about the intended application of that rod. They don’t tell you everything about how that rod is actually going to behave. Recovery plays a role in that overall feel. A rod that settles quickly after loading tends to feel crisp and responsive. A rod that continues oscillating longer may feel softer. That can also influence how consistent the rod feels during the cast. So when you find yourself thinking: “I don’t know why… this rod just feels better.” There may actually be a physical reason behind it. What Determines How Quickly A Fishing Rod Recovers? A few different things can influence rod recovery. One of the biggest is the construction of the blank itself. Higher-quality materials can allow rod designers to build a blank with the stiffness and characteristics they want without needing as much material. Less material means less mass. And generally, less mass means there’s less weight moving around after the rod unloads. But the blank isn’t the only thing that matters. The components attached to it matter, too. Guides are a great example. Heavier guides add more mass to the blank, especially toward the upper portion of the rod. That additional weight can contribute to more oscillation. Lighter guide trains help reduce that unnecessary mass and can contribute to that crisp, responsive feeling you’ll often notice in a well-designed premium rod. This is why simply comparing the words printed on two rod blanks doesn’t tell you the entire story. Blank materials, taper, construction, components, and overall design all work together. And that’s part of what you’re paying for when you move into a better-designed rod. That said, spending more money does NOT automatically mean you’re getting a better rod. And you definitely don’t need an expensive fishing rod to catch fish. I’ve caught plenty of fish on inexpensive setups. The point is simply that when a premium rod is designed well, there are performance characteristics happening behind the scenes that you won’t find printed on the spec sheet. Final Thoughts Rod recovery is one of those things most anglers will never actually see. But once you watch it happen in slow motion, it helps explain why certain rods feel noticeably lighter, crisper, and more responsive than others with seemingly similar specifications. It’s also one more thing to think about the next time you’re comparing fishing rods. Because length, power, and action are important… But they’re not the whole story. Have you ever picked up two rods with nearly identical specs and immediately noticed that one felt WAY better than the other? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions What is rod recovery on a fishing rod? Rod recovery describes how quickly a fishing rod blank stops oscillating and returns to its neutral position after being loaded and released, such as during a cast. Does faster rod recovery make a fishing rod better? Not necessarily for every situation, but quicker recovery can contribute to a rod feeling lighter, crisper, and more responsive. The ideal rod still depends on the fishing technique and the characteristics you prefer. Why do two fishing rods with the same power and action feel different? Rod specifications such as power and action don’t describe every characteristic of a rod. Blank materials, construction, taper, guide weight, overall mass, and rod recovery can all affect how a rod feels. Do lighter fishing rod guides matter? They can. Guides add mass to the rod blank, and heavier components can affect how the blank behaves after it is loaded. Premium rods often use lightweight guide systems to help minimize unnecessary weight. Are expensive fishing rods always better? No. Price alone does not guarantee better performance. A well-designed premium rod may use better materials, lighter components, and more refined construction, but anglers can still catch plenty of fish using less expensive rods. What fishing rod had the fastest recovery in this test? Of the rods I tested for this video, the Slot Machine had the quickest recovery time. It was designed to be lightweight, crisp, responsive, and consistent while casting.

items.title: Which Hardbait Should You Throw? Here’s How I Decide
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Most anglers have a favorite hardbait. But that doesn’t mean it’s the right one to throw. A small change in the conditions can completely change which lure gives you the best shot at getting bit. And sometimes, the lure I reach for is NOT the one mos
items.search_text: Most anglers have a favorite hardbait. But that doesn’t mean it’s the right one to throw. A small change in the conditions can completely change which lure gives you the best shot at getting bit. And sometimes, the lure I reach for is NOT the one most anglers would expect. In the video below, I break down the clues I look for before choosing a hardbait and what tells me it’s time to switch. And once you see it, you’ll have a much better idea of which lure to tie on first… and the confidence to know when it’s time to make a change. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Insiders: You just saw how much the RIGHT hardbait can matter. Now go grab your FREE plug for September 2026 and put it to work. Claim your free plug here. Featured Gear Moonwalker Topwater Skinny Lipper Floater-Diver Fat Lipper Wake Bait Wake Mullet Shallow-Running Crankbait Flea Flicker Slow-Sinking Twitchbait Bundle (Save 20%): Hardbody Bundle Salt Strong Insiders get exclusive savings on all of these hardbaits at FishStrong.com. Moonwalker: When Fish Are Feeding On The Surface The Moonwalker is a walk-the-dog topwater lure built for one very specific situation: Fish actively feeding on the surface. That could mean redfish chasing baitfish, trout popping shrimp, or snook blowing up on bait along a shoreline. And despite what you may have heard, topwater fishing is not limited to early mornings or low-light conditions. If fish are feeding on the surface, a topwater can work at almost any time of day. I especially like throwing the Moonwalker when there is a little chop on the water. That surface movement helps the lure blend into the surrounding commotion while its rattle helps fish track it down. The Moonwalker also comes rigged with strong inline hooks. These hooks are less likely to bend when a larger fish strikes, giving you a better chance of getting that fish all the way to the boat. There is also a Silent But Deadly version for situations where a loud rattle may be too much. Best conditions for the Moonwalker: Fish visibly feeding on the surface A light to moderate chop Active redfish, trout, or snook Fish chasing shrimp or baitfish Skinny Lipper: When Fish Are Feeding Just Below The Surface The Skinny Lipper is probably the most versatile hardbait in this lineup. It floats at rest, dives when twitched, and then rises back toward the surface. That makes it an excellent option when fish are feeding shallow but are not fully committing to a topwater. You may see fish following your Moonwalker, slapping at it, or blowing up behind it without getting hooked. That is a strong sign that it may be time to switch to a subsurface presentation. The Skinny Lipper can be worked several different ways. You can twitch it, pause it, and allow it to float back toward the surface. You can also use a steady jerking retrieve to keep it underwater and moving erratically. When you need to cover more water, simply reel it straight back. Its wide side-to-side wobble gives the lure plenty of action without requiring much additional work from the angler. It can even be trolled behind a kayak or small boat while moving between nearby fishing spots. Best conditions for the Skinny Lipper: Fish feeding just beneath the surface Fish missing or refusing a topwater Shallow water with active baitfish Covering water with a straight retrieve Trolling between nearby spots Fat Lipper: When You Need Noise, Vibration, And A Big Wake The Fat Lipper is a true wake bait. Its wide body produces a large side-to-side wobble while staying right near the surface. It also creates a noticeable wake, plenty of vibration, and a loud rattle. That combination can be extremely effective when fish are aggressive and need help locating your lure. I especially like throwing the Fat Lipper in slightly stained or muddy water. The sound and vibration allow fish to detect the lure even when visibility is limited. It is also a great choice when there is chop on the water and fish are aggressively chasing bait in the shallows. However, this lure can sometimes be too aggressive around heavily pressured or spooky fish. When the water is slick calm and the fish are cautious, I usually reach for something quieter and more subtle. Best conditions for the Fat Lipper: Choppy water Stained or muddy water Aggressive fish feeding shallow Areas with lower fishing pressure Situations where extra noise and vibration help Wake Mullet: When You Need To Find Fish Fast The Wake Mullet is a shallow-running crankbait that dives to roughly 12 inches. It has a wide profile, a strong wobble, and an internal rattle that can call fish in from a distance. But one of its biggest advantages is how easily it covers water. This is a cast-and-retrieve lure. Throw it out, reel it straight back, and let the lure do the work. That makes the Wake Mullet an excellent search bait when you are fishing a new area or are not yet sure where the fish are holding. It works especially well over shallow grass flats when fish are feeding aggressively. The Wake Mullet is also another strong option when fish are striking at a topwater but failing to connect. It stays just beneath the surface, putting the lure directly in front of fish that may not want to fully break through the top. Best conditions for the Wake Mullet: Searching unfamiliar water Covering large grass flats Aggressive fish feeding shallow Fish missing a topwater lure Anglers who want a simple cast-and-retrieve presentation Flea Flicker: When The Bite Gets Tough The Flea Flicker is different from every other lure on this list. While the other hardbaits are primarily built for aggressive fish, the Flea Flicker shines when fish are spooky, picky, or unwilling to chase. It is a very slow-sinking twitchbait designed to remain in the strike zone for a long time. That slow fall allows you to place the lure in front of a fish and leave it there until the fish finally decides to strike. I love using the Flea Flicker during the heat of summer when fish are holding shallow but do not want to expend much energy chasing prey. It can also be excellent during winter afternoons after the sun warms the shallows and fish begin pushing into skinny water. The biggest mistake anglers make with this lure is fishing it too fast. I will often pause the Flea Flicker for seven to ten seconds between twitches. That may feel painfully slow, but the pause is what gives hesitant fish enough time to inspect and eat the lure. If you have tried the Flea Flicker without getting bites, slow down even more. Best conditions for the Flea Flicker: Tough or slow bites Spooky and pressured fish Calm water Hot summer conditions Sunny winter afternoons Fish holding shallow but refusing to chase Final Thoughts Most hardbaits work best when fish are actively feeding. The Moonwalker shines when they are eating on the surface. The Skinny Lipper gets just below them. The Fat Lipper and Wake Mullet help you cover water and trigger aggressive fish with vibration and noise. But when the fish stop chasing, the Flea Flicker gives you a slower and more subtle option. Hardbaits also have another major advantage during a fast bite. Once you land a fish, you can usually unhook it and immediately make another cast without fixing, replacing, or rerigging your lure. The key is not finding one hardbait that works everywhere. It is recognizing what the fish are doing and choosing the lure that fits that exact situation. Which of these hardbaits gives you the most confidence, and what conditions do you like to throw it in? Frequently Asked Questions What hard bait should I use for inshore fishing? It depends on what the fish are doing and the conditions you are fishing. If fish are feeding aggressively near the surface, a topwater or wake-style bait can be a great choice. If they are spooky, pressured, or unwilling to chase, a slower and more subtle hard bait can be much more effective. When should I throw a topwater lure? Topwater lures are a strong option whenever fish are actively feeding at the surface. That can happen early in the morning, but it is not limited to low-light conditions. If you see bait getting chased or fish blowing up on top, it is usually worth trying a topwater. What should I throw if fish keep missing my topwater? If fish are swiping at or blowing up on your topwater without getting hooked, try switching to a lure that runs just below the surface. A subsurface hard bait can often convert those missed strikes into hookups. Are hard baits good in stained or dirty water? Yes. Hard baits that create more vibration, wobble, and noise can be especially effective in stained water because they give fish more ways to detect the lure when visibility is reduced. What is the best hard bait for a slow bite? When the bite is tough, a slower presentation is usually the better choice. A slow-sinking twitchbait like the Flea Flicker can stay in the strike zone longer and give hesitant fish more time to commit. How fast should I retrieve a hard bait? That depends on the lure. Some hard baits are designed for a simple steady retrieve, while others perform best with twitches, pauses, or an erratic cadence. One of the biggest mistakes anglers make is fishing a finesse-style hard bait too quickly. Can I use hard baits for redfish, trout, and snook? Absolutely. Hard baits can be very effective for redfish, speckled trout, snook, and other inshore predators, especially when those fish are actively feeding on baitfish or shrimp.

items.title: Where To Find Big Redfish During Summer
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Think the big redfish disappeared when the water heated up? They didn’t. Big summer redfish are actually pretty predictable if you know what to look for. I created this video to show you the four types of spots I look for when targeting big redfish i
items.search_text: Think the big redfish disappeared when the water heated up? They didn’t. Big summer redfish are actually pretty predictable if you know what to look for. I created this video to show you the four types of spots I look for when targeting big redfish in the summer. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software Smart Fishing Spots Why Big Redfish Move In The Summer As water temperatures rise, bigger redfish become more focused on conserving energy. They’re looking for places that provide: Cooler water Current Easy access to food Instead of roaming around shallow flats all day, they’ll often position themselves near deeper water and let bait come to them. That’s why I like to think in terms of feeding zones and safety zones. Shallow areas provide feeding opportunities, while nearby deeper water gives the fish a place to retreat when temperatures climb. Finding areas that offer both is one of the keys to catching larger summer reds. Fish Edges And Drop-Offs One of the first places I look is a shallow flat that borders deeper water. Big redfish may feed shallow early in the day, but once the sun gets high, they’ll often slide off into nearby channels or deeper troughs. Instead of staying on top of the flat all day, I like to work the edges where shallow water meets deeper water. Those transition areas can hold some of the biggest fish around. Focus On Points With Current Points are natural feeding funnels. Current pushes bait around the tip of the point, and big redfish simply sit in position and wait for food to come to them. If you don’t have strong tidal current in your area, wind-blown points can accomplish the same thing. The key is movement. If a point isn’t getting current or wind pushing bait through it, I’ll usually move on and find a better area. Funnels Concentrate Fish Another area I love targeting is anywhere water gets squeezed. Examples include: Creek mouths Passes Inlets Narrow channels These areas force baitfish into predictable paths, making it easier for larger redfish to feed without expending much energy. Big fish are efficient. They don’t want to chase meals all over the bay when they can sit in one location and let the current deliver food right to them. Structure Near Deep Water Is Critical Docks, bridges, and oyster bars can all hold fish, but only if they’re connected to deeper water. An isolated shallow dock or oyster bar often looks great, but it may not hold bigger fish during the heat of summer. What I really want to find is: Structure next to a channel Oyster bars with nearby troughs Bridges with current and depth Docks positioned along deeper edges Those combinations create ideal feeding opportunities while giving fish quick access to cooler water. Ask Yourself These Three Questions Before I spend much time fishing an area, I ask myself three questions: Is there current? Moving water helps position bait and brings food to the fish. Is there deep water nearby? Big redfish want quick access to safety and cooler temperatures. Is there bait? If there isn’t food present, there’s usually no reason for the fish to stay. If the answer is no to any of those questions, I’ll often leave and find another area instead of wasting time fishing dead water. Final Thoughts Big summer redfish aren’t gone. They’ve simply moved to areas that offer current, depth, and easy feeding opportunities. So instead of changing lures every few casts, spend more time looking for edges, points, funnels, and structure near deeper water. Find those areas, and you’ll find fish no matter what state you live in. And if you want help finding those spots faster, Smart Fishing Spots and the Salt Strong Insider Club can make the process much easier.

items.title: What Luke Is Throwing for BIG Inshore Fish This Fall
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: See Luke’s favorite fall lure for targeting big inshore fish, why it works so well, and when he switches to a different presentation.
items.search_text: Fall can completely change the way you should approach inshore fishing. Luke has been testing one particular strategy lately, and it’s been producing some of his biggest fish. But it only works when the conditions are right. Here’s when he uses it… and when he switches away from it. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Want to fish the Skinny Lipper XL this fall? It’s included FREE in the Ultimate Fall Bundle 2026, along with our hand-picked lures for the fall feeding frenzy. [GET THE FALL BUNDLE HERE] Featured Gear Skinny Lipper XL Why Bigger Plugs Shine During the Fall For years, Luke primarily relied on soft plastics. And they still have an important place in his tackle box. But when fish are aggressively feeding, he’s found hard plugs offer a few major advantages. First, they can cast a LONG way. Second, they allow you to cover water quickly. And third, a larger plug with single inline hooks can help filter out some of the smaller fish. Luke regularly sees small trout and other undersized fish swipe at a larger plug without getting hooked. That commotion can even attract the attention of a larger predator nearby. That bigger fish sees what looks like another fish trying to grab an easy meal and comes charging in. During aggressive feeding periods, Luke now reaches for plugs far more often than he used to. And fall is one of the BEST times to take advantage of that. Fish the Feeding Window, Not Just the Lure This is probably the most important takeaway from the entire conversation. The Skinny Lipper XL isn’t automatically the best choice all day. Luke’s recent trip was a perfect example. Early in the morning, the fish were actively feeding around schools of mullet. Luke was throwing the Skinny Lipper XL while his dad was fishing a Prawn XT Jr. During that aggressive window, Luke could cast roughly 30 to 40 feet farther, cover more water, and get his lure in front of fish his dad simply couldn’t reach. He caught the biggest trout and biggest redfish during that stretch. But then the conditions changed. The sun came up. The wind died. The water got calmer. And the plug bite slowed down. Luke switched to a much quieter soft plastic presentation and started catching fish again. That gives us a simple rule: Aggressive fish = cover water with plugs. Slower, pressured fish = slow down with soft plastics. Soft plastics can catch fish during BOTH feeding conditions. But when fish are really fired up, a plug can give you a serious advantage in how much water you can effectively fish. How To Retrieve the Skinny Lipper XL One of the advantages of the Skinny Lipper is that you can change the retrieve as the bite changes. The lure floats and has a small lip that makes it dive just below the surface when twitched. When Fish Are Aggressive Early in the morning, Luke fishes it FAST. He uses a quicker retrieve with repeated twitches, making the lure dart erratically like an injured baitfish. The goal is simple: Create commotion and cover water. The built-in rattle adds sound while the erratic movement mimics vulnerable bait. This is the retrieve Luke likes when fish are actively chasing bait and competing for food. As the Bite Slows Down As the sun gets higher and the fish become less aggressive, Luke slows everything down. Instead of continuously working the lure, he gives it a single twitch. The lure dives several inches below the surface and then slowly floats back up. Then he repeats it. This lets you keep using the same plug while presenting it much more slowly. Eventually, though, there comes a point when even that becomes too aggressive. That’s when Luke puts the plug away and switches to a soft plastic. Why Casting Distance Matters So Much for Big Fish Casting farther isn’t just about covering more water. It can also help you catch fish that would otherwise know you’re there. The biggest fish have usually survived long enough to become pretty good at detecting danger. Your boat, kayak, footsteps while wading, or even your presence can shut them down before you ever get a lure in front of them. The farther away you can make an effective presentation, the better your odds of reaching those fish before you spook them. That becomes especially important during fall when schools of larger redfish can move onto shallow flats. Sometimes those schools pop up just outside normal casting range. Being able to make one long cast without pushing the boat closer can be the difference between hooking into a giant redfish and watching the entire school disappear. And remember: Ten or twenty extra feet might not seem like much on ONE cast. But over 100 or 200 casts, that extra distance adds up to a huge amount of additional water covered. Final Thoughts There isn’t one lure that’s going to dominate from sunrise until you head back to the ramp. The better approach is matching your lure to the feeding mood of the fish. When fall fish are aggressive, especially around active bait schools, a bigger plug can help you: Cast farther Cover more water Create more commotion Reach fish before they detect you Potentially weed out some smaller fish But once the sun gets high and the bite slows down, don’t force it. Slow down and switch to a quieter soft plastic presentation. That ability to recognize when the feeding window changes is much more important than blindly sticking with one lure all day. What’s your favorite lure for targeting BIG redfish in the fall? Let us know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Are bigger lures better for redfish in the fall? Bigger lures can be extremely effective when redfish are actively feeding, particularly around larger baitfish such as mullet. They can also help reduce some strikes from smaller fish. However, bigger lures are not always the best choice once fish become less aggressive. When should I throw a plug instead of a soft plastic? Luke prefers plugs during strong feeding windows when fish are actively chasing bait and willing to move for a meal. As conditions get calmer, the sun gets higher, or fish become less aggressive, he switches to quieter soft plastics. How should I retrieve the Skinny Lipper XL? When fish are aggressive, use a faster retrieve with repeated twitches to imitate an injured baitfish and cover water. When the bite slows down, use individual twitches and allow the lure to float back toward the surface between movements. Why is casting distance important for redfish? Longer casts allow you to present your lure farther away from the boat or angler. That can be especially important for larger fish that may detect your presence before you get close enough to make a normal cast. Should I use a plug when it’s windy? Plugs can work very well in wind, but Luke prefers models with larger lips and more vibration when the water becomes heavily disturbed. In calmer conditions, he favors the Skinny Lipper-style presentation.

items.title: What Happens To Redfish When it’s Hot? [And What To Use]
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Most anglers see a blazing-hot afternoon and assume the redfish bite is DONE. But that’s not always true. In fact, once you understand what’s happening to redfish when water temps push into the 90s, you can start predicting exactly where they’ll move
items.search_text: Most anglers see a blazing-hot afternoon and assume the redfish bite is DONE. But that’s not always true. In fact, once you understand what’s happening to redfish when water temps push into the 90s, you can start predicting exactly where they’ll move and what they’ll want to eat. And there’s one BIG reason deeper, moving water can become such a productive place to look. Watch the video below to see the science behind this summer pattern, how I rig blue crab for these fish, and the artificial lures I trust when the heat is cranked up. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear: Rod: Slam Stick 7’6 Medium Heavy Reel: Diawa BG MQ 3000 Lure 1: Prawn XT OG Lure 2: Prawn XT JR Hook 1: Hoss Round Eye Jighead Hook 2: Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead Hook 3: Hoss Football Jighead Hook 4: Hoss Weedless Football Jighead Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 20lb Leader: Ande 20lb Mono Leader You can find the tackle featured in this video at FishStrong.com . Why Redfish Move To Deeper Water In Hot Weather Redfish can tolerate water temperatures above 90 degrees, but extreme heat creates an interesting problem. As water temperatures rise, a redfish’s metabolism increases. That means the fish needs MORE food and energy just to maintain normal bodily functions. But at the same time, warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen. So the fish has an increased demand for oxygen right when there’s less of it available. That combination can make certain areas much more attractive than others during the hottest part of the day. Deeper water is often cooler near the bottom, while moving water helps reoxygenate the water column. That’s why deeper channels, current seams, and other areas with consistent water movement can be excellent places to search for summer redfish when shallow water gets extremely hot. Best Bait For Redfish In Hot Summer Conditions When redfish are dealing with extremely warm water, an easy meal can be hard to beat. That’s where cut bait shines. A chunk of blue crab sitting on the bottom doesn’t require a redfish to burn much energy chasing it down. For the crab rig shown in the video, remove the legs, trim the pointed edges of the shell, and cut the crab in half. Then run your jighead through the rear leg or flapper hole and out through the shell. You’re left with a compact chunk of natural bait that can sit right in the strike zone. And as you saw in the video, a big redfish had no problem finding it. Major and minor feeding periods can also help stack the odds in your favor. The fish in this trip ate right in the middle of a major feeding period, which is another piece of information worth paying attention to when planning a summer trip. Best Artificial Lures For Summer Redfish Cut bait isn’t your only option. If you want to target these fish with artificial lures, larger profiles can work extremely well during the summer. Baitfish are typically larger this time of year, and a bigger lure presents redfish with exactly what they’re looking for: A BIG, easy meal. Four- to five-inch lure profiles are a great starting point. For paddletails, I like pairing them with a round-eye jighead. If I’m fishing relatively clean bottom without much structure, I’ll use an open-face jighead to maximize hookups. If there are oysters, rocks, or other snaggy structure around, I’ll switch to a weedless version. Best Jighead For Paddletails And Shrimp Lures Jighead style can also make a difference depending on the lure profile you’re fishing. I prefer a round-eye jighead with paddletails because the visible eye matches the profile of a baitfish and gives predators another target to key in on. Shrimp are different. For shrimp profiles like the Prawn, I prefer a football-style jighead. The football head helps the lure sit naturally on the bottom and allows the shrimp profile to stand up. Again, match the hook style to the structure you’re fishing. Use an open hook when the bottom is relatively clean. Go weedless when you’re fishing around heavy structure or areas where snagging is a concern. And if you want something that can survive multiple fish and multiple trips, the new Prawn XT is made from an extra-tough material designed for exactly that. Final Thoughts Extremely hot summer afternoons don’t automatically mean you should stop fishing for redfish. You just need to understand what those fish are dealing with. Hotter water increases their metabolism while simultaneously reducing dissolved oxygen, which can make deeper, moving water especially attractive. Find cooler water with current, give those fish an easy meal, and you can still put some impressive reds in the boat even during the hottest part of the day. And whenever you’re fighting fish in extreme heat, make sure to take your time during the release and let the fish fully recover before it swims away. What’s your go-to strategy for catching redfish during the hottest part of summer? Let me know in the comments!

items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Your phone already takes pictures, checks the tides, and probably distracts you more than it should. But it can also record your fishing trips, organize your catches, save private spots, and help reveal the conditions that produce your best days on t
items.search_text: Your phone already takes pictures, checks the tides, and probably distracts you more than it should. But it can also record your fishing trips, organize your catches, save private spots, and help reveal the conditions that produce your best days on the water. It is basically a fishing data cruncher in your back pocket. Luke has been digging into these features and finding some amazing use cases. Boat GPS on steroids? Whatever we call it, this thing does some seriously cool stuff. Here is how it works. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots What Are Routes in Smart Fishing Spots? Routes help you map out a fishing trip before you hit the water. Luke likes creating them on his computer because the larger screen makes it easy to study an area and mark the water he wants to explore. As soon as he saves a route, it appears on his phone. You can research an area from home, mark the zones you want to fish, and have that plan in your pocket when the trip begins. What Are Fishing Tracks? Routes show what you planned. Tracks show what you actually did. Turn tracking on at the start of a trip, and Smart Fishing Spots records your movement throughout the day. Afterward, you can review the water you covered, compare your drifts, and see exactly where the action happened. Luke recently used this while drift fishing for trout. His track showed that most of the strikes came along the deeper outside edge of a grass flat, not on top of the shallow section. When he returned to the area, he could focus on the zone that had already produced fish. That is much better than getting home and saying, “I think we caught them somewhere over there.” What Information Does the Catch Log Save? Every catch can become a private data point inside Smart Fishing Spots. Depending on the information available with your photo, the app can organize catches using details such as: Date and time Tide cycle Wind direction and speed Temperature Barometric pressure Moon phase Lure and trip notes You can upload catches directly to the tool or add photos through an Insider Community fishing report. Either way, your personal catch pins stay private unless you deliberately share them. Can Smart Fishing Spots Organize Older Fishing Photos? Yes, and this is one of the coolest features. If your old fishing photos contain time and location information, the app can place those catches on your private map. It can also retrieve the historical tides and weather from when each fish was caught. Those forgotten photos sitting in your camera roll can suddenly become useful fishing information. Instead of only remembering that you crushed the trout “a few summers ago,” you can see the month, tide, wind, conditions, and location associated with that trip. How Does Your Catch History Help You Find Patterns? Once you build a catch history, you can filter it by month, tide cycle, wind, temperature, pressure, moon phase, and other conditions. That helps answer questions like: Where do I consistently catch redfish in August? Which areas produce during an incoming tide? What wind direction has been best for trout? Where have I caught fish under conditions similar to today? Most anglers save spots. This lets you save the story behind each spot. A waypoint tells you where something happened. Your catch history helps explain when and why it may have happened. Are Your Fishing Spots Private? Yes. Your routes, tracks, waypoints, and catch pins are private by default. Other members cannot see them unless you choose to share something. Private member catches are also NOT used to generate the recommended Smart Spots inside the app. Smart Spots are built separately using areas evaluated by fishing professionals. The system considers factors such as season, tide cycle, wind direction, and current conditions to highlight promising areas. You get the benefit of Smart Spots while keeping your personal fishing history private. Can You Access Your Fishing Data From Different Devices? Yes. Your information is connected to your profile instead of being trapped on one piece of equipment. You can study an area on your computer, save a route or waypoint, and access it from your phone. Your tracks and catches stay with you whether you are fishing from your boat, a friend’s boat, a kayak, a paddleboard, or from shore. For Luke, that was a huge benefit. Instead of installing another expensive unit on his paddleboard, he can use the same fishing information he has already saved in Smart Fishing Spots. Is Smart Fishing Spots Only for Beginners? Not even close. New anglers can use it to shorten the learning curve, but the trip planning and catch analysis tools are valuable for experienced fishermen, too. Professional captains and highly accomplished anglers are already using the app to organize information, study patterns, and preserve what they learn from every trip. It is not about whether you are a beginner or a pro. It is about using better information to catch more fish consistently. How Do You Start Using Routes and Tracks? Try this on your next trip: Study the area inside Smart Fishing Spots. Create a route showing the water you want to explore. Add private waypoints to interesting areas. Turn on tracking when the trip begins. Save your catches. Review everything afterward. Every trip adds more information to your private fishing history and makes the app even more valuable. If you are already an Insider member, open Smart Fishing Spots and start playing around with routes and tracks. If you are not a member yet, click here to learn more. Final Thoughts The best fishing tools are the ones that help you learn from every trip. Smart Fishing Spots does more than save a few pins on a map. It helps you record where you fished, connect catches with real conditions, and recognize patterns you might otherwise miss. The more you use routes, tracks, waypoints, and the catch log, the more valuable your personal fishing history becomes. What Smart Fishing Spots feature should we break down next? Let us know in the comments!

items.title: This Is Why I Love Fishing Docks In The Summer
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: When the water gets hot, fish do not always feed the way we want them to. They get less aggressive and tuck closer to structure, where they can stay comfortable and ambush easy meals. That was exactly the situation on this trip. The tide was not grea
items.search_text: When the water gets hot, fish do not always feed the way we want them to. They get less aggressive and tuck closer to structure, where they can stay comfortable and ambush easy meals. That was exactly the situation on this trip. The tide was not great, the shallow bite never really fired up, and the fish were not chasing much. But by targeting docks with the right lure setup, I was still able to catch snook, trout, flounder, and grouper in less than 2 hours of fishing. This was a great case study in why docks can be one of the best places to fish during the summer. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Insiders, if you want to give this rigging a shot for yourself, June’s Tackle Tester is the Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead. Claim yours here. Featured Gear Deep Structure Setup Rod: Slam Stick Medium Heavy Reel: Daiwa Saltist 4000 Line: Daiwa J-Braid 30lb Leader: Ande 40 lb Mono Lure: Prawn Original Rigging: 1/4 oz Weedless Round Eye Jighead (4/0 Hook) Light Tackle Setup Rod: Slot Machine Medium Power Reel: Otis 2500 Line: Daiwa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 20lb Mono Lure: Prawn Jr Rigging: 1/4 oz Weedless Round Eye Jig Head (3/0 Hook) Why Docks Matter in the Summer During the summer, fish often slide deeper and hold tighter to structure. That does not mean they will not eat. It just means you usually have to put an easy meal right in front of them. On this trip, the deeper docks were the most productive area because they had shade, depth, pilings, rubble, grass, and current breaks. That combination gave fish a comfortable place to sit and ambush prey. The key was getting the lure close to the structure, letting it sink, and slowly bouncing it along the bottom. The Retrieve That Got The Most Strikes The best retrieve was simple. I skipped the lure under the dock, let it get down to the bottom, and worked it back with slow twitches and bottom contact. Nothing fancy. The goal was to make it look like an easy meal sitting right in the strike zone. That slower bottom-bouncing retrieve produced most of the action. Why The Shallows Did Not Produce After the dock bite, I moved to shallower oysters and mangroves to try to find redfish. I did see some fish, but they were very finicky and did not want to commit. That was a big lesson from this trip. Even though the tide started moving later, the shallow bite was still not as good as the deeper dock bite during the slower tide window. When the water is hot, deeper structure can give you a much better chance of getting bites, especially when fish are not aggressive. Final Thoughts This trip was a good reminder that summer fishing is not always about covering more water. Sometimes it is about finding the right structure and slowing down. If the flats, oysters, or mangroves are not producing, do not be afraid to target deeper docks, bridges, rocks, or other hard structure nearby. Get your lure down, keep it close to structure, and make it easy for those fish to eat. That can be the difference between a slow summer trip and a really fun day on the water.

items.title: This Is What Fishing a New Spot REALLY Looks Like
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: One of the biggest challenges in fishing isn’t figuring out how to catch fish. It’s figuring out where to begin. That’s especially true when I’m launching into an area I’ve never fished before. Every shoreline looks promising. Every creek seems worth
items.search_text: One of the biggest challenges in fishing isn’t figuring out how to catch fish. It’s figuring out where to begin. That’s especially true when I’m launching into an area I’ve never fished before. Every shoreline looks promising. Every creek seems worth exploring. Every point has potential. So how do I decide where to make my first cast? For this trip, I intentionally launched into water I’d never fished before and walked through every decision I made along the way. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: Lure 1: Prawn Jr. Lure 2: Mulligan Paddletail Rigging for Prawn Jr: 2/0 Hoss Round Eye Jighead (1/8 oz) Rigging for Mulligan: 4/0 Hoss Helix Hooks (1/8 oz) Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Every Trip Starts With a Plan When I launch into unfamiliar water, my first goal isn’t catching fish. It’s finding the highest-percentage water. Before I even make my first cast, I’ll often use Smart Fishing Spots to identify a handful of promising starting locations. From there, it’s all about letting the conditions tell the story. Instead of making random casts, I’m constantly looking for clues: Current flow Shoreline shape Water depth Bait activity Wind direction Bottom composition Areas that naturally funnel fish Every observation helps eliminate unproductive water and narrows down where fish are most likely to be. Think of it like solving a puzzle instead of playing the lottery. The Reality of Fishing New Water If you watch enough fishing videos online, it can feel like everyone catches fish every time they launch. The truth is, most days aren’t like that. This trip was a perfect example. The fishing was slow. There weren’t fish around every corner, and every decision mattered. But that’s exactly why I wanted to share it. The lessons you learn on difficult days often stick with you far longer than the lessons from an easy bite. Success Isn’t Always Measured by Fish in the Boat At the end of the day, the fish count didn’t tell the whole story. We found multiple redfish in a completely unfamiliar area. In fact, this trip was only a few casts away from looking completely different. One cast landed too close to a cruising redfish, spooking not one, but two fish. Another opportunity ended when my lure caught the shoreline before reaching another fish. Those fish never made it into the kayak, but they proved something important: The process worked. The fish were there. The opportunities were there. The execution simply wasn’t perfect. That’s an encouraging place to be because it’s much easier to improve your casting or presentation than it is to find fish that don’t exist. Judge the Process, Not Just the Results One mistake I see anglers make is judging every trip solely by how many fish they catch. While catching fish is always the goal, it isn’t the only way to measure progress. Did you eliminate unproductive water? Did you identify a pattern? Did you find bait? Did you locate fish? Did you learn where you’d start next time? Those are all wins that build toward consistently successful trips. A few years ago, I might have left this area thinking there simply weren’t any fish there. Today, I leave knowing exactly where I’d start the next time I launch. That’s progress. And sometimes, that’s the most valuable catch of the day. Final Thoughts Fishing new water will always come with a little uncertainty. That’s part of what makes it fun. The goal isn’t to have every trip go perfectly. It’s to leave the water knowing something you didn’t know when you launched. Every clue you uncover, every area you eliminate, and every fish you find makes the next trip that much better. Stick with the process, keep paying attention to what the conditions are telling you, and before long you’ll be able to break down unfamiliar water with confidence. That’s a skill that will help you catch more fish no matter where you launch.

items.title: This Is My Favorite Way To Catch Snapper and Grouper Inshore
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: One lure. One drift. A whole lot of action. I headed to Boca Grande Pass to test the durability of the new Prawn XT, and I chose one of the easiest ways to put it in front of a ton of fish: dropping it straight down and bouncing it along the bottom a
items.search_text: One lure. One drift. A whole lot of action. I headed to Boca Grande Pass to test the durability of the new Prawn XT, and I chose one of the easiest ways to put it in front of a ton of fish: dropping it straight down and bouncing it along the bottom as I drifted through the pass. Watch the video below to see this easy jigging technique in action, and how the lure held up through it all. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear: Rod: Slam Stick Medium-Heavy Power Reel: Saltist MQ 3000 Line: 20 lb J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 30 lb Ande Monofilament Lure: Prawn XT 4.3″ rigged on 3/4 oz Hoss Weedless Football Jighead How to Catch Saltwater Fish by Vertical Jigging Passes and Inlets The technique is incredibly simple. Position your boat at the beginning of a productive stretch, drop a weedless shrimp lure to the bottom, and let the current carry you through the pass. Use short, controlled lifts to make the shrimp rise and fall. Most strikes will come as it drops back toward the bottom. The biggest key is keeping your line as vertical as possible. I used the trolling motor to stay over the lure instead of letting it trail far behind the boat. This made it easier to: Feel the bottom Detect light strikes Avoid snags Pull grouper away from structure The action started almost immediately. I missed a few smaller taps before hooking a solid grouper near a drop from approximately 40 to 60 feet. More grouper, mangrove snapper, and jacks followed as we drifted through the pass. At times, the lure didn’t make it through more than a few bounces before another fish hit. How to Find Productive Ledges, Holes, and Bottom Structure You can drift randomly and catch fish, but knowing what’s beneath the boat makes this technique much more effective. I used the high-resolution shaded-relief imagery inside Smart Fishing Spots to locate: Deep holes Rocky ledges Underwater boulders Sharp depth changes I could watch the boat drift across those features in real time and anticipate when the bottom was about to get deeper or shallower. That matters because the best action often occurs along the edges of holes and ledges. Grouper and snapper use those areas to hide from current while waiting for shrimp, crabs, and baitfish to pass overhead. Once we drifted beyond the main structure, the bite slowed dramatically. That’s your clue to return to the productive area and make another pass. Don’t keep drifting across empty bottom and assume the fish suddenly stopped biting. How to Rig a Weedless Shrimp Lure for Deep-Water Jigging Passes and inlets hold fish because they contain structure, but that same structure can steal a lot of tackle. A weedless setup allows you to bounce the lure through rocks, ledges, and uneven bottom with fewer snags. For this trip, I rigged the Prawn XT on a 3/4-ounce weedless football-style jighead. That was enough weight to maintain bottom contact in 40 to 70 feet of water with minimal current. Use the lightest jighead that still lets you feel the bottom and keep your line reasonably vertical. Shallower water and weaker current will usually call for less weight. The lure also needs to sit straight. Insert the hook through the center of the nose, bring it out through the underbelly, and slide the lure firmly against the jighead. Then mark where the hook naturally meets the body and push it straight through. A properly rigged lure will fall naturally without spinning or bunching. The Prawn XT’s durability was the biggest surprise. The lure featured in this video had already been used on six trips and caught at least 40 fish. After another drift filled with fish and missed strikes, the head and tail were still intact. That means more time fishing and less time reeling up from 70 feet to replace torn soft plastics. When You Need an Easy Way to Find Action This is one of my favorite techniques when the current is weak, the wind disappears, or the regular inshore bite gets tough. Instead of running around searching for active fish, locate a pass or inlet with good depth changes and hard structure. Then let the boat carry a weedless shrimp past the fish. It works particularly well during summer, when warm water pushes many species toward deeper areas with stronger water movement. And the species list can get interesting. Depending on where you fish, this same setup could produce: Grouper Mangrove snapper Redfish Snook Flounder Sheepshead Tarpon Cobia That mystery is part of what makes it so much fun. Every drop could produce a different fish, and when the boat passes through the right stretch, the strikes can come unbelievably fast. Final Thoughts This is one of my favorite ways to find action when the current is weak, the wind disappears, or the regular inshore bite gets tough. Find a pass or inlet with good bottom structure, drop a weedless shrimp lure straight down, and keep it near the bottom. That simple approach can catch grouper, snapper, redfish, snook, flounder, sheepshead, and plenty of surprise species. Best of all, you never know what will be on the other end when the rod bends. Find the structure, keep your line vertical, and hold on! Then come back and let me know what you caught in the comments!

items.title: This Is How To Sight Fish Redfish & Black Drum In Shallow Water
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Sight fishing doesn’t get much better than this. Joe and I spent an awesome morning in Louisiana getting shots at big redfish, chunky black drum, and even one absolutely MASSIVE bycatch. And while the fishing was a blast, one thing became VERY clear…
items.search_text: Sight fishing doesn’t get much better than this. Joe and I spent an awesome morning in Louisiana getting shots at big redfish, chunky black drum, and even one absolutely MASSIVE bycatch. And while the fishing was a blast, one thing became VERY clear… If you can’t put your lure where it needs to be, those fish may never give you a second chance. Check out the video below to see some of our best catches from the trip, the casts that got those fish to eat, and how to recover when one misses the mark. You’ll know exactly what to do when a big fish suddenly shows up in front of you. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: Medium Setup Rod: Slam Stick Traveler 7’6″ – Medium Power (Fast Tip) Reel: Otis 3000 – Coming Soon ( Otis 2500 is available here ) Line: 15 lb Daiwa J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 30 lb Ande Mono Lure: Prawn XT 3.5″ rigged on a 3/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jighead 1/4 oz Medium-Heavy Setup Rod: Slam Stick Travel 7’6″ – Medium-Heavy Power (Fast Tip) Reel: Otis 3000 – Coming Soon ( Otis 2500 is available here ) Line: 20 lb Daiwa J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 30 lb Ande Mono Lure: Mulligan Bomber 5″ rigged on a 4/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/8 oz Casting Accuracy Was EVERYTHING These fish made it pretty obvious when they liked a cast… and when they didn’t. Especially with the black drum, the lure often had to land RIGHT in front of their face to get a reaction. Too far away and they ignored it. Too much splash and you risked spooking them. The goal wasn’t simply to cast near the fish. It was to quietly put the lure exactly where that fish could see it and react without having to chase it very far. The 3 Casts That Got Us Bites We ended up using three different casts depending on how far away the fish was and how calm the water was. Sidearm Cast: Great when the fish was too far away for a pitch but we still wanted a low, quiet lure entry. Underhand Pitch: Perfect for close-range opportunities when accuracy and minimal splash mattered most. Overhand Cast: Best when we needed more distance, especially when we could cast beyond the fish and bring the lure into its path. Being comfortable with all three gave us a much better chance of making the right presentation when a fish suddenly appeared. You Can Still Save A Bad Cast Not every cast lands perfectly. One of the biggest lessons from this trip was that a slightly off-target cast doesn’t automatically mean the opportunity is over. On one of the drum, my lure landed farther left than I wanted. Instead of immediately retrieving it and recasting, I raised the rod tip and moved it off to the side as I retrieved the lure. That changed the lure’s path and allowed me to guide it directly in front of the fish. Once it reached the strike zone, I centered the rod, dropped the lure right in front of its face… And it ate. Learning how to redirect your lure after it lands can save a LOT of sight fishing opportunities. Your Rod Matters More Than You May Think Sight fishing puts a lot of demands on your rod. You need it to make accurate casts, properly work the lure, feel subtle strikes, drive the hook home, and then control a fish once it takes off. That’s one reason Joe and I were putting the Slam Stick Traveler through its paces on this trip. We brought both Medium and Medium-Heavy setups so we could adjust depending on the size of the fish and lure we were throwing. The Medium setup paired perfectly with the smaller Prawn XT Jr. for the reds and drum. Then when we spotted a giant gar, I switched over to the Medium-Heavy setup with a 5-inch paddletail. That turned into one of the craziest catches of the entire trip. Final Thoughts This was one of those mornings that reminded me why sight fishing is so addicting. You’re watching the fish. You’re trying to make the perfect presentation. And when everything lines up, you get to watch the whole eat happen right in front of you. But it also shows just how important casting accuracy can be. Practice your sidearm cast, underhand pitch, and overhand cast BEFORE you need them, because when a big redfish or drum suddenly appears 20 feet from the boat, you may only get one shot. What’s your favorite way to sight fish, and which of these casts do you use the most? Let me know in the comments! Tight Lines! Frequently Asked Questions What is the best cast for sight fishing? It depends on the distance and conditions. An underhand pitch is excellent for close fish, a sidearm cast helps create a quieter lure entry at moderate distances, and an overhand cast is useful when you need additional distance. Where should you cast when sight fishing redfish or black drum? Whenever possible, place the lure slightly ahead of the fish and close enough that it can easily see the bait without requiring a long chase. On this trip, some of the drum wanted the lure almost directly on their nose before they would eat. How do you fix a bad cast while sight fishing? If your lure lands slightly off target, you can sometimes use your rod angle to redirect its path during the retrieve. Raise the rod and move the tip to one side or the other to guide the lure back toward the strike zone. What lure did we use for sight fishing? Our best results came on the Prawn XT 3.5″ rigged weedless on a 1/4 oz Hoss Weedless Football Jighead . Where was this sight fishing trip filmed? This trip was filmed in Venice, Louisiana while fishing with Capt. Hollywood.

items.title: This Has To Be The Easiest Way To Catch Seatrout [Case Study]
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: If I want to catch a bunch of seatrout in a saltwater bay, this is the strategy I trust most, even when the tide is weak. You don’t need a trolling motor, expensive marine electronics, or live bait. All you need is something that floats, a couple lur
items.search_text: If I want to catch a bunch of seatrout in a saltwater bay, this is the strategy I trust most, even when the tide is weak. You don’t need a trolling motor, expensive marine electronics, or live bait. All you need is something that floats, a couple lures, and a plan for setting up productive drifts. In this case study, I’ll show you exactly how to: Choose high-percentage summertime seatrout spots Use your phone as a powerful fishing GPS Plan and repeat productive drifts Catch fish during a tough slack-tide window I also put my two favorite seatrout lures head-to-head. One of them was the clear winner for both the quality and quantity of strikes. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear: Rod: Slot Machine 7’6″ Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Line: 8 lb Daiwa J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 20 lb Ande Mono Lure 1: Skinny Lipper – Slam Shady Lure 2: The 2.0 – Slam Shady rigged on 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye 1/4oz Other: Boat: 22′ Micro Draft Sunglasses: Smith – Guide’s Choice Pliers: Danco Pro Series Where To Find Seatrout In Saltwater Bays The most important part of catching seatrout is finding the right zone. For this trip, I focused on grass flats located next to deeper water, channels, bridges, and other areas with current flow. I also looked for signs of life, including baitfish and diving birds. The key wasn’t simply finding a good-looking flat. It was identifying the specific depth where the trout were feeding. During my first few drifts, most of the action came along the deeper edges of the grass. Once I recognized that pattern, I could stop wasting time in water that was too shallow or too deep. That’s when the catch rate really started to improve. How To Set Up Productive Drifts A controlled drift lets you cover water without constantly running the trolling motor or making noise around the fish. After completing a drift, I reviewed my track and marked where the strikes happened. I could then reposition the boat and make another drift through a slightly different section of the productive zone. The goal isn’t to follow the exact same line repeatedly. Instead, use each drift to learn where the fish are holding and then adjust your next pass accordingly. That process helps you quickly eliminate dead water and maximize the amount of time your lure spends in front of feeding fish. How Smart Fishing Spots Helps You Find Fish Faster One of the biggest challenges, especially in a new area, is deciding where to begin. Smart Fishing Spots helps narrow the search by highlighting areas that match the conditions. Instead of randomly working miles of shoreline, you can focus on locations with the highest probability of holding fish. The tracking feature is especially valuable when drift fishing. It shows exactly where the boat traveled, making it easy to compare productive and unproductive passes. You can also use it to: Find high-percentage fishing zones Monitor your location and drift direction Safely navigate unfamiliar water Mark catches directly on your private map Return to productive areas on future trips It essentially turns your phone into a powerful fishing GPS that you can use anywhere on the boat. Hard Plug vs. Paddletail For this trip, I alternated between two Slam Shady lures: The Skinny Lipper The 2.0 paddletail I started by making three casts with one lure and then switching to the other. That gave both lures repeated opportunities in the same water and under the same conditions. The Skinny Lipper generated the most strikes early in the trip and produced some of the better trout. Its larger profile and erratic action appeared to trigger fish even when they weren’t feeding aggressively. As the sun climbed higher, the paddletail began performing better. Its ability to stay deeper in the water column made it more effective once the fish settled lower. The big lesson is that lure performance can change throughout the day. Test different profiles and depths instead of assuming one lure will always be the best choice. Why Every Angler Should Keep A Catch Log Every fishing trip teaches you something, but only if you remember the details. Recording where you caught fish, along with the tide, wind, weather, season, and lure, helps reveal patterns that would otherwise be easy to miss. The Smart Fishing Spots catch log makes this process simple. When you upload a photo from your phone, it can automatically associate the catch with its location, time, weather, and tide information. Over time, you can filter your catches by factors such as: Month or season Tide cycle Current flow Wind direction and speed Air temperature Barometric pressure Moon phase Lure selection That turns each trip into useful information you can apply the next time you’re on the water. Eventually, your private catch log becomes one of the most valuable fishing tools you own. Final Thoughts You don’t need expensive equipment or a complicated boat setup to catch a bunch of seatrout. The winning formula is simple: Find grass flats near deeper water and current. Look for bait, birds, and other signs of life. Use controlled drifts to cover water. Track where your strikes occur. Repeat your drifts through the most productive depth. Match your lure to the depth and activity level of the fish. A tool like Smart Fishing Spots can dramatically shorten the learning curve by helping you find promising areas, structure your drifts, and save everything you learn. That means less time searching—and more time catching fish. Have you tried this style of drift fishing for seatrout? What lure produces the most strikes for you? Let me know in the comments!

items.title: This 3-Rod Cut Bait Setup is DESTROYING Big Redfish (Guide Secret)
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Most anglers fishing cut bait simply spread out a few rods and wait. World-record holder Captain Peter Deeks takes a different approach. His three-rod technique gives each bait a specific job, and the way he combines that spread with wind and current
items.search_text: Most anglers fishing cut bait simply spread out a few rods and wait. World-record holder Captain Peter Deeks takes a different approach. His three-rod technique gives each bait a specific job, and the way he combines that spread with wind and current may completely change how you approach a mangrove shoreline. There’s also one bite most anglers consider a nuisance that he actually wants to see. Watch the video below to see exactly how Capt Peter positions his three rods, why he chooses the windy shoreline, and what happens when he puts the complete system to the test. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Where Should You Fish Cut Bait For Redfish? Use Smart Fishing Spots to find windblown shorelines where moving water can carry your bait’s scent toward likely redfish holding zones. Before launching, check the wind and tide. Then use the satellite imagery, seagrass and oyster layers, and 1-foot depth contours to look for: Mangrove shorelines exposed to the wind Sandy potholes surrounded by grass Oyster edges and depth changes Docks, fallen trees, points, and current funnels Save several promising areas as waypoints rather than relying on a single spot. Once you arrive, position yourself with the wind and current at your back. Look for moving water and signs of life, such as large mullet jumping nearby. During higher water, skip your bait beneath overhanging mangroves. On grass flats, place it in a sandy pothole where redfish can both smell and see it. If there’s no wind or current and the fish aren’t moving, switch to a live bait or artificial lure that allows you to cover more water. What Is The Best Cut Bait And Rig For Redfish? Fresh, oily bait is best. Mullet, ladyfish, and blue crab are all excellent options. Hook the bait through the thinner end, close to the edge, and leave the circle hook exposed. This helps it cast farther, skip accurately, and hook fish cleanly. A 4/0 circle hook is a good starting point for most redfish. Around mangroves or heavy structure, use strong tackle: 7-foot-6-inch medium-action rod like our Slam Stick Medium 50-pound braided line 50-pound leader On open flats, you can drop to 15- or 20-pound line for longer casts. Always check your local bait and redfish regulations before fishing. How Does The 3-Rod Cut Bait Setup Work? Cast one unweighted bait down the middle. Then place a lightly weighted bait on either side to keep the spread separated: Weighted bait – Unweighted bait – Weighted bait In heavy wind or current, approximately a 1/2-ounce weight on each outside rig is usually enough. Watch the rod tips closely. A catfish often makes the tip dance and stop, while a redfish typically loads the rod and swims away. When that happens, pick up the rod and steadily reel until the circle hook comes tight. Don’t use a hard hookset. And don’t be too quick to retrieve a bait when a catfish starts picking at it. That commotion releases scent and food particles that can attract a larger redfish. Final Thoughts Cut bait fishing doesn’t need to be complicated. Use fresh bait, find moving water, cast where redfish can easily locate the bait, and spread your rods across the strike zone. Then sit back, relax, and wait for one to bend over.

items.title: The Incredible Impact of Releasing ONE 20″+ Trout
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Discover the incredible impact of releasing a speckled trout over 20 inches and how one simple decision could help future fish populations.
items.search_text: What if releasing just ONE big speckled trout could help produce millions of future fish? Sounds pretty wild, right? Well, there’s some fascinating science behind it. I recently caught up with my buddy David Fladd, founder of Release Over 20 , to talk about what happens when we give bigger fish a chance to keep growing and spawning. And what started as a simple idea to protect trophy trout has turned into something MUCH bigger. Check out our conversation below! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Learn More About Release Over 20 Why 20 Inches Matters Here’s something I didn’t know until I first met David several years ago. Most speckled trout over 20 inches are females. And those larger females play an incredibly important role in producing the next generation of fish. According to David, a 20-inch female trout can potentially produce around 20 MILLION eggs in a single spawning season! And here’s where it gets even more interesting. Unlike fish that spawn just once a year, speckled trout can spawn repeatedly throughout the warmer months. In fact, David explained that females may release portions of their eggs every four to five days during spawning season. And as those trout get bigger? Their egg production can increase dramatically. A 23- or 24-inch trout may produce considerably more eggs than a 20-inch fish. Now, that doesn’t mean every egg becomes another trout. Far from it. But when you consider how many eggs a single large female can produce, you start to see why giving some of those bigger fish another chance can make a difference. One fish today could potentially contribute to thousands of fish in the future. Pretty cool stuff! The Impact Is Already Adding Up Here’s where this story gets REALLY exciting. When David started Release Over 20, he wasn’t trying to create some massive conservation movement. He simply wanted to catch more big trout around Charleston, South Carolina. So he made a personal decision. Every speckled trout he caught over 20 inches was going back into the water. That was it. No new fishing regulations. No complicated rules. Just one angler making a choice to help improve his local fishery. Fast-forward to today, and thousands of anglers have joined the movement. During our conversation, David shared that more than 17,000 speckled trout over 20 inches had been recorded through the program. Using an estimated 20 million eggs per fish over one spawning season, that represents a theoretical spawning potential of approximately 345 BILLION eggs! Of course, that’s not a count of actual eggs produced or fish that survived. But it helps put the potential impact into perspective. And I’m especially proud of how our Salt Strong community has gotten involved. Multiple Salt Strong chapters are participating, and our Charleston chapter even earned recognition as the top organization in the program’s inaugural awards. Our St. Pete chapter had already surpassed its goal of 500 releases for 2026 when David and I recorded this conversation. That’s what I love about this whole thing. Anglers coming together to make fishing better for EVERYONE. It’s Bigger Than Speckled Trout While Release Over 20 started with speckled trout, David and his team have expanded the program to include five species: Speckled trout Redfish Flounder Sheepshead Striped bass And each species has its own interesting story. Take flounder, for example. David explained that male flounder generally don’t grow nearly as large as females. That means the keeper-sized flounder we’re catching in his region are overwhelmingly females. Pretty fascinating, right? Then there’s redfish. David and I discussed how protecting spawning fish can be especially important in areas where redfish populations have declined. And sometimes, helping those fish doesn’t necessarily mean releasing everything we catch. It might mean releasing a particularly large fish. Or giving spawning fish a break during certain times of the year. Or simply keeping a few fish for dinner instead of taking home a full limit. The goal isn’t to stop enjoying the fishery. It’s to help make sure there’s an abundance of fish to enjoy for years to come. And that’s something I think just about every angler can get behind. How YOU Can Get Involved One of the coolest things about Release Over 20 is how easy they’ve made it to participate. They’ve even turned conservation into a fun challenge with prizes! Here’s how it works: Download the FREE Release Over 20 app. Create your profile. Catch and release an eligible fish over 20 inches. Log your release in the app. Get entered for a chance to win fishing gear! That’s right. You can actually win tackle, hats, shirts, and other fishing goodies just for participating. The app doesn’t collect your GPS coordinates. You only need to provide the state where you caught and released the fish. David and his team are anglers, too. They understand how important it is to protect those hard-earned fishing spots! They’ve also created leaderboards for fishing clubs, organizations, and individual anglers. So if you’re part of a Salt Strong chapter, this is an awesome way to get everyone involved. Learn More About Release Over 20 Final Thoughts One thing I really appreciate about David is his approach to conservation. He’s not trying to tell everyone how they should fish. And neither am I. I love catching fish. I love eating fresh fish. And I love seeing families bring home a few fish for dinner. There’s absolutely nothing wrong with enjoying the harvest side of fishing within the regulations. But I also love the idea that one simple decision on the water could help create better fishing opportunities for our kids and grandkids. Imagine what our fisheries could look like if thousands of anglers made small decisions like that throughout the year. More fish. Bigger fish. And more incredible memories on the water. That’s a future worth working toward! So a HUGE shoutout to David Fladd and everyone involved with Release Over 20. Keep up the awesome work! And if you haven’t already, check out their free app and consider joining the movement. Now I’ve got a question for you… Do you have a personal size limit for releasing bigger trout, redfish, or other inshore species? Or have you participated in Release Over 20 already? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Why should you release speckled trout over 20 inches? Larger speckled trout are often females capable of producing millions of eggs during spawning season. Releasing these fish gives them additional opportunities to reproduce and potentially contribute to future trout populations. How many eggs can a 20-inch speckled trout produce? According to David Fladd of Release Over 20, a 20-inch female speckled trout may produce approximately 20 million eggs over a spawning season. This is an estimate, not an exact number. Actual egg production varies based on factors such as the fish’s size, age, and reproductive condition. What species qualify for Release Over 20? Release Over 20 currently includes speckled trout, redfish, flounder, sheepshead, and striped bass. Anglers can record qualifying releases through the organization’s free app. Is the Release Over 20 app free? Yes! The Release Over 20 app is completely free. Anglers can record qualifying releases, participate in leaderboards, and receive entries into fishing gear giveaways. The app also protects your fishing spots by not collecting GPS coordinates. Does Release Over 20 mean you shouldn’t keep fish? Not at all! Release Over 20 encourages voluntary conservation and responsible fishing practices. Anglers can still enjoy keeping fish for dinner while making personal decisions about releasing larger fish that may be particularly valuable to future spawning populations. The goal is to help create healthier, more abundant fisheries for future generations.
