items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: There are dozens of knots, and if you spend a few minutes online, you’ll quickly find people claiming theirs is the strongest, the easiest, or even the mythical “100% knot.” The truth? You don’t need to learn a dozen knots to become a better angler.
items.search_text: There are dozens of knots, and if you spend a few minutes online, you’ll quickly find people claiming theirs is the strongest, the easiest, or even the mythical “100% knot.” The truth? You don’t need to learn a dozen knots to become a better angler. In this video, Luke and I break down the one fishing knot every beginner should master first, why it works so well across different applications, and when it makes sense to start learning more advanced knots. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Why The Uni Knot Is Perfect For Beginners When you’re first getting into fishing, simplicity matters. The Uni Knot is one of the most versatile knots you can learn because it can be used for several different connections, including: Tying directly to hooks Connecting to swivels Tying braid to monofilament or fluorocarbon leaders (Double Uni) Mono-to-mono connections Instead of memorizing several different knots, beginners can gain confidence by mastering one knot that works in almost every situation. Why There Is No Such Thing As A “100% Knot” One of the biggest misconceptions in fishing is the idea of a “100% knot.” As Luke explains, every knot creates bends and pressure points in your fishing line. Those stress points naturally become the weakest part of the system. After years of controlled knot testing, Luke found that nearly every properly tied knot eventually breaks at the knot itself, not somewhere else along the line. That’s why it’s important to focus less on marketing claims and more on learning knots you can tie correctly every single time. When To Upgrade To More Advanced Knots The Uni Knot is an excellent place to start. But as your skills improve, there are advantages to learning more specialized knots. For example, Luke recommends the FG Knot for braid-to-leader connections because controlled testing has consistently shown it to be stronger and significantly slimmer than the popular Double Uni Knot. That combination creates smoother casts while maximizing line strength. The key is progression. Master one versatile knot first, then expand your knot selection as your fishing experience grows. Test Your Own Knots One of the best tips from this discussion is to test your own knots. You don’t need expensive equipment. Tie your favorite knots between two solid anchor points and gradually apply pressure until they break. Doing this helps you build confidence while identifying any weak points before you’re on the water fighting a trophy fish. Even small improvements in your knot strength can make a big difference when that one bite finally comes. Final Thoughts If you’re just getting started, don’t worry about learning every fishing knot out there. Master the Uni Knot first, tie it consistently, and build your confidence from there. Once you’re ready, you can begin adding more specialized knots like the FG Knot to maximize your performance on the water.

They simply move to areas that give them everything they need. That’s why I spend so much time fishing spoil islands. These areas usually have shallow grass flats, sand potholes, and deeper water all within a short distance. Trout can slide shallow to feed early in the morning, then move into deeper water once the sun gets high without traveling very far. If I can find bait around these areas, I’m usually confident there’s a good chance trout won’t be far behind. How I Find These Areas On this trip, I noticed the productive islands all had a few things in common. There was plenty of bait activity, birds working nearby, and shallow structure sitting right next to deeper water. Once I recognized that pattern, I pulled up Smart Fishing Spots and started looking for other spoil islands with those same characteristics. Instead of guessing where the fish might be, I simply looked for more spots that matched what was already producing. That’s a pattern you can repeat almost anywhere you fish. Three Things That Made A Big Difference Finding the right spot is only half the battle. The way you fish it matters just as much. First, I always try to avoid running directly over the area I want to fish. I’ll make a wide loop and ease back into casting range so I’m not spooking fish before I even pick up my rod. Second, I pay close attention to exactly where I’m getting bites. On this trip, the trout were holding shallower while the ladyfish were slightly deeper. Little details like that help me stay around the fish instead of making random casts. Finally, don’t underestimate boat noise. After changing my drift to eliminate hull slap, the bite picked right back up. Staying quiet is one of the easiest adjustments you can make, and it often pays off immediately. It stayed just below the surface, matched the baitfish I was seeing, and held up much better than soft plastics with all the pufferfish around. Looking back, I’d probably switch to the medium-light section of the Traveler Rod next time to help keep more fish pinned near the boat. Final Thoughts If you’re struggling to catch trout during the summer, don’t assume they’ve left the area. Start looking for spoil islands, shallow structure next to deeper water, and plenty of bait activity. Combine that with a quiet approach, and you’ll put yourself around a lot more fish this summer.

items.title: Stop Overlooking This Summer Fishing Window (PM Bite)
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Ask almost any angler when to fish during summer, and they will tell you to get on the water before sunrise. They are not wrong. But summer often creates a second feeding window, and most anglers are already off the water before they realize it is ha
items.search_text: Ask almost any angler when to fish during summer, and they will tell you to get on the water before sunrise. They are not wrong. But summer often creates a second feeding window, and most anglers are already off the water before they realize it is happening. It starts with a predictable chain of changes that makes bait more active and pulls predators back into striking range. So, what triggers the second bite, and how can you tell when it is about to begin? Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: Lure 1: Moonwalker topwater Lure 2: 4-inch Mulligan paddletail Lure 3: Wake Mullet crankbait Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots What Creates the Second Summer Feeding Window? Early morning fishing is productive because several favorable conditions happen at the same time. The water has had all night to cool, baitfish become active, and low light helps predators approach their prey. As the sun climbs, shallow water heats faster than deeper water. Fish are cold-blooded, so many will move toward deeper, cooler areas during the hottest part of the day. That is one reason the afternoon bite can feel so difficult. The process begins reversing as the sun gets lower. Shallow water is no longer receiving the same direct heat, so it begins cooling. Baitfish become more comfortable and start moving into shallow feeding areas. At the same time, fading light gives predators the cover they need to follow. Cooler shallows, active bait, and lower light begin recreating many of the same conditions that made the morning bite so productive. What Signs Show That the Evening Bite Is Starting? The exact timing can change from one day to another, so do not rely only on the clock. Instead, watch what is happening around you. Signs of increasing feeding activity may include: Baitfish becoming active near the surface Wading birds moving into shallow water Diving birds working over bait Predators striking at the surface Fish pushing wakes across a flat Increasing activity along shorelines and shallow edges Afternoon storms can also accelerate the transition. Clouds block sunlight, rain can help cool the surface, and wind can disturb and oxygenate shallow water. Together, these changes may encourage fish to become active earlier. Always wait until a storm has completely passed before returning to the water. Lightning is never worth the risk. Where Should You Fish During the Evening Window? Look for shallow feeding areas with deeper water nearby. Fish can remain in comfortable depths during the hottest part of the day, then move into the shallows as conditions improve. Productive areas may include: Flats bordering channels Shorelines near a drop-off Points connecting shallow and deep water Creek mouths Oyster bars near deeper troughs Grass lines beside channels Sandbars next to deeper cuts The most important feature is the relationship between deep and shallow water. When those areas are close together, fish do not have to travel far to take advantage of the evening feeding opportunity. Which Lures Work Best in Low Light? You do not need an entirely different tackle box for evening fishing. Many of the same lures that catch fish around sunrise will also produce as daylight fades. A topwater lure is an excellent choice when fish are feeding near the surface. It can cover water quickly, imitate fleeing bait, and call fish from a distance. A built-in rattle gives predators another way to locate it. A 4-inch paddletail is another strong option. The larger profile produces more vibration, which can help fish track the lure as visibility decreases. A shallow-running crankbait such as the Wake Mullet stays close to the surface while producing vibration and sound. Final Thoughts Most anglers schedule their summer trips around the morning bite. If early morning works for you, take advantage of it. Just do not assume it is your only opportunity. As the sun gets lower, shallow water begins cooling, bait becomes active, and predators move back into feeding areas. You may also find fewer boats and much less fishing pressure. Watch the bait, birds, light, weather, and nearby depth changes. When those clues begin coming together, move shallow and get ready. Have you caught more summer fish during the morning bite or during the final few hours before sunset?

items.excerpt: See how one skeptical angler tested a simple lure, caught more trout, and gained confidence fishing without bait.
items.search_text: If you’ve always relied on live bait, switching to artificial lures can feel like a gamble. Why mess with something that already catches fish? One Salt Strong Insider felt the exact same way. He’d watched our videos, heard what we had to say, and still wasn’t convinced artificial lures could compete with live bait. Then one fishing trip gave him the perfect chance to finally put it to the test. And what happened completely changed the way he looks at fishing. By the end of this video, you’ll know a simple way to test artificial lures for yourself and gain confidence fishing without relying on live bait. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Lure 1: Slam Shady 2.0 Lure 2: Prawn Jr. Bundle and Save: Inshore Slammer Bundle Start Somewhere You KNOW Has Fish This angler wasn’t struggling to catch fish. Quite the opposite. He had spent around $100 on live bait for the day, and once they got to one of his spots, the fish were feeding like crazy. But they were burning through shrimp almost as quickly as they could put them in the water. Eventually, he looked down and saw a pack of Slam Shady 2.0 paddletails he had never used. So he rigged one up and gave it a shot. That’s what makes this such a good way to start experimenting with artificial lures. You don’t have to completely change the way you fish. Go somewhere you already have confidence. Let the live bait prove the fish are there. Then pick up an artificial lure and give it an honest shot. Artificial Lures Help You Cover More Water This was the big aha moment. Once he started throwing the paddletail, he could cast farther, retrieve faster, and work more water around the boat. And instead of constantly replacing stolen shrimp, he could just keep fishing. Before long, he was actually catching more trout than the anglers still using live bait. That ability to cover water is one of the biggest advantages of artificial lures. Luke learned the same lesson years ago. He used to spend huge chunks of fishing trips searching for live bait before he would even start fishing. Once he was forced to use artificial lures from a kayak, he quickly realized how much more water he could cover and how much faster he could learn where the fish were actually holding. That’s the bigger lesson here. Artificial lures aren’t just about replacing live bait. They can help you become better at finding fish . You DON’T Need A Tackle Box Full Of Lures This is where a lot of anglers make things harder than they need to. If you’re just getting started with artificial lures, keep it VERY simple. Start with: A 3.5-inch paddletail and A 3.5-inch shrimp imitation That’s it. If you’re seeing baitfish, a paddletail is an easy choice. If shrimp seem to be the main forage, such as when you’re seeing wading birds feeding on them, go with the shrimp imitation. And if you just want one lure that can handle a huge variety of situations, the Slam Shady 2.0 is a great place to start. You can always get more specialized later. First, build confidence with a couple of proven lures. Final Thoughts The coolest part of this story wasn’t simply that an artificial lure caught fish. It was what happened afterward. This angler no longer felt like he HAD to find live bait before he could go fishing. No worrying about the marina selling out of shrimp. No spending the morning throwing a cast net. No livewell required. He knew he could grab a couple of lures, hit the water, and still have confidence that he could catch fish. That’s a pretty big change. And if you’ve been hesitant to try artificial lures yourself, you don’t have to quit live bait overnight. Bring a paddletail or shrimp lure to a spot where you KNOW fish are feeding… And see what happens. Do you still primarily fish with live bait, or have you already made the switch to artificial lures? Let me know in the comments! FAQ Are artificial lures better than live bait for inshore fishing? Not necessarily in every situation. One major advantage of artificial lures is that they allow you to cast repeatedly, cover more water, and search for actively feeding fish without constantly replacing bait. What artificial lure should a beginner start with? Keep it simple with a 3.5-inch paddletail and a 3.5-inch shrimp imitation. Those two lure styles can cover a huge range of inshore fishing situations. When should I throw a paddletail instead of a shrimp lure? If you’re seeing baitfish, start with the paddletail. If shrimp appear to be the primary forage, a shrimp imitation is an easy choice. Do these lures only work in Florida? No. These same lure styles have been successfully used for inshore species throughout the Southeast, including Louisiana, Texas, and Virginia.

items.title: STOP Making These Travel Rod Mistakes
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Travel rods are one of those pieces of fishing gear that make you wonder why you didn’t get one sooner. They’re easy to throw in the truck, pack for a vacation, stash on a boat, or bring anywhere a full-size rod would be a pain. And a GOOD travel rod
items.search_text: Travel rods are one of those pieces of fishing gear that make you wonder why you didn’t get one sooner. They’re easy to throw in the truck, pack for a vacation, stash on a boat, or bring anywhere a full-size rod would be a pain. And a GOOD travel rod can still give you the feel and performance you expect from a serious fishing setup. That convenience is exactly why I love them. But there are a few simple things every travel rod owner should know to keep their rod performing properly and lasting for years. In the video below, I’ll show you the biggest travel rod mistakes to avoid, plus the right way to assemble, clean, break down, and store your rod so it’s ALWAYS ready for the next trip. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. The Slam Stick Traveler featured in this video is 50% OFF MSRP for Salt Strong Insiders during Fish Strong Week. If you’ve been wanting a full-performance inshore rod that breaks down for easy travel and storage, this is the week to grab one. This offer ends September 8th, 2026, so don’t wait! [Click Here To Get The Traveler Deal Before It’s Gone.] Featured Gear Rod: Slam Stick Traveler Why Travel Rods Are So Useful A good travel rod gives you a ton of flexibility without forcing you to give up the performance you expect from a quality fishing rod. You can keep one in the truck, pack it for a flight, stash it in a small boat, or bring it along anywhere a full-length rod would be inconvenient. That means more opportunities to fish without having to plan your entire day around hauling a full-size setup. And when the rod is built well, you can still get the crisp feel, casting performance, and fish-fighting ability you want. That’s what makes travel rods so useful. They give you convenience without turning your fishing setup into a compromise. The key is knowing a few simple things about how to assemble, clean, and store them so they keep performing the way they should. How To Keep A Travel Rod Performing Like It Should Most travel rod problems come down to the connection points between the rod sections. When putting the rod together, the sections should be snug, but you do not need to force them together as tightly as possible. Push the sections together until they feel secure, then give them a slight twist. You also want to make sure the rod guides are lined up properly with the reel. If the sections are too loose, they can twist while casting or even separate. That can throw the guides out of alignment and hurt your casting performance. A quick check before you start fishing can prevent a lot of frustration later. Clean, Dry, And Break It Down After Every Trip This is especially important if you fish saltwater. Salt, sand, dirt, and moisture can collect around the ferrules and connection points. After each trip, rinse the rod with fresh water, wipe down the ferrules, and let everything dry completely before storing it. And one of the biggest advantages of a travel rod is that it can be broken down. Use that advantage. Leaving the rod assembled for days, weeks, or months can allow salt and debris to build up inside the joints, which can eventually cause the sections to seize together. Breaking it down regularly keeps those connection points cleaner and makes sure the rod is ready to pack up whenever you need it. Protect The Parts That Keep Your Rod Fishing Right A travel rod is easy to break down, but you still want to handle it correctly when taking the sections apart. Never grab the guides and pull. Instead, hold the rod blank itself, then gently twist and pull the sections apart. The same goes for putting the rod together. Apply pressure to the blank, not the guides. You also want to avoid using the guides as hook keepers. That extra pressure can bend a guide or damage the insert. Use the rod’s built-in hook keeper whenever possible. And don’t reel your lure all the way into the rod tip. Repeated impacts from a jighead, lure, or weight can damage the top guide or even break the tip. These are all small habits, but together they help keep your rod feeling right and fishing the way it should. Final Thoughts Travel rods are one of the easiest ways to make fishing more convenient. They’re easy to transport, easy to store, and give you a lot more flexibility when space is limited. And if you take care of the connection points, guides, and rod tip, they can stay ready to fish trip after trip. A few simple habits can make a big difference in how long your rod lasts and how well it performs. Do you use a travel rod regularly, or are you thinking about adding one to your setup? Let us know in the comments! Travel Rod FAQ Are travel fishing rods worth it? Yes. Travel rods are a great option if you want a rod that is easier to transport, pack, or store without giving up the convenience of having a full fishing setup ready to go. Do travel rods perform as well as one-piece rods? A quality travel rod can still offer excellent casting performance, sensitivity, and fish-fighting ability. The biggest difference is the added convenience of being able to break the rod down for transport and storage. How tight should the sections on a travel fishing rod be? The sections should be firmly seated and snug, but you generally do not need to force them together as tightly as possible. Insert the section until secure and use a slight twisting motion to help lock it in place. Why do fishing rod sections get stuck together? Salt, sand, dirt, moisture, and long-term storage while assembled can cause rod sections to seize together. Cleaning and drying the ferrules after fishing and storing the rod broken down can help prevent this. Should you leave a travel rod assembled? It’s better to break a travel rod down after fishing, especially if it has been exposed to saltwater. This helps keep the ferrules clean and reduces the chance of the sections becoming stuck together. Can you pull a fishing rod apart by the guides? No. Grab the rod blank itself when separating the sections. Pulling or pushing on the guides can bend or damage them. Can reeling a lure into the rod tip damage a fishing rod? Yes. Allowing a lure, jighead, sinker, or other terminal tackle to repeatedly strike the rod tip can damage the top guide or potentially break the rod tip.

items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Learn when to switch fall fishing lures! Coach Tony shares how to adjust your lure strategy based on feeding activity and water depth.
items.search_text:
Fall is one of my FAVORITE times to get out on the water! But here’s the deal… As the water cools and baitfish start moving around, the fish aren’t always going to be feeding the same way. And if you’re throwing the wrong lure at the wrong time, you could be missing out on some BIG fish! In this quick video, I’ll show you how I adjust my lure strategy in the fall to stay on the bite! ﻿
Featured Gear Moonwalker Topwater Plug Skinny Lipper XL Prawn Shrimp Lure 5″ Mulligan Bomber Paddletail Ultimate Fall Lure Bundle (Free Skinny Lipper XL) 1. Start With WHERE the Fish Are Feeding Here’s something I always keep in mind when I’m fishing in the fall… Just because fish are feeding doesn’t mean they’re feeding on top! During those cooler early mornings, I love starting with a topwater like the Moonwalker when fish are actively feeding near the surface. There’s nothing quite like watching a redfish or trout come up and absolutely CRUSH a topwater plug! But what happens when you’re seeing baitfish getting chased and the topwater isn’t getting any love? That’s when I’ll switch things up. The Skinny Lipper XL is a great option when fish are chasing bigger baitfish just BELOW the surface. It creates plenty of action and commotion without requiring fish to come all the way up to eat. The lesson here? Don’t force a topwater bite if the fish are telling you something different! Pay attention to where the action is happening and adjust your presentation accordingly. 2. Know WHEN to Slow Things Down Not every fall fishing trip is going to be nonstop explosions and aggressive strikes. Sometimes the fish just aren’t in the mood to chase. And that’s when I see anglers make a BIG mistake… They keep working the same fast-moving lures, hoping something will eventually bite. Instead, I’ll slow things down and give those fish an easier meal. A shrimp imitation like the Prawn is one of my favorite ways to do that. I’ll work it around areas like: Grass edges Structure Deeper pockets Areas where fish can sit and ambush prey The goal is to keep that lure in the strike zone and give less aggressive fish an opportunity to eat. Remember, you don’t always need to change spots when the bite slows down. Sometimes you just need to change your presentation! 3. Match the Bigger Baitfish One of the things I love about fall fishing is the opportunity to target BIGGER predators feeding on larger baitfish. But just because there’s bigger bait around doesn’t mean you should blindly throw the biggest lure you’ve got. You still need to think about WHERE those fish are feeding. When I’m targeting bigger fish along drop-offs and deeper feeding zones, the 5″ Mulligan Bomber is a great option. That larger paddletail profile helps imitate bigger baitfish, and I can adjust how I’m fishing it based on the situation. And here’s something you don’t want to overlook… That same lure can work in the shallows, too! Rig it weedless, and you can fish shallower areas where predators may be hunting larger baitfish. The important thing is matching both the baitfish AND the depth where predators are feeding. Final Thoughts If there’s ONE thing I want you to take away from this quick lesson, it’s this: Fall fishing success isn’t just about WHAT lure you’re throwing. It’s knowing WHEN and WHERE to throw it! Pay attention to the baitfish, watch how predators are feeding, and don’t be afraid to switch things up. Those little adjustments can make a BIG difference in how many fish you catch! Now I’ve got a question for you… What’s your confidence lure when the fall bite starts heating up? Let me know in the comments below! Frequently Asked Questions What’s the best lure to throw for fall inshore fishing? There’s no single lure that’s best for every situation! I like having options that cover different depths and feeding behaviors. Topwaters, subsurface plugs, shrimp imitations, and paddletails all have their place depending on what the fish are doing. When should I switch from topwater to a subsurface lure? If I’m seeing fish chasing bait near the surface but they’re not committing to a topwater, that’s a good sign to try something just below the surface. A lure like the Skinny Lipper XL can be a great adjustment. What should I throw when fish aren’t aggressively feeding? That’s when I like slowing things down with a shrimp imitation like the Prawn. Working it around grass edges, structure, and deeper pockets can be effective when fish aren’t willing to chase faster-moving lures. Are bigger lures better for fall fishing? Not always! When larger baitfish are present, a bigger profile like the 5″ Mulligan Bomber can be a great match. But the key is still matching the forage and fishing the right depth, not simply throwing the biggest lure in your box.

items.search_text: How many fish do you expect to catch before a soft plastic gets absolutely DESTROYED? Five? Ten? How about 40+ fish on the SAME lure?! Luke has been putting the new Prawn XT through the wringer with snapper, grouper, flounder, trout, and more… And this thing just keeps catching fish! But durability is only part of the story. There are some BIG differences between the Prawn XT and original Prawn, plus a few rigging tricks you’ll want to know. Check it all out below! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear Lure 1: Prawn XT OG Lure 2: Prawn XT JR Rigging 1 (OG Deep Water): 4/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jig 1/2 oz Rigging 2 (JR): 2/0 Hoss Roundeye Jighead 1/4 oz Rigging 3 (Shallow OG): 4/0 Hoss Weedless Football 3/16 oz Rigging 4 (Shallow JR): 3/0 Hoss Weedless Football 3/16 oz What Makes The Prawn XT Different From The Original Prawn? The biggest difference is durability. The original Prawn is made from Plastisol and is easier to rig. The Prawn XT uses a much tougher material that can withstand significantly more abuse from fish. And no, the original Prawn isn’t going away. We’ll continue offering it as long as our members want it. The tradeoff with the Prawn XT is that the tougher material can be more difficult to rig, especially on a Hoss Helix Hook. But once you get it rigged correctly, it stays put incredibly well. How Do You Rig The Prawn XT? The Prawn XT can be rigged on traditional exposed jigheads, weedless jigheads, and Hoss Helix Hooks. When fishing deeper rocks and structure, Luke has been using a weedless Hoss Football Jighead. The key is choosing the lightest jighead that still gets your lure to the bottom . For example, Luke used a 1/2-ounce jighead around a bridge in 15 to 30 feet of water with strong current. When fishing roughly 35 feet of water around the Tampa Bay shipping channel, he went as heavy as 3/4 ounce. In shallower water with less current, a 1/4-ounce jighead may be plenty. How Do You Fish A Shrimp Lure Around Deep Structure? Get the lure down to the bottom and start bouncing it through the structure. Luke specifically targets rocks, ledges, bridges, and other hard structure where species such as mangrove snapper, grouper, and flounder commonly hold. Pay close attention to what you feel through your rod. When you start feeling rocks, make another cast to that area. Those little pieces of structure can concentrate predators, especially during the summer when many fish move toward deeper water. And this is where a weedless Prawn XT really shines. You can work it through some nasty structure without constantly getting snagged or having fish destroy your lure. What Leader And Line Should You Use For Deep-Water Fishing? For the deep structure shown in this video, Luke used: 30 lb mono leader Approximately 4 feet of leader 20 lb braid Prawn XT OG 4/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jig 1/2 oz The longer leader provided extra protection around tall rocks and ledges. Luke still had to retie when the mono became chafed, so make sure you regularly check your leader when fishing around heavy structure. Final Thoughts The Prawn XT costs more per lure and takes a little more effort to rig than a traditional soft plastic. But when one lure can survive dozens of fish, including lure-destroying species such as snapper and grouper, that tradeoff starts looking pretty darn good. Luke has already caught more than 40 fish on a single Prawn XT, and we’re going to keep pushing these things to see just how much abuse they can handle. Now we want to hear from you! What’s the most fish you’ve ever caught on ONE soft plastic? Let us know down in the comments!

items.title: Plug vs Paddletail: The Distance Difference Shocked Me
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: When fish are feeding aggressively, the ability to cover more water without spooking fish can make a huge difference in your catch results. And one of the easiest ways to do that is by casting farther. But that raises a couple of interesting question
items.search_text: When fish are feeding aggressively, the ability to cover more water without spooking fish can make a huge difference in your catch results. And one of the easiest ways to do that is by casting farther. But that raises a couple of interesting questions… 1. Which lure actually casts farther: a plug or a paddletail? 2. How much farther exactly can one outcast the other? I’ve noticed differences over the years, but I wanted real numbers. So I decided to put the longest-casting 4-inch plug I’ve ever used against the longest-casting 4-inch paddletail I’ve ever used in a head-to-head casting distance test. Note: I weighted the paddletail with a jighead to make sure they were equal in weight. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine 7’6″ Medium Power Reel: Otis 2500 Line: 10 lb J-Braid 8 Grand Lure 1: Skinny Lipper Lure 2: Mulligan Paddletail rigged on 3/0 Weedless Round Eye Jig Head 3/16 oz Luke 3: Mulligan Paddletail rigged on 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/8 oz The Test For this experiment, I compared: Skinny Lipper (4″) Mulligan Paddletail (4″) rigged on a 3/0 Weedless Round Eye Jig Head 3/16 oz Mulligan Paddletail (4″) rigged on a 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/8 oz The Results Here’s how the tests ended up after averaging out the distances they traveled: Mulligan On Hoss Helix Hook: 105 feet Mulligan On Weedless Round Eye Jig Head: 118 feet Skinny Lipper: 135 feet The shortest cast with the Skinny Lipper was still longer than the best cast from any of the paddletail setups. In other words… The plug wasn’t just winning… it was dominating. Why Does It Matter? An extra 15 to 30 feet may not sound like much at first. But over the course of a fishing trip, that can be significant (especially if you’re fishing next to someone who can’t cast as far). To put it in perspective, an extra 30 feet per cast means you’ll cover an additional football field of water every 10 casts. Longer casts allow you to: Cover more water Reach fish before they see the boat Present lures farther away from potential disturbances Increase your chances of connecting with larger, more cautious fish That’s especially important when targeting bigger redfish, snook, trout, and flounder in shallow water. Why The Plug Casts Farther The biggest factor is design. The Skinny Lipper features weight-shift technology that moves weight toward the rear of the lure during the cast. That helps it fly more efficiently and maintain momentum throughout the cast. The paddletail setups cast well, but they simply can’t match the aerodynamic advantages built into a lure specifically designed for maximum casting distance. My Biggest Takeaway I expected the plug to cast farther. I didn’t expect the difference to be this large. For situations where fish are actively feeding and lure selection isn’t the deciding factor, a long-casting plug can help you cover water more efficiently and keep your bait in front of more fish throughout the day. That’s one of the reasons I’ve been reaching for plugs more often lately. Not only am I covering more water, but I’m also getting my lure farther away from the boat where bigger fish are often more comfortable feeding. Final Thoughts If your goal is to maximize casting distance and cover as much water as possible, this test showed a clear winner. The paddletail performed well, but the Skinny Lipper consistently delivered the longest casts and the greatest water coverage. Have another lure you’d like to see tested? Let us know in the comments below.

But these calm and hot weather days can still be very productive as long as we make the necessary adjustments. First, we need to be very mindful of any noise or vibration we emit while approaching our target spots… that’s crucial. But we also need to be very selective in which lures we decide to throw. items.excerpt: Summer can be a great time of year to target big reds. And if you’re using artificial lures, one continues to earn a permanent spot in my tackle bag… The Prawn Original. The key isn’t necessarily the lure itself. It’s rigging it correctly for the typ
items.search_text: Summer can be a great time of year to target big reds. And if you’re using artificial lures, one continues to earn a permanent spot in my tackle bag… The Prawn Original. The key isn’t necessarily the lure itself. It’s rigging it correctly for the type of water you’re fishing. In this video, I’ll show you the three ways I rig a Prawn for redfish and when to use each. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Looking to stock up before your next trip? We’ve put together some great deals on tackle, gear, and bundles as part of our Summer Slam Savings Event. Check them out here. Featured Gear: Rod 1: Slot Machine Medium Heavy Power Rod 2: Slot Machine Medium Reel 1: 3000 Diawa BG MQ Reel 2: Otis 2500 Lure: Prawn Original Hook 1: Hoss Helix Hook 3/0 1/16oz Hook 2: Hoss Football Jighead Hook 3: Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead Rattles: Battle Rattles Scent: Pro Cure Shrimp & Inshore Saltwater Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 15lb – 40lb Mono Leader Free Rigging Guide Cheat Sheet Depth control with soft plastic lures is extremely important, so we created a helpful single-page guide that shows you exactly which jighead to pair with the given lure for certain depth ranges. Click here to see the Rigging Guide When To Use A Football Jighead? If I’m fishing deeper water with a relatively clean bottom, I’ll usually rig the Prawn on a HOSS Football Jighead. This setup excels in: Channels Drop-offs Deep potholes Current-swept areas The football head helps keep the lure near the bottom where redfish often feed, while also allowing you to feel the lure better as it moves across the structure. As a general rule, this is my preferred setup anytime I’m fishing water deeper than about four feet and I’m not worried about getting snagged. When To Use A Weedless Jighead? Many of the best redfish spots often include oysters, rocks, dock pilings, and other structure that can quickly eat up traditional jigheads. That’s where the HOSS Weedless Round Eye Jighead shines. This setup allows me to fish the same deeper water while greatly reducing the chances of hanging up on structure. I typically choose this option when: Fishing oyster bars Working rocky shorelines Targeting fish around docks Fishing areas with scattered debris You still get the benefit of a weighted presentation, but with much better snag resistance. My Favorite Shallow Water Setup When I’m fishing shallow flats, grass, potholes, or shallow oyster bars, I usually switch to a HOSS Helix Weedless Hook. This setup allows the Prawn to move naturally through areas where redfish commonly feed while helping avoid grass and other obstacles. For water four feet deep or less, this is often my go-to choice. I’ll adjust the weight depending on the current and depth, but the weedless design helps keep the lure fishing clean throughout the retrieve. Should You Add Rattles And Scent? Sometimes. When I’m fishing deeper water or dealing with dirty water conditions, I like adding a few extra attractors. Battle Rattles can be inserted directly into the body of the Prawn. These rattles create additional sound that can help fish locate the lure when visibility is limited. I’ll also frequently add Pro-Cure Shrimp Scent. Redfish already expect shrimp to smell like shrimp, so adding scent can help make the presentation even more convincing. Neither of these additions are mandatory, but they can absolutely help in tougher conditions. Rod, Reel, And Line Setup My tackle setup changes slightly depending on where I’m fishing. For deeper water and heavier structure, I prefer a medium-heavy rod like the Slot Machine Rod. The additional power helps: Feel the lure better Maintain bottom contact Pull fish away from structure For open flats and less demanding situations, I’ll often use a medium-power rod. As for line, I typically use: 10-15 lb braid in open water 20-30 lb braid around structure 15-25 lb leader in open water 30-40 lb leader around heavy cover A 2500 to 3000 size spinning reel handles most redfish situations perfectly. Finding The Right Spot Still Matters Most The Prawn is a proven redfish lure. The rigging matters. The tackle matters. But none of it matters if you’re fishing in the wrong place. Big redfish are often surprisingly predictable when you understand where they position based on tides, depth, bait, and structure. That’s why spending time learning fish behavior and finding productive areas will usually make a bigger difference than switching lures. Final Thoughts The Prawn is one of the most versatile redfish lures I use. By matching your rigging to the depth and structure you’re fishing, you’ll spend more time presenting the lure effectively and less time dealing with snags. If you’re looking for a reliable artificial shrimp presentation for redfish, this setup is hard to beat.

items.title: Mistakes That Spook Fish Before You Even Make a Cast
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Quick question… Have you ever wondered if YOU’RE the reason that perfect-looking spot never produces? Because 2 incredibly common mistakes kill your chances before your lure even hits the water. Watch the video below to see if you’re guilty of them…
items.search_text: Quick question… Have you ever wondered if YOU’RE the reason that perfect-looking spot never produces? Because 2 incredibly common mistakes kill your chances before your lure even hits the water. Watch the video below to see if you’re guilty of them… Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Mistake #1: Running Straight to the Shoreline When I first transitioned from bass fishing to inshore saltwater fishing, I made the same mistake almost every trip. I’d find a promising shoreline, run straight to it, fish every inch of it, and leave wondering why I never got a bite. The problem wasn’t the shoreline. The problem was how I approached it. Many anglers assume the fish are tight against the bank, but that’s often not the case. Depending on the tide, wind, water temperature, and where the bait is holding, fish may be 20, 30, or even 50 yards off the shoreline. By running directly to the bank, you may be parking your boat right on top of the fish before you ever make your first cast. Fish Your Way Into the Spot Instead of driving straight to the shoreline, stop well short of your destination. As a general starting point, I like to shut down at least 75 yards away in shallow water. The exact distance depends on water depth and conditions, but the goal is always the same: Give yourself time to observe before you move in. Those extra 20 to 30 seconds can completely change your game plan. Look for: Schools of baitfish Mullet activity Pinfish flashes Nervous water Fish wakes or pushes Current seams Oyster bars Potholes Changes in bottom depth These clues tell you where predators are most likely positioned. Rather than guessing where the fish are, you’re letting the conditions show you. Remember: Fish Move One mistake many anglers make is assuming fish will always be in the same place. A shoreline that held fish last week may be empty today. Why? Because conditions changed. On grass flats with significant tidal movement, fish constantly reposition themselves based on water depth, bait movement, and available cover. For example, a flat may have: Very shallow water near shore An intermediate depth zone A deeper edge farther out At different stages of the tide, fish may be using any one of those three areas. That’s why it’s so important to fish your way into a spot instead of assuming they’re already on the shoreline. Mistake #2: Making Too Much Noise Even if you stop far enough away, you can still ruin the opportunity if you approach too loudly. I see this happen all the time. Anglers shut down the outboard just a short distance away, drop the trolling motor into the water, crank it up on high speed, slam hatches, stomp around the deck, and start casting. Sometimes they’ll still catch fish. But many times, they’ve already warned every cautious fish on the flat that something isn’t right. The shallower the water, the more important it becomes to stay quiet. Think Like You’re Hunting One mindset shift can make a huge difference. Don’t think of yourself as driving to a fishing spot. Think of yourself as trying to sneak up on a wild animal. Imagine trying to walk within bow range of a deer. You wouldn’t stomp through the woods, slam doors, or yell to your buddy. You’d move slowly. You’d stay quiet. You’d pay attention to every little detail. That’s exactly how you should approach shallow-water fish. They’re not sitting around trying to solve puzzles. They’re simply reacting to anything that feels out of place. After spending their entire lives avoiding sharks, dolphins, birds, and anglers, they’ve become incredibly cautious. Any unusual sound or disturbance can be enough to send them somewhere else. Small Changes Lead to More Fish Successful fishing isn’t just about finding good spots. It’s about arriving at those spots without announcing your presence. The next time you’re approaching a shallow flat, remember these simple steps: Shut down early. Slow down. Observe before you move in. Fish your way into the area. Keep your approach as quiet as possible. Those few extra seconds of patience can be the difference between fishing water that looks perfect and actually presenting your lure to willing fish. Sometimes the fish were there all along. The only difference is whether you gave yourself the chance to catch them. Final Thoughts Most anglers spend hours planning a fishing trip. They check the tides, study the weather, rig the right lures, and pick what looks like the perfect spot. But all of that preparation can be wasted if you make the wrong approach. Before you ever fire your first cast, ask yourself: Am I stopping far enough away? Have I taken a few seconds to observe what’s happening? Am I fishing my way into the area instead of running straight to the shoreline? Am I keeping my approach as quiet as possible? Those simple habits won’t guarantee a fish every trip, but they’ll make sure you’re giving yourself the best chance to catch the fish that are already there. Because sometimes the difference between a slow day and a great one isn’t finding a better spot… It’s approaching the right spot the right way. Be honest… what’s one thing you see other anglers do that instantly makes you think, “They’re about to spook every fish”?
items.content_headings: Mistake #1: Running Straight to the Shoreline Fish Your Way Into the Spot Remember: Fish Move Mistake #2: Making Too Much Noise Think Like You’re Hunting Small Changes Lead to More Fish Final Thoughts

The first thing you’ll notice about the Wake Mullet is the oversized lip. That lip creates a tremendous amount of vibration and action without requiring any special retrieve. Simply cast it out and reel it back in. The lure does the work for you. That’s one of the reasons it has become one of my favorite shallow-water plugs. It covers water efficiently, stays easy to fish, and consistently gets the attention of nearby predators in churned-up water. When The Wake Mullet Really Shines Not every lure excels in every situation. One of the things I like most about the Wake Mullet is how effective it can be when water clarity isn’t perfect. The combination of vibration, wobble, and water displacement helps fish locate it even when visibility is reduced. Redfish, snook, and trout all rely heavily on their lateral lines to detect movement in the water, and this lure creates a strong presence that can help trigger reaction strikes. The Results Have Been Impressive The Wake Mullet was originally released through our Tackle Tester Program, and the feedback started rolling in almost immediately. Members have been catching quality redfish, snook, trout, jack crevalle, and even largemouth bass on it. One of my favorite things has been seeing how quickly anglers gain confidence with the lure. There’s very little learning curve. Cast it out, keep it moving, and let the lure do what it was designed to do. Final Thoughts The Wake Mullet has been producing for redfish, snook, trout, and a variety of other species, all while being one of the easiest lures in my arsenal to fish effectively. If you’re looking for a shallow-water plug that creates plenty of vibration, covers water efficiently, and flat-out catches fish, it’s definitely worth checking out. items.title: Is This The Best Rod for Wade Fishing? (Feat Wader Dave)
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: When it comes to wade fishing, most anglers spend a lot of time thinking about lures, reels, braid, and leader. But one of the biggest factors in your success is something many anglers overlook: Your fishing rod. And after years of testing rods from
items.search_text: When it comes to wade fishing, most anglers spend a lot of time thinking about lures, reels, braid, and leader. But one of the biggest factors in your success is something many anglers overlook: Your fishing rod. And after years of testing rods from nearly every major manufacturer, Wader Dave recently made a surprising statement… A rod he didn’t expect to become his favorite has officially earned that title. In this podcast, Dave shares what made this rod stand out, why casting distance matters so much when targeting redfish, trout, snook, and flounder, and the features he believes make the biggest difference during a long day of wade fishing. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod 1: Slot Machine Medium Rod 2: Slam Stick Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Why Casting Distance Matters For Wade Fishing One of the biggest advantages of wade fishing is stealth. Without a boat nearby, you’re able to approach fish quietly and naturally. But that advantage disappears quickly if you can’t reach fish before they know you’re there. Every extra foot of casting distance allows you to cover more water, stay farther away from fish, and present your lure in less pressured areas. That may not sound like much. But over the course of a trip, an extra 10 feet per cast can add up to hundreds of yards of additional water covered. When you’re making cast after cast across grass flats, potholes, sandbars, mangrove shorelines, or surf zones, those small gains become significant. For anglers targeting spooky redfish or trout in shallow water, distance can often be the difference between a hookup and a blown opportunity. The Features That Matter Most In A Wade Fishing Rod While distance is important, it’s only one piece of the puzzle. According to Wader Dave, the best wade fishing rods share several key characteristics: Lightweight Construction Wade fishermen make a lot of casts. Whether you’re spending three hours on a flat or six hours covering miles of shoreline, rod weight matters. A lighter rod reduces fatigue and makes it easier to maintain accuracy throughout the day. Sensitivity Feeling subtle changes in bottom composition can help you locate productive areas. Shell. Sand. Grass. Mud. A sensitive rod helps you understand what’s happening beneath the surface and detect subtle strikes that might otherwise go unnoticed. Accuracy Distance is great. But accuracy puts fish in the boat. Whether you’re sight-casting to a tailing redfish or skipping a lure under mangroves, placing a lure exactly where it needs to be is often more important than simply casting farther. Proper Balance A balanced rod and reel combo feels almost weightless in your hands. When the setup isn’t fighting against you all day, fishing becomes easier, more enjoyable, and ultimately more productive. Why Rod Length Plays Such A Big Role Many anglers automatically assume longer equals farther. While that can be true, rod design matters just as much as overall length. A properly designed 7’6″ rod gives anglers more casting leverage and increased tip speed, which can translate into greater casting distance with less effort. The key is finding a rod that’s long enough to maximize performance without becoming cumbersome during a full day of fishing. For many inshore anglers, the 7’6″ medium-power spinning rod continues to be one of the most versatile options available. It offers enough backbone for larger fish while still handling lighter lures commonly used for redfish, trout, and snook. Durability Still Matters One thing often overlooked when discussing high-performance rods is durability. Lighter rods are typically built using more advanced materials and thinner blanks designed for maximum sensitivity and casting performance. That means proper handling becomes even more important. The biggest mistake many anglers make is “high-sticking” a fish. This occurs when the rod is raised beyond a safe fighting angle, placing excessive pressure on the upper section of the blank. Instead, keep pressure on the lower portion of the rod and let the drag do its job. When handled correctly, today’s high-performance rods are more than capable of landing oversized redfish, snook, and even larger species. The Best Rod Is The One That Fits Your Fishing Style At the end of the day, there isn’t a single perfect rod for every angler. Beginners may prioritize durability. Tournament anglers may prioritize sensitivity. Wade fishermen often place a premium on casting distance, weight, and comfort. The important thing is understanding what matters most for the type of fishing you do. If you spend most of your time wading shallow flats, covering long stretches of shoreline, or targeting fish in clear water, investing in a lightweight, sensitive rod can have a bigger impact on your results than almost any lure you’ll tie on. Final Thoughts The best wade fishing rod isn’t necessarily the most expensive one. It’s the rod that helps you cast farther, fish longer, stay comfortable, and put your lure where the fish actually are. And when you’re making hundreds of casts in a day, those advantages add up quickly. Watch the full podcast above to hear Wader Dave and Luke break down exactly what they look for in a wade fishing rod and why those details matter on the water.

items.title: Introducing the Prawn XT: Our Toughest Shrimp Lure Yet
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Soft plastic shrimp lures catch an incredible number of fish. Unfortunately, fish also know how to tear them up. Pinfish swipe the tail. Snapper bite off pieces. Grouper drag them through reefs. Sometimes, one good bite is all it takes to ruin a lure
items.search_text: Soft plastic shrimp lures catch an incredible number of fish. Unfortunately, fish also know how to tear them up. Pinfish swipe the tail. Snapper bite off pieces. Grouper drag them through reefs. Sometimes, one good bite is all it takes to ruin a lure. That is exactly why I am so excited to introduce the new Prawn XT OG (4.3″) and Prawn XT Jr. (3.5″) . Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. GET THE PRAWN XT OG (4.3″) GET THE PRAWN XT JR. (3.5″) Rigging Options For 4.3″ OG Size: 4/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jighead (Recommended) 4/0 Roundeye Jighead 4/0 Football Jighead Rigging Options For 3.5: Jr. Size: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jighead (Recommended) 2/0 Roundeye Jighead 2/0 Football Jighead Weight Selections For Depth Coverage: 3/16th oz: 3 to 7 ft 1/4 oz: 5 to 10 ft 1/2 oz: 10 to 25 ft 3/4 oz: 20 to 50 ft 1 oz: 50 to 90 ft 2 oz: 80 to 150 ft Note: The depth ranges listed above assume low to moderate current flow… if the current is moving fast, you’ll need to go up a weight level or two to compensate for the added drag on the line. What Makes the Prawn XT Different? The Prawn XT is made from the toughest soft plastic material we have ever used in a shrimp lure. However, durability alone would not mean much if the lure did not move naturally in the water. Fortunately, this new material is still flexible enough to give the Prawn XT the lifelike action that made the original Prawn so effective. It glides naturally as it falls, maintains a realistic shrimp profile, and can be retrieved in several different ways. The streamlined body also helps it cast well. There are no unnecessary appendages catching the wind or interfering with its movement through the water. Most importantly, you can fish it around the structure where shrimp, and the predators that eat them, naturally live. The Prawn XT can be rigged weedless for fishing around rocks, oysters, grass, docks, bridge pilings, and reefs. It can also be rigged on a traditional jighead when fishing open water. That combination of natural action, versatility, and extreme durability allows the Prawn XT to fish almost like a hard plug. Instead of stopping to replace a damaged soft plastic every few fish, you can keep casting while the bite is hot. Two Sizes: Prawn XT OG and Prawn XT Jr. The Prawn XT is currently available in two proven sizes: Prawn XT OG: Three lures per pack Prawn XT Jr: Four lures per pack Both match the established Prawn sizes that anglers have already been using successfully for years. The OG is the larger option. It is ideal when fish are feeding on full size shrimp, when you want a larger profile, or when you are targeting bigger fish. The Jr. gives fish a smaller and more compact target. It is a great choice when the available shrimp and bait are smaller, the fish are being selective, or you simply want to downsize your presentation. We also plan to introduce an even smaller Prawn XT later this year. The Best Way to Rig the Prawn XT Our preferred setup is a weedless football jighead . The Prawn XT OG pairs well with a 4/0 hook , while the Prawn XT Jr. pairs well with a 3/0 hook . Here is how to rig it correctly. Step 1: Insert the Hook Through the Center Start by inserting the hook point directly into the center of the lure’s head. Run it approximately half an inch into the body before bringing the point out through the middle. Keeping the hook centered helps the finished lure sit straight and move naturally in the water. Step 2: Push the Lure Up to the Weight Thread the Prawn XT down the hook. As you apply pressure, the lure will naturally turn around the bend of the hook. Continue pushing until the head of the lure sits firmly against the weight. We prefer to pin the lure’s head directly against the jighead. This creates a clean profile, helps the lure skip, and gives it a more natural appearance in the water. Step 3: Mark the Hook’s Natural Entry Point Hold the lure straight alongside the hook to see where the hook point naturally meets the body. Pinch that location with your thumb. This marks the spot where the hook should pass through the lure. Step 4: Rotate and Insert the Hook Turn the lure approximately 90 degrees and guide the hook point through the marked location. When rigged correctly, the lure should sit straight without being stretched, compressed, or bent to one side. This gives you a weedless shrimp presentation that can be bounced around rocks, oysters, grass, pilings, and other structure with a much lower risk of snagging. One Important Hookset Tip The Prawn XT material is tougher and slightly stickier than a traditional soft plastic. That helps the lure remain securely attached to the hook and keeps the presentation weedless. However, it also means the hook may require a little more force to break free from the lure during a strike. There are two easy ways to compensate: Put a little more authority into your hookset. Gently loosen the material around the hook point before fishing. You do not need to expose the hook completely. Simply make sure the lure can slide down the hook quickly when a fish strikes. That small adjustment will help improve your hookups while maintaining the weedless benefits of the rig. Can You Use the Prawn XT on a Traditional Jighead? Yes. The Prawn XT can be rigged on football, round eye, and other traditional jigheads. The tougher material just requires more effort to push over a standard bait keeper. If the keeper is especially large, you can carefully flatten it with pliers before rigging the lure. This makes it easier to slide the material into place. Start the hook directly through the center of the Prawn XT. As you feed the lure onto the hook, gradually angle the point toward the top of the lure. Before bringing the hook point out, check that you have threaded enough material onto the hook. The front of the lure should begin angling back toward the jighead. Push the hook point through at that location. Then, work the lure over the keeper and up to the head. It takes more effort than rigging a traditional soft plastic, but once the Prawn XT is in place, it holds extremely well. We also have new jigheads in development with clean hook shanks and no traditional bait keepers. These will make rigging the Prawn XT on an exposed hook setup much easier. When Should You Fish It Weedless? The weedless football jighead is our top recommendation when fishing around: Rocks Oyster bars Grass Dock pilings Bridge structure Nearshore reefs Offshore structure These are the areas where many of the best fish hold. They are also the places where an exposed hook is most likely to snag. Heavier weedless football jigheads can be extremely effective for nearshore and offshore fishing. This setup has already produced grouper, mangrove snapper, cobia, snook, and big redfish. When fishing open flats, beaches, or other relatively snag free areas, a traditional exposed hook jighead can give you an advantage. The key is matching the rigging style to the structure you are fishing. How to Retrieve the Prawn XT You do not need a complicated retrieve to catch fish with this lure. In most situations, the best approach is to bounce the Prawn XT along the bottom and allow it to glide back down after each movement. That falling glide is often when the strike happens. A steady retrieve can also work, especially when fish are actively feeding or holding higher in the water column. Experiment with your speed and cadence throughout the trip. Let the fish show you whether they want a slow bottom presentation, a more aggressive bounce, or a steady retrieve. A Shrimp Lure Built to Keep Fishing The Prawn has become one of our most trusted lures for producing both numbers and quality fish. Now, the Prawn XT takes that proven profile and adds a level of durability that can keep you fishing much longer without replacing torn or damaged lures. The Prawn XT costs slightly more per pack than a traditional soft plastic. However, when a single lure can survive dozens of fish, aggressive bait stealers, and repeated trips around heavy structure, the long-term value becomes easy to see. The Prawn XT OG and Jr. are both available now . GET THE PRAWN XT OG GET THE PRAWN XT JR Give them a try and put them through your own durability test. As always, if you do not think they are awesome, you can get your money back. Have any questions about the new Prawn XT, choosing the right size, or rigging it correctly? Let me know in the comments below!

The wait is OVER! After selling thousands of our original Dr. Popper popping corks, we heard from a LOT of anglers about what they loved and what they wanted us to improve. And we listened! The result is the NEW Dr. Popper XT , a tougher, more durable popping cork with some exciting upgrades based directly on YOUR feedback. Here’s what’s changed, why we made these improvements, and why I’m so excited about this new cork.
Featured Gear NEW Dr. Popper XT A Stronger, Tougher Popping Cork One of the things anglers loved most about the original Dr. Popper was its flexible shaft. Unlike traditional rigid popping corks, you could bend it, and it would straighten right back out without permanently kinking. We wanted to keep that feature while making the cork even tougher. So we made one BIG change. We replaced the original monofilament shaft with a flexible steel cable. This gives the Dr. Popper XT some important advantages: Improved durability: The steel cable is tougher and more resistant to fraying. White on the bottom: Designed to blend in better with the bright sky when fish look up from below. The goal? Make the cork easier for anglers to see while potentially making it less noticeable to fish. If you buy the Dr. Popper XT and don’t like it, we’ll give you your money back. But here’s the kicker… YOU GET TO KEEP THE CORK! That’s how confident we are in this new design. And that’s exactly what we did. items.excerpt: ICAST this. ICAST that. Closet Insiders? A larger Otis reel? Tougher Prawns, with a Micro Prawn on the way? Luke and I just returned from our 11th ICAST, so we sat down to talk about what stood out at the show and catch everyone up on what has been h
items.search_text: ICAST this. ICAST that. Closet Insiders? A larger Otis reel? Tougher Prawns, with a Micro Prawn on the way? Luke and I just returned from our 11th ICAST, so we sat down to talk about what stood out at the show and catch everyone up on what has been happening at Salt Strong. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. GET THE PRAWN XT OG (4.3″) GET THE PRAWN XT JR. (3.5″) Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear: Lure 1: Prawn XT OG (4.3″) Lure 2: Prawn XT Jr. (3.5″) Lure 3: Prawn XT Micro (2.5″) (Coming Soon) Reel: Otis 3000 (Coming Soon) Was the New Fishing Gear at ICAST Worth the Hype? ICAST is one of the largest fishing industry events in the world. Roughly 14,000 manufacturers, retailers, media members, guides, and other fishing professionals gather to see the newest rods, reels, lures, electronics, and accessories. Before the internet, this was where tackle dealers went to discover what manufacturers were releasing next. Today, it is still an incredible place to reconnect with people and get your hands on new products. But was there any revolutionary new fishing gear this year? Honestly, not much. There were plenty of bigger, stronger, and more expensive versions of products that already existed. One of the biggest trends was the sea urchin style lure currently taking over freshwater bass fishing. It catches a ton of air when cast, but anglers are buying them so quickly that companies are making tackle trays specifically for them. Will it work for redfish? Luke bought a few to find out. We also found two interesting lures inside smaller international booths. We are not revealing much until Luke can properly test them, but they looked promising enough to bring home. The odds are always against a new lure making the cut. For every custom lure we release, Luke has usually tested 10 to 20 others that did not perform noticeably better than what was already available. Still, these two earned a trip to the water. One of the best ICAST moments had nothing to do with gear. Bill Dance received an award recognizing his impact on fishing. Steve Harvey helped present it and shared an incredible story about watching Bill Dance on display televisions while he was homeless and trying to become a comedian. Those fishing lessons helped Steve catch food during one of the hardest periods of his life. That was easily one of the most powerful moments of the show. Why Experienced Anglers Are Quietly Using Smart Fishing Spots Captain Peter Deeks recently introduced us to a new term: Closet Insider. These are experienced anglers, guides, and lifelong fishermen who are Salt Strong Insider members but rarely post in the community or talk about it publicly. Peter will be talking with someone who clearly knows how to catch fish, and that person will casually mention marking a spot inside Smart Fishing Spots. That is when Peter realizes he has found another closet Insider. We met several of them at ICAST. Many were using Smart Fishing Spots to: Track complete fishing routes Log catches on a private map Review tides and weather from past trips Filter catches by month, tide, and wind Find patterns they might otherwise forget The GPS tracking feature can continue recording while your phone is in sleep mode. After the trip, you can review the entire route and see exactly where the action happened. That can quickly reveal your 90/10 zone. You may discover that most of the trip was spent covering unproductive water while nearly every strike occurred along one small ledge, point, shoreline, or depth change. Your catch log helps preserve those lessons. It is easy to remember your last trip. It is much harder to remember the exact tide, wind, route, and productive areas from one year ago. Logging that information allows every fishing trip to make the next one better. The New Fish Strong Gear Luke Is Testing Outside of the ICAST discussion, Luke also shared a few exciting Fish Strong updates. The first is a larger version of our Otis spinning reel. The Otis 2500 has been used and abused by anglers from Texas to Virginia for roughly three years. Before releasing it, we tested dozens of reels and built a pretty impressive reel graveyard in the process. Now, Luke is testing a new 3000 size version. The sample weighs just 7.6 ounces, which is extremely light for a saltwater capable reel in this size. It has the same smooth feel as the 2500, with more capacity and power for larger fish. Luke’s next job is to put it against big snook, redfish, and hopefully a tarpon. He also shared a first look at a tiny 2.5 inch shrimp lure made from our new extra tough material. The original sample arrived in a color that looked like it came straight from Chernobyl. Luke hated the color. The snook did not. His first drop produced a snook around 30 inches. That same tiny lure went on to catch roughly 20 snook without showing meaningful damage. The new Prawn XT OG and Prawn XT Jr. use the same extra tough material. Luke has already put individual Prawn XT lures through dozens of grouper, snapper, jacks, and other fish. Even after being bounced around reefs and rocky structure, the tails and bodies remained intact. The material is extremely tough while still being flexible enough to move naturally. It takes slightly more effort to rig than a traditional soft plastic. But once it is properly rigged on a jighead, it stays in place extremely well. Is it pufferfish proof? We are not making that claim yet. Luke still wants to find a pufferfish flat, set up a few underwater cameras, and see what happens. Final Thoughts ICAST is still one of the best places to reconnect with the fishing industry and discover products that might otherwise go unnoticed. But the biggest booth does not always have the best product. The most hyped lure does not always catch the most fish. And the angler who never posts in the community might secretly be using every Smart Fishing Spots feature available. items.title: I Was Bad At Inshore Fishing… Until I Learned This
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: For years, I thought catching more fish meant buying more lures. When that didn’t work, I bought different colors. Then different rods. Different reels. I convinced myself the anglers who consistently caught fish knew about some secret lure or hidden
items.search_text: For years, I thought catching more fish meant buying more lures. When that didn’t work, I bought different colors. Then different rods. Different reels. I convinced myself the anglers who consistently caught fish knew about some secret lure or hidden spot that I didn’t. Looking back, I wasn’t struggling because of my tackle. I was struggling because I didn’t understand fish behavior. Once I learned that, everything changed. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software Smart Fishing Spots – helps take the guesswork out of pre-trip planning by showing you where fish are most likely to be based on conditions. Instead of wondering where to start, you can spend more time focusing on the food, comfort, and safety factors Pat discusses in this lesson. Why Most Anglers Struggle To Catch Fish One of the biggest mistakes anglers make is focusing on tackle before understanding the fish. Many anglers start by asking: What lure should I throw? What color should I use? What rod is best? But that’s like walking into a hardware store and buying tools before you even know what project you’re building. The fish determine the task. The lure is simply the tool. Before choosing a lure, it’s important to understand what the fish are doing, why they’re there, and what conditions they’re looking for. Once you understand that, finding fish becomes much easier. Fish Behavior Matters More Than Tackle The anglers who consistently catch fish aren’t necessarily using better gear. They simply understand fish behavior. They know: Why fish are in a particular area Why fish move When fish feed When fish stop feeding Instead of guessing, they’re making informed decisions based on conditions and fish movement. Most fish behavior can be simplified into three basic needs: Food Comfort Safety When you find an area that provides all three, you’re much more likely to find feeding fish. Principle #1: Fish Follow Food One of the most important lessons in fishing is that predator fish follow their food. When bait moves, predators often move with it. That’s why a spot that was loaded with fish yesterday can be completely empty today. The structure may be the same. The tide may be similar. But if the bait leaves, the predators often leave too. Before making a cast, look for signs of life: Mullet schools Shrimp activity Nervous bait Diving birds Surface disturbances Stingrays and other wildlife activity These clues often reveal far more than lure selection ever will. If there isn’t food in the area, there’s a good chance feeding fish won’t be there either. Principle #2: Fish Seek Comfort Fish are constantly looking for conditions that help them conserve energy and survive. What creates comfort changes throughout the year. During winter, fish often move into rivers, creeks, and backwater areas where water temperatures remain more stable. These areas allow fish to escape sudden cold fronts and quickly move shallow when conditions improve. During summer, the opposite is often true. Fish frequently seek cooler water with higher dissolved oxygen levels. That may mean deeper water, open bays, passes, oyster reefs, bridges, or nearby surf zones. The fish haven’t changed. Their needs have. Instead of relying on yesterday’s fishing report, ask yourself: “Where would a fish want to be today?” That question can dramatically improve your pre-trip planning. Principle #3: Fish Need Safety Fish spend their lives avoiding predators. Redfish, snook, trout, and flounder may be predators themselves, but they can also become prey for larger predators such as dolphins and sharks. Because of that, fish often position themselves near areas that provide protection. Examples include: Oyster bars Dock pilings Bridge structure Mangrove shorelines Grass edges Shallow water These areas allow fish to feed while still having a place to escape if danger appears. When an area provides food, comfort, and safety at the same time, it often becomes a high-percentage fishing location. The Three Questions I Ask Before Every Trip Today, before I ever tie on a lure, I ask myself three simple questions: 1. Where Is The Food? Are there baitfish, shrimp, crabs, or other forage nearby? 2. What Do The Fish Need Today? Are they looking for warmer water, cooler water, oxygen, current, or protection from changing conditions? 3. Where Is The Safety? What nearby structure or habitat allows fish to feed while remaining protected from predators? Answering these questions usually tells me far more than any lure package ever could. Final Thoughts Lure selection matters. Rods matter. Reels matter. But they shouldn’t be the starting point. The day I stopped asking: “What lure should I throw?” And started asking: “Why are fish here?” Was the day I became a better inshore angler. Because at the end of the day, fish don’t care what lure you’re holding if there isn’t a reason for them to be there in the first place.
