items.search_text: Ever pull up to brand-new water and think, “Where the heck do I even start?” When everything looks fishy, it’s easy to burn the best part of the morning in the wrong place. In this video, you’ll see how to narrow the search down to three promising areas, then evaluate them under real fishing conditions. You’ll walk away with a simple game plan to stop guessing, keep solid backup options, and spend more time fishing high-percentage water. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear: Rod: Slot Machine Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Lure 1: The Mulligan 4″ Paddletail Hook: 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/16oz Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 15lb Mono Leader How To Find Spots In New Water When fishing an unfamiliar area, avoid building the entire trip around one location. Coach Tony used Smart Fishing Spots to select three promising areas with different types of structure: A shallow shoreline An island point with cuts and a protected cove An area containing points, oyster beds, islands, and backwater habitat Selecting different types of spots allows you to test multiple patterns. Redfish may be holding tight to a shoreline, feeding around a windblown point, or moving through protected backwater. If all three selected spots feature the same structure, you may continue testing the same unproductive pattern throughout the trip. Before finalizing the plan, also consider the tide, wind, water level, and time of day. This trip began before sunrise, while summer water temperatures were still relatively cool. Slack tide was approaching, but an incoming tide was expected to begin moving water shortly afterward. The goal is to choose several high-percentage areas that provide options as the conditions change. How To Approach And Evaluate A Spot Selecting the spot is only the first step. How you approach it can determine whether you get an opportunity. Extremely low water and thick grass made reaching the first area more difficult than expected. Slowing down revealed bait and fish activity before the actual spot was reached. A weedless four-inch paddle tail was used to search the grass. The best casts were directed toward sections with ripples on the surface, where the vegetation remained slightly below the water. Those observations led to two redfish before reaching the first planned area. When approaching a Smart Spot, watch for: Tailing fish Surface wakes Nervous or showering bait Feeding birds Rippled openings in thick grass Shoreline corners Points and cuts Oyster beds Wind-driven current These signs can reveal where fish are concentrated within or around the larger area. Avoid running directly into the center of the spot. Begin watching the water as you approach, and be ready to stop if you see activity. Once there, evaluate the area efficiently. If there are no signs of bait or gamefish, move to the next option rather than forcing an inactive spot to produce. How To Save Productive Fishing Patterns After the trip, the route and catches can be reviewed inside the app. Logging each catch preserves useful information such as: Catch location Time and tide stage Wind and weather conditions Moon phase Air temperature The route taken through the area This creates a record of which spots held fish, which areas lacked activity, and where opportunities appeared along the approach. Over time, these logs can reveal repeatable seasonal patterns. If redfish consistently appear near similar shorelines, points, grass openings, or tide stages, that information can help guide future Smart Spot selections. Instead of starting from scratch on the next trip, you can build on what the fish already taught you. See a more detailed overview of the catch log and tracking feature here. Final Thoughts A three-spot game plan makes unfamiliar water much easier to approach. Use Smart Fishing Spots to select several high-percentage areas with different types of structure. Then let the conditions on the water refine the plan. Watch for bait, birds, wakes, tails, grass openings, and moving water as you approach each spot. Be willing to stop early when you see activity, and move on when an area shows no signs of life. Smart Fishing Spots can narrow down where to begin. Careful observation helps identify exactly where to cast.

items.title: I Launched… Now What? (How I Choose Where To Fish)
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Every fishing trip starts with a decision. You launch your boat, step into your kayak, or walk onto a shoreline and immediately face a question that can determine how the rest of your day unfolds: Where do I fish first? For years, I made this decisio
items.search_text: Every fishing trip starts with a decision. You launch your boat, step into your kayak, or walk onto a shoreline and immediately face a question that can determine how the rest of your day unfolds: Where do I fish first? For years, I made this decision the same way many anglers do. I’d start with a spot I liked, a place I’d caught fish before, or an area that simply looked “fishy.” Sometimes it worked. A lot of times it didn’t. What eventually changed my fishing wasn’t finding more secret spots. It was learning how to choose my spots strategically before I ever made my first cast. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots : Before your next trip, use Smart Fishing Spots to pick out 3–5 potential starting locations before you ever leave the ramp. Use the map layers to find high-percentage areas based on the conditions you’ll be fishing, whether that’s oyster bars, seagrass, contour lines, or other key habitat. Then drop waypoints on each of those locations so you already have a game plan when you launch. If your first stop doesn’t have the bait or conditions you’re looking for, you’ll already have several backup options ready to go, saving time and helping you spend more of your day fishing productive water instead of searching for it. And don’t forget to log your catches, privately or publicly, to build a library of historical data you can use to make even better decisions on future trips. The Biggest Mistake Happens Before You Launch Most anglers think the decision starts at the ramp. It doesn’t. The biggest mistake many anglers make is waiting until they launch to decide where they’re going to fish. At that point, you’re often making a decision with very little information. You’re looking at water, shorelines, points, creeks, and flats, but you haven’t taken the time to think about what the fish are likely doing. Instead of asking: “Where should I fish?” Start by asking: “What are the fish likely doing today?” That small shift changes everything. Start With The Conditions Before every trip, I try to identify the factors that are most likely influencing fish behavior. Three of the biggest are: Season Tide Wind These don’t tell you exactly where the fish are. They tell you where fish are more likely to be. For example, an outgoing tide often concentrates bait and creates feeding opportunities around drains, creek mouths, and other funnel points. A strong wind can reposition bait and influence where predators set up. Seasonal patterns often determine whether fish are likely to be shallow, deep, spread out, or concentrated. The goal isn’t to find fish yet. The goal is to understand what fish want. Find Areas That Match The Conditions Once you have a game plan, it’s time to look for areas that fit it. This is where many anglers get backwards. Instead of looking for your favorite spot, look for spots that match today’s conditions. If moving water is important, look for areas that concentrate current. If bait movement is a key factor, look for locations that naturally funnel bait. If seasonal patterns point toward a particular depth range or type of habitat, focus your attention there. The question isn’t: “Where did I catch fish last time?” The better question is: “What type of area best fits today’s conditions?” That approach works in Florida, Texas, Louisiana, North Carolina, and just about everywhere in between. Narrow The Water Down One of the biggest advantages of having a game plan is that it helps eliminate water. Most fisheries contain far more water than you could realistically fish in a day. The goal isn’t to find every possible place fish could be. The goal is to identify the highest-probability starting location. By the time I launch, I’ve usually narrowed my options down to just a handful of areas. Now the decision becomes much easier. Instead of choosing between hundreds of acres of water, I’m choosing between a few locations that already fit the conditions. Pick The Spot With The Most Evidence When several areas look good, I look for overlap. Where do multiple factors come together? Maybe a point has: Moving water Bait activity A favorable wind Seasonal positioning That’s a lot of evidence pointing toward one location. I’m not looking for the perfect spot. I’m looking for the spot with the most things going for it. Fishing is rarely about certainty. It’s about stacking odds in your favor. Let The Fish Vote Even the best game plan isn’t perfect. That’s where the fish come in. Once I arrive at my starting location, I’m looking for signs that support or challenge my decision. Things like: Bait activity Nervous water Follows Blowups Strikes Visible fish movement The conditions help me decide where to start. The fish help me decide whether to stay. A good plan gets you in the neighborhood. The fish tell you if you’re standing at the right house. Final Thoughts Many anglers start looking for fish when they arrive at the ramp. I prefer to start much earlier. By taking a few minutes to understand the conditions, identify what fish are likely doing, and match those conditions to specific types of locations, you can dramatically improve your chances of starting in the right place. The next time you launch, don’t ask: “Where should I fish?” Ask: “What are the fish likely doing today?” Answer that question first, and the choice of where to fish becomes much easier.

items.search_text: Ever pull up to a spot that screamed FISH, only to discover the fish didn’t get the memo? A few easy-to-miss factors can turn a great spot into dead water, even when everything looks perfect. That’s why we built Smart Fishing Spots. In this video, I’ll show you how to uncover hidden structure, find public access, save waypoints, turn catch photos into fishing intel, and avoid the biggest Smart Spot mistake. You’ll also learn my simple ABC method for deciding whether to stay or move on. Watch this before your next trip and stop donating hours to fishless water! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Beginner? Intermediate? Advanced? Start Your Fishing School Journey Here. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Start With The Smart Spots The highlighted areas on the map are called Smart Spots. These zones have a higher probability of holding feeding fish based on factors such as: Date and season Time of day Tide cycle Wind and weather Barometric pressure Structure Water movement You can move the time bar to see how the recommended areas change throughout the day. Smart Spots should be treated as high-probability zones, not guaranteed fishing locations. Fish and bait move, and changing conditions can make a normally productive area temporarily unproductive. Use the platform to identify the right neighborhoods. Once you arrive, look for bait, birds, current, surface strikes, and other signs of life. If a spot is not producing, move to the next promising area. Evaluate Every Spot With The ABC Method Once Smart Fishing Spots guides you to a promising zone, evaluate it using the ABC Method: Ambush points Bait Current Redfish, speckled trout, snook, and flounder are ambush predators. Look for shoreline points, creek mouths, oyster bars, grass lines, mangroves, dock pilings, ledges, and depth changes. The best locations often combine multiple types of structure. A dock with shade, oyster-covered pilings, seagrass, and deeper water will usually have more potential than a dock surrounded by featureless sand. Next, confirm that bait is present. Maps can show structure and predict water movement, but they cannot confirm exactly where the bait will be. Look for jumping mullet, flickering baitfish, working birds, nervous water, and visible feeding activity. Finally, look for current. Moving water carries food past structure and allows predators to feed efficiently. When ambush points, bait, and current are all present, you have found a high-probability fishing area. Use The Map Layers To Find Better Targets Smart Fishing Spots includes several layers that help you investigate each zone. The one-foot contour layer reveals ledges, channels, holes, and sharp depth changes. These features are especially useful around bridges or in murky water where the bottom cannot be seen. Instead of fishing every bridge piling, focus on pilings near strong depth changes. These areas can combine structure, current, shade, and deeper water. The oyster layer helps identify another valuable form of structure. Oysters attract baitfish and crabs while creating feeding opportunities for redfish, trout, snook, and other predators. Isolated oyster bars can be especially productive because they concentrate activity. You can also use the maps to find docks and shorelines that stand out from the surrounding area. Look for: Docks extending into deeper water Isolated docks with extra space around them Large docks producing more shade Shoreline points beside channels Multiple forms of structure in one location For shore and kayak anglers, the public-access layer can help locate legal access near promising water. Street View can also be used to check parking, signs, launches, and access conditions before the trip. Build Your Plan With Waypoints And Catch Logs Once you identify promising areas, save them using waypoints. You can mark oyster bars, depth changes, docks, creek mouths, shoreline points, and public access areas. Not every waypoint needs to fall inside a highlighted Smart Spot. If an area has good structure and appears promising, save it and investigate it. Creating several waypoints also gives you backup options if your first location does not produce. The catch-log feature helps you learn from previous trips. You can import fishing photos from your phone, and the platform can connect each catch with information such as: Catch location Date and time Tide stage Weather conditions Wind Moon phase Fish species Over time, this creates a private fishing database based on your own results. You can use that information to identify which locations, tides, seasons, and conditions produce the most fish for you. Final Thoughts Smart Fishing Spots is designed to make fishing research faster and more effective. Before your next trip: Select the date and time you plan to fish. Review the highlighted Smart Spots. Look for ambush points within each zone. Use the contour and oyster layers to find better targets. Save several promising areas as waypoints. Build a route with backup locations. Once you reach the water, approach each area quietly and look for bait, current, birds, and feeding activity. Smart Fishing Spots helps you build the plan and reach high-probability water. Your observations help you choose the exact place to cast. items.title: How to Catch Redfish on Cut Bait in Summer
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Hot summer day. Water temperatures in the low 90s. Redfish buried DEEP inside the mangroves. Sounds like a tough bite, right? It usually is. But one simple technique can turn those hiding redfish into a feeding FRENZY. Watch the video below to see ho
items.search_text: Hot summer day. Water temperatures in the low 90s. Redfish buried DEEP inside the mangroves. Sounds like a tough bite, right? It usually is. But one simple technique can turn those hiding redfish into a feeding FRENZY. Watch the video below to see how it works! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots What Is The Best Tide For Catching Mangrove Redfish? The first two to three hours of the outgoing tide are usually the best time to use this technique. During the summer, redfish often move into mangrove root systems to find food, shade, and protection. When the tide is high, those fish can push surprisingly far back into the roots. That makes them difficult to reach. As the tide begins to fall, the redfish are forced out of the mangroves and closer to the edge. That is the opportunity anglers are looking for. There is still enough water for the fish to feel comfortable, but they are no longer sitting several feet beyond casting range. While the water is still high, baits may need to be cast deep into the mangrove openings to get bites. As the water continues falling, the fish often begin moving closer to the outside edge. This is why knowing the tide stage before a trip is so important. Smart Fishing Spots provides tide predictions using local tide stations, making it easy to identify the first few hours of the outgoing tide and plan trips up to two weeks in advance. The high-resolution satellite imagery and changing Smart Spots can also help identify which mangrove shorelines are expected to become more productive as the tide changes. How To Rig Cut Bait For Redfish The rig for this technique is incredibly simple. The setup includes: Fresh cut pinfish 3/0 circle hook Small split shot 25-pound leader Start by cutting the head and tail off the pinfish. Remove the sharp fins from each side as well. This gives the bait a cleaner profile and reduces the chance of a redfish getting poked by a fin and dropping it. Place a small split shot just above the hook. Only enough weight to keep the bait near the bottom and prevent it from moving out of the strike zone is needed. Then cast it into a promising opening and let it sit. Cut bait releases scent while remaining in one place. That makes it perfect for hot summer conditions when redfish are tucked into the shade and may not want to chase a fast-moving lure. Cut bait can also be placed under a float. The float allows the current to carry the bait along the mangrove edge and cover more water. When the float shoots underwater, there is no mistaking the bite! Use the bottom rig to target one specific mangrove pocket. Use the float to drift the bait along the shoreline and search for active fish. Where Should Cut Bait Be Cast Around Mangroves? Bait placement can make or break this technique. A bait can sit just outside a mangrove opening for 20 minutes without getting a bite. Cast that same bait five feet farther into the opening, and a redfish may eat it almost immediately. Five feet can make the difference. When the tide is still high, get the bait as far into the openings as safely possible. Look for: Gaps between mangrove branches Small pockets behind the outer edge Drains carrying water out of the trees Shaded areas with enough depth Openings with visible current Accurate casting matters much more than casting distance. The goal is to place the bait close to the fish without wrapping the line around a branch. Once a bite comes from one opening, cast back into the same area. Redfish often hold together, and one small mangrove pocket can produce several fish. When a fish eats, keep the rod tip low and apply steady pressure. A low rod angle helps keep the line away from overhanging branches while guiding the fish out of the roots. Once the redfish reaches open water, the drag can be loosened and the fight can slow down. Final Thoughts Cut bait is one of the most reliable ways to catch redfish around mangroves during the hottest days of summer. The setup is simple. The real key is combining it with the right tide and accurate bait placement. Focus on the first two to three hours of the outgoing tide. Cast deep into the openings while the water is high. Move closer to the edge as the water falls. And if one mangrove pocket produces a fish, KEEP FISHING IT! There may be an entire group sitting in the same small area. This trip even produced a solid Tampa Bay redfish with zero spots. What do you call a redfish without a spot? Let everyone know in the comments!

items.search_text: Summer high tides can sometimes make redfish feel impossible to find. Many anglers assume the fish have disappeared when the water gets high. In reality, they’ve simply moved. Instead of roaming open flats, redfish often push up into shoreline cover where they have access to food and protection from predators. If you know where to look, and how to present your lure, you can have some incredible days fishing even during the highest tides of summer. In this video, I’ll show you exactly how I approach high-tide redfish while exploring new waters, including the retrieves, lure choices, and locations that consistently produce. Featured Gear: Shrimp Lure Setup: Rod: Slot Machine 7’6″ Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Line: 10 lb Daiwa J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 15 lb Ande Mono Bite Tippet: 30 lb Ande Mono Lure: Prawn Jr rigged on 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jig Head 3/16oz Jerk Lure Setup: Rod: Slot Machine 7’6″ Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Line: 8 lb Daiwa J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 15 lb Ande Mono Bite Tippet: 30 lb Ande Mono Lure: Polk County Tweaker rigged on 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/8oz Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Other: Boat: 22′ Micro Draft Sunglasses: Smith – Guide’s Choice Solar Hoodie: Sky Camo Performance Solar Hoodie Why High Tide Can Be One Of The Best Times To Catch Redfish Of all the popular inshore species, redfish are some of the most willing to move into extremely shallow water. During high tide, they frequently push tight against mangroves, grass shorelines, oyster bars, creek mouths, and other shoreline structure to feed on crabs, shrimp, and baitfish that become accessible only when the water rises. Many anglers continue fishing open water. The better approach is to fish where the water has just opened up new feeding opportunities. Fish Tight To Structure The biggest mistake anglers make during high tide is not casting close enough. When redfish move into shoreline cover, they often position only inches from mangrove roots, grass edges, or shoreline points. That means your lure needs to land as close to the structure as possible. Sometimes that even means casting over mangrove branches or through shoreline vegetation before bringing your lure back into the strike zone. The closer your presentation gets to the cover, the better your odds. Why Weedless Lures Shine Around Mangroves Fishing this tight to cover is almost impossible with an exposed hook. A weedless setup allows you to: Skip under mangroves Cast through shoreline grass Retrieve over roots and branches Keep your lure in the strike zone much longer In several of the catches from this trip, being weedless was the difference between landing a fish and getting hung in the mangroves. Adjust Your Lure If Fish Become Spooky Not every lure lands the same. During calm summer conditions, even a quality presentation can spook fish if the lure enters the water too aggressively. If you notice fish reacting to the splash instead of the retrieve, consider downsizing your presentation or switching to a lighter setup. A quieter entry often gives fish just enough confidence to stay put long enough to eat. Small adjustments like this can completely change your results. Spend More Time In The Strike Zone Another key adjustment during high tide is knowing where the fish actually are. Most bites happen within the first few feet of shoreline cover. Once your lure has moved away from the structure, the odds of getting bit drop dramatically. Rather than slowly working the lure all the way back to the boat, make your presentation near the cover, fish it thoroughly, then reel in quickly and make another cast. More casts into productive water usually mean more fish. How To Find High-Tide Redfish Spots When looking for productive summer high-tide areas, I focus on locations that combine several key ingredients: Healthy mangrove shorelines Shallow backwater areas Seagrass Oyster bars Nearby deeper water The shallow water provides excellent feeding opportunities during high tide, while nearby deeper water gives redfish a place to retreat as the tide falls and temperatures rise. These transition areas consistently produce throughout the summer. Use Smart Fishing Spots To Narrow Your Search One of the easiest ways to find these areas before leaving the dock is with Smart Fishing Spots . I primarily use it to identify: High-resolution satellite imagery Mangrove shorelines Oyster bars Seagrass Smart Fishing Spots Marine charts Hourly tide and weather forecasts Personalized Game Plans Launch locations Private catch logs Being able to compare satellite imagery with tides, weather, structure, and historical catches makes finding productive water much faster than relying on trial and error. If you haven’t already, make sure you’re logging your catches as well. Your catch log can be kept private or public , giving you valuable historical data to help identify patterns and improve future trips. Final Thoughts Summer high tides don’t make redfish harder to catch. They simply change where you need to look. Fish tight to shoreline structure, use weedless lures that let you make aggressive casts, pay attention to how fish react to your presentation, and focus your time where the fish actually live during high water. Those adjustments can completely change your success when the tide is high.

items.title: How To Catch More Fish In Highly Pressured Areas
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Learn how to catch highly pressured redfish and trout using stealth, lighter presentations, better timing, and a few simple adjustments.
items.search_text: Highly pressured fish can be some of the MOST frustrating fish to catch. You know they’re there… But one wrong move can shut the whole thing down. On this trip, a few small adjustments made a BIG difference with both redfish and trout. And once you see what changed, you’ll know exactly what to look for and how to adjust the next time pressured fish just WON’T cooperate. Watch below to see how I approach fish that have seen it ALL. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine Medium Lure 1: 2.0 (Black Ice) Lure 2: Tweaker (Black Ice) Rigging: 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/16 oz Salt Strong Insiders can save 20% on proven tackle we use and trust at Fish Strong. Go Smaller, Lighter, And Different One of the first things I change in pressured water is my presentation. Instead of throwing what everyone else is throwing, I want something smaller, lighter, or just a little different. I started with a 3.5-inch black and silver paddletail on a 1/16 oz Hot Helix Hook. That gave me a smaller profile, a quieter entry, and a color the fish probably weren’t seeing as often. That produced both trout and redfish. Later in the morning, I went even more finesse with a black and silver Tweaker rigged completely weightless. The goal was simple: slow everything down and make the presentation as subtle as possible. Around pressured fish, sometimes LESS really is more. Stealth And Timing Matter You can have the perfect lure tied on and still ruin a spot before you ever get a cast. Early in the morning, there wasn’t another boat around me. That gave me a shot at fish before they had been disturbed. Once those fish get spooked, though, your window can close fast. That’s why trolling motor speed, boat noise, and movement all matter in shallow water. Avoid sudden bursts from the trolling motor. Gradually increase or decrease speed, and use quieter options like a push pole, paddle, or natural drift whenever possible. Later in the trip, I used the wind to drift along a grass line and make longer casts with the wind at my back. Less noise. Less movement. More distance from the fish. That can make a HUGE difference. Make The First Cast Count Pressured fish may only give you one good opportunity. That means casting distance and accuracy matter. I was using a 7’6” medium power, fast action Slot Machine rod paired with a lightweight 2500-size reel. I also downsized from 10 lb braid to 8 lb braid and used a 12 to 15 lb leader. Then I lengthened my leader from the 18 to 24 inches I normally use to roughly 4.5 to 5 feet. All of those little changes helped me stay farther away, cast more quietly, and present the lure more naturally. And that’s really the goal. Give the fish as few reasons as possible to know you’re there. Final Thoughts When fish are getting hammered by anglers every day, don’t immediately start searching for a magic lure. Ask yourself: Can I go smaller? Can I go lighter? Can I make a longer cast? Can I fish earlier? Can I be quieter? But most importantly: How can I make this fish have no idea I’m here? That mindset can be the difference between watching pressured fish refuse everything and getting one to eat. What adjustment has helped YOU the most when fishing highly pressured areas? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Should you downsize lures for pressured fish? Yes, it can be very effective. Smaller, lighter lures create a more subtle presentation and can look different from what pressured fish regularly see. Does lighter fishing line help? Lighter braid can improve casting distance and help create a more finesse-oriented setup. On this trip, I dropped from 10 lb braid to 8 lb braid. Should you use a longer leader? A longer leader can help create more separation between your lure and braided main line. I increased mine to roughly 4.5 to 5 feet on this trip. How do you avoid spooking fish in shallow water? Reduce noise and movement, use your trolling motor sparingly, avoid sudden speed changes, make longer casts, and use wind or current to drift whenever possible. What is the best time to fish pressured areas? Getting there before heavy fishing activity begins can give you a big advantage. Early morning is often a great opportunity before fish have been disturbed.

items.title: How To Catch Freshwater Redfish & Flounder
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Redfish and flounder in 100% freshwater? Yep. Luke and I just got back from one of the wildest fishing trips we’ve taken in a long time, and there were moments when you genuinely had no clue what was going to eat your lure next. A largemouth bass? A
items.search_text: Redfish and flounder in 100% freshwater ? Yep. Luke and I just got back from one of the wildest fishing trips we’ve taken in a long time, and there were moments when you genuinely had no clue what was going to eat your lure next. A largemouth bass? A flounder? A big redfish? All of them were swimming in the SAME water. But the craziest part wasn’t just what we caught. It was how ridiculously repeatable the pattern became once we figured out the one type of spot these fish kept stacking around. And this wasn’t some Louisiana-only trick. If you fish coastal rivers, marshes, creeks, or backwaters anywhere from Texas to the Carolinas, you’re going to want to see this. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. This offer ends September 8th, 2026, so don’t wait! Click Here To Get The Traveler Deal + See All The Other BIG Fish Strong Week Savings Before They’re Gone. Featured Gear Lure: Prawn XT Jr. Rigging: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jighead 1/4 oz Rod: Slam Stick Traveler Reel: Otis 2500 (3000 Coming Soon) Line: 10 lb J-braid Leader: Ande 30 lb mono leader The Prawn XT Jr. was the star of the trip. Luke fished the same soft plastic for all three days and landed at least 60 fish on it, while most of the fish we caught overall came from bouncing that shrimp imitation along the bottom. Yes, Redfish And Flounder Can Live In Freshwater This trip was in the Venice, Louisiana area, but we weren’t fishing what most anglers would think of as traditional saltwater. We literally dipped our fingers into the water and tasted it. No salt. Yet we were catching redfish, black drum, flounder, and other saltwater species right alongside freshwater species like largemouth bass and gar. That alone made the trip pretty surreal. But more importantly, it showed just how far certain inshore species can push into coastal freshwater systems when the habitat and food are right. And these weren’t random fish. We caught more redfish, drum, and especially flounder than we had on any of our previous Louisiana trips. Luke estimated we caught at least 30 flounder during the first two days alone. Find Creek Intersections And Fish The Bottom This was the biggest lesson from the entire trip. We kept targeting places where a smaller creek met another creek, river, canal, or larger body of water. These intersections create natural funnels. And around the mouth of those smaller creeks, there’s often a depression or drop caused by moving water. That little depth change is PERFECT for ambush predators. Flounder can sit right on the bottom. Redfish and black drum can patrol the edges. And bait gets pushed right through the strike zone. Our approach was incredibly simple: Fish one point of the creek mouth. Fish the other point. Fish through the middle. Then work a little farther down either side. It was rare for us to fish one of these intersections without getting at least one bite, and some held multiple redfish or flounder. The other thing we watched for was bait and birds . If we saw mullet working a shoreline or multiple egrets hanging around a creek mouth, that spot immediately moved up the list. Those clues helped us find the most productive intersections much faster. Why Bouncing A Shrimp On Bottom Crushed The Fish Popping corks are extremely popular in Louisiana. And they absolutely catch fish. But for what we were targeting, getting the lure all the way to the bottom was the difference maker. The flounder were sitting down in those depressions near the creek mouths. Black drum often had their heads down feeding. And many of the redfish were eating close to the bottom too. We watched other anglers fish similar areas with popping corks, then came through afterward and caught flounder they had completely missed. Our primary presentation was a Prawn XT Jr. on a 1/4 oz jighead , bouncing along the bottom through those deeper zones. We also made sure we had enough weight to maintain bottom contact whenever the current picked up. And surprisingly, the water was extremely murky, but we didn’t need crazy colors, excessive noise, or complicated presentations. Put a natural-looking shrimp in the right zone and keep it near the bottom. The fish handled the rest. Final Thoughts Freshwater redfish and flounder sound strange until you see it happen. But the biggest takeaway from this trip wasn’t Louisiana, freshwater, or even the ridiculous number of fish we caught. It was how transferable the pattern was. Find a creek or drain entering a larger body of water. Look for the points and deeper depression around that intersection. Confirm there’s bait or bird activity nearby. Then put your lure on the bottom and work the entire zone. Luke uses the same basic strategy in Florida, Texas, and other marsh systems, and it worked almost immediately for us in Louisiana too. Have you ever caught a redfish, flounder, or another saltwater species WAY farther into freshwater than you expected? Let me know in the comments! Freshwater Redfish & Flounder FAQs Can redfish live in freshwater? Yes. Redfish can move into freshwater portions of coastal rivers, creeks, and marsh systems. On this trip, we were catching redfish in water where we couldn’t taste any salt at all. Can flounder live in freshwater? Flounder can also move well into low-salinity and freshwater coastal systems. We caught roughly 30 flounder during the first two days of this trip while fishing freshwater creek systems. Where should you look for redfish and flounder in coastal creeks? Focus on creek intersections, especially where a smaller creek or drain enters a larger creek, river, or bay. These spots often have deeper depressions near the mouth that attract feeding fish. What lure worked best? The Prawn XT Jr. on a 3/0 Hoss Weedless Football Jighead 1/4 oz caught the vast majority of the fish. We worked it slowly along the bottom through creek mouths, points, and deeper holes. Do you need a popping cork? No. In fact, bouncing the lure directly along the bottom was much more productive for the flounder and bottom-feeding fish we were targeting on this trip. Does incoming or outgoing current matter? We caught fish during both incoming and outgoing flow. Luke’s takeaway was that being in the right creek intersection and keeping the lure near the bottom mattered more than obsessing over current direction.

items.title: Gold vs. Silver Flash: What Happened After One Morning Test
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: When it comes to dark-colored lures, most anglers focus on the silhouette. But there’s another variable that’s easy to overlook… The flash. For this trip, I wanted to compare two nearly identical paddletails, one with gold flash and one with silver f
items.search_text: When it comes to dark-colored lures, most anglers focus on the silhouette. But there’s another variable that’s easy to overlook… The flash. For this trip, I wanted to compare two nearly identical paddletails, one with gold flash and one with silver flash, and see if changing light conditions throughout the morning made any noticeable difference. The goal wasn’t to prove that one is better than the other. I wanted to take one trip, keep everything else as consistent as possible, and see if any interesting patterns emerged. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Insiders, July’s Tackle Tester is Black Ice, the same color Tony used in this video, and you can choose from three different lure profiles . Claim yours here. Featured Gear: Rod: Slot Machine Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Lure 1: Mulligan 4″ Paddletail – Black Ice Lure 2: Mulligan 4″ Paddletail – Gold Digger Hook: Hoss Helix Hook 3/0 1/8oz Mainline: Diawa J-Braid 10lb Leader: Ande 15lb Mono Leader Scent: Pro-Cure Inshore Saltwater Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots What I Observed To keep the test as fair as possible, I used identical setups and switched between lures every three casts. Early in the morning, the gold flash lure got the first bite, a snook that unfortunately came unbuttoned. Later, after the sun climbed higher, the silver flash lure produced two landed redfish. Those results lined up with the theory that gold can perform well in lower light while silver may become more effective as more sunlight is available. But it’s important to remember… This was just one morning on the water. That’s nowhere near enough data to say one flash color is better than the other. One Lesson Had Nothing To Do With Lure Color One of the biggest differences on this trip wasn’t the lure at all. After the first area slowed down, I made a move to a completely different spot using Smart Fishing Spots . That decision put me around active fish, which gave me the opportunity to keep comparing the two lures. Final Thoughts After one trip, I wouldn’t declare a winner. What I would say is that the results were interesting enough that I’ll keep testing. If you’re fishing dark lures, it may be worth paying attention not only to the color of the bait, but also to the type of flash inside it and how that matches the available light. I’m looking forward to running this comparison on more trips to see if the same pattern continues. Want me to test out anything in particular? Comment below!

items.title: Florida’s Bold Plan for Better Fishing (Florida’s Coastal Corridor)
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Florida now has roughly $15 million on the table to improve fishing around the state. But this is NOT just another artificial reef program. The Florida Coastal Corridor could eventually connect and improve habitat from our estuaries and seagrass flat
items.search_text: Florida now has roughly $15 million on the table to improve fishing around the state. But this is NOT just another artificial reef program. The Florida Coastal Corridor could eventually connect and improve habitat from our estuaries and seagrass flats all the way out to nearshore and offshore waters. In this episode, Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida Executive Director Nick Wiley reveals where the money is going, how quickly they want to use it, and how anglers can help decide where new habitat is needed. If you fish anywhere in Florida, you need to hear this! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Click Here To Learn More About Florida’s Coastal Corridor. What Is Florida’s Coastal Corridor? Nick described Florida’s Coastal Corridor as one big umbrella for improving the state’s coastal resources. The initial funding and first projects will focus on artificial reefs and adding structure to the water. But the long-term vision is much broader. Nick said the initiative could eventually include habitat restoration and protection involving mangroves, seagrass, salt grass, estuaries, living shorelines, reefs, and corals. The goal is to identify gaps in Florida’s fisheries habitat and create a connected system that supports fish from the estuaries all the way offshore. Nick said the program will maintain a “laser focus” on enhancing fisheries habitat, boosting fish stocks, and creating more opportunities for anglers, boaters, and divers. Where Will The Money Go? Deploying an artificial reef requires approved materials, environmental clearances, contractors, barges, cranes, and other heavy equipment. According to Nick, many counties want to build more fisheries habitat, but they have not had enough funding to get larger projects into the water. Some counties already have suitable reef material stockpiled and ready to go. Nick said this new funding can serve as the catalyst that finally gets those projects deployed. The program technically has about four years to spend the money, but Nick wants it in the water much sooner. He said they would love to spend it within a year if the right projects and partnerships come together. Their working goal is to use the money within two or three years, if not sooner. Nick also said they want to see some major deployments happen within the next year. Areas being considered include the Gold Coast around Miami and Fort Lauderdale, the Emerald Coast and Panhandle, and the stretch from Jacksonville through Merritt Island. How Will Anglers Be Involved? FWC will develop a strategic framework to determine where Florida’s greatest fisheries habitat needs and gaps exist. Nick said that process will include anglers, scientists, stakeholders, and coastal communities. FWC plans to hold a series of public meetings across the state. There will also be electronic ways for anglers to provide input if they cannot attend a meeting. Those public input channels were not open at the time of this conversation, but Nick said information about the meetings and other ways to participate would be announced over the following months. Nick wants anglers to identify areas where structure or habitat is missing. That input will then be considered alongside the science and the economic needs of Florida’s coastal communities. The program will also have to report annually to the Florida Legislature and FWC. Reef deployments will be monitored to document how the reefs develop and what benefits they provide. Nick said success means more than simply spending the money and completing contracts. The reefs must be placed in the right areas, improve fisheries, benefit coastal economies, and create results anglers can see. If the program can prove that it works, Nick believes it can attract additional legislative, corporate, and philanthropic funding for even more fisheries habitat. Final Thoughts A new reef can begin attracting fish on day one. Over the following year or two, it can become a living reef that supports baitfish, larger fish, spawning areas, production, survival, and the broader food web. Now the challenge is getting the right habitat into the right places. Nick specifically asked anglers to help hold the program accountable and participate when FWC opens its public meetings and feedback channels. Where do you think Florida needs more fisheries habitat? Let us know your area and what is missing in the comments! And if you know a Florida angler who needs to hear about this new program, please TAG or SHARE this article with them.

items.title: Finicky Summer Redfish? My Go-To Simple Lure In Calm, Shallow Water
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Redfish can be weird. They’ll explode on bait ten feet away, then develop trust issues the second you try to catch them. Luckily, a few small adjustments can be all it takes to get them to commit. When it’s calm and they’re shallow, spooky, and aller
items.search_text: Redfish can be weird. They’ll explode on bait ten feet away, then develop trust issues the second you try to catch them. Luckily, a few small adjustments can be all it takes to get them to commit. When it’s calm and they’re shallow, spooky, and allergic to commitment, I reach for the Polk County Tweaker . It doesn’t make a scene. It just hangs around looking easy to eat. I created this video to show you how I work the Tweaker for shallow, spooky redfish. And break down two simple retrieves, including one you probably wouldn’t think would work. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: Lure: Polk County Tweaker Rigging 1: 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook Weightless Rigging 2: 3/0 Hoss Helix Hook 1/8 oz Rigging 3: 2/0 Hoss Round Eye Jighead 1/4 oz Great Lure For Spooky Summer Redfish? A subtle soft-plastic jerk lure like the Polk County Tweaker is an excellent option when redfish are holding in shallow, calm water. These fish often don’t want to chase a fast-moving lure during the hottest part of summer. The Tweaker can be worked with very little movement, allowing it to remain in the strike zone and look like an easy meal. Its slim profile also creates less commotion than a lure with a hard-thumping tail, which can be important when targeting pressured or spooky fish. How Should You Retrieve A Lure For Finicky Redfish? Start with two light twitches followed by a pause. Cast beyond the feeding activity, allow the Tweaker to settle to the desired depth, and then use the following retrieve: Give the lure two subtle twitches. Let it pause. Repeat the sequence slowly. Increase your speed only if the fish are feeding aggressively. Avoid making the twitches too sharp. Hot water and calm conditions can make redfish hesitant to chase. An aggressive retrieve may create more action than they want and cause them to turn away. If the grass is topped out and the bait is holding near the surface, rig the lure weightless to keep it above the vegetation. A Slow Retrieve Can Catch Extra-Spooky Redfish Sometimes even subtle twitches are too aggressive. If the fish continue refusing the lure, let it settle to the desired depth and begin reeling it slowly. Don’t twitch the rod or try to add any extra action. In areas without heavy grass, allow the lure to make occasional contact with the bottom. This slow-drag presentation creates an easy target that doesn’t appear to be escaping. It can be especially effective after redfish follow or refuse a traditional twitch-and-pause retrieve. Should You Rig The Polk County Tweaker Weightless? A weightless rig works best when redfish are feeding in extremely shallow water or holding above topped-out grass. Without additional weight, the lure remains higher in the water column and is less likely to collect vegetation. A weighted hook is a better option when you need additional casting distance or want the Tweaker to run slightly deeper while remaining weedless. In deeper water without much grass, a jighead allows you to reach the bottom and maintain contact throughout the retrieve. Cast Ahead Of Feeding Redfish Even the perfect lure and retrieve won’t produce if the bait never reaches the fish. Watch and listen for signs of feeding activity, including: Bait scattering across the surface Redfish pushing water Small splashes or boils Fish slurping bait Activity along the edges of grass When you see or hear a redfish feeding, react quickly, but avoid landing the lure directly on top of it. Cast beyond or ahead of the activity and bring the Tweaker through the strike zone. This gives the redfish an opportunity to discover the lure without being startled by its entry into the water. Final Thoughts Tough summer conditions don’t always mean the redfish have stopped feeding. Sometimes they simply want an easier meal. Keep your presentation subtle, match the rigging to the depth, and let the fish tell you whether they want a twitch-and-pause retrieve or a slow drag. Have you tried the Polk County Tweaker for shallow-water redfish? Let me know your favorite way to retrieve it in the comments! And if you know an inshore angler struggling with the summer bite, please TAG or SHARE this article with them.

items.title: Fall Fishing: How to Find Tripletail and BIG Redfish
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Learn where to find tripletail and BIG bull redfish this fall! Luke shares proven fishing patterns, lure tips, and the best areas to target.
items.search_text: Fall is one of the BEST times of year to fish, but there are a couple of opportunities that many anglers completely overlook. Luke just got back from an awesome tripletail fishing trip, and there’s a good reason these fish are showing up right now. But that’s not all… MASSIVE schools of big redfish are also moving into certain areas! In the video below, Luke and I break down two exciting fall fishing patterns, where to find these fish, and how to catch them. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Lure 1: Prawn XT Jr. (3.5″) Rigging: Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead Lure 2: Skinny Lipper XL Lure 3: Mulligan 5″ Bomber Crab Trap Buoys Are Fall Fishing GOLDMINES When crab trap buoys start appearing along the coast, it’s time to start looking for tripletail! Fall is Luke’s favorite season for targeting these fish, and the arrival of crab traps creates an incredible opportunity. Here’s why. Crab traps naturally attract smaller fish and other marine life, creating a steady source of food that draws in larger predators. Tripletail take advantage of this by positioning themselves underneath the floating buoys, where they can ambush unsuspecting prey. And they’re not limited to offshore waters! You can find tripletail around: Crab trap buoys in bays and nearshore waters. Channel markers and other floating structures. Buoys along beaches and coastal shorelines. Floating debris and vegetation. Luke has even encountered tripletail in water as shallow as TWO FEET! The key is to keep your eyes open. As you’re traveling between fishing spots, take a few extra minutes to inspect nearby buoys. Sometimes you’ll spot a fish immediately. Other times, you might check dozens of buoys before finding one. But when you do find one, the action can be incredible! The Biggest Mistake Anglers Make When Targeting Tripletail One of Luke’s biggest takeaways from years of targeting tripletail? DON’T overcomplicate it! Many anglers assume they need live shrimp or other live bait to consistently catch these fish. But Luke has found that a small artificial shrimp can be incredibly effective. His current favorite is the Prawn XT Jr. rigged on a jighead. And there’s an important reason he prefers this setup. Sink Rate Makes a HUGE Difference Tripletail frequently sit just beneath the surface, waiting to ambush anything that drifts into their feeding zone. To trigger a strike, Luke wants his lure to drop directly in front of the fish. He previously experimented with weedless hooks that allowed the lure to fall more slowly. The problem? His strike ratio dropped considerably! Switching to a jighead helped him get the lure into the strike zone much more effectively. For anglers concerned about snagging the buoy rope, Luke recommends using a weedless jighead, such as the Hoss Weedless Round Eye. The basic strategy is simple: Locate a tripletail hanging around a buoy or marker. Cast close enough to get the lure in front of the fish without snagging the rope. Allow the lure to drop naturally through its strike zone. Watch your line carefully for the strike! And don’t give up after one rejected presentation. Luke and Joe have encountered tripletail that refused numerous casts before finally deciding to eat. Persistence can pay off! Want BIG Bull Redfish? Stop Fishing ONLY the Shorelines! While tripletail are gathering around floating structure, another incredible fall fishing pattern is developing across expansive grass flats. Massive schools of oversized redfish are moving into the shallows! These aren’t your typical small schools of slot redfish. We’re talking about schools containing HUNDREDS of fish, including bull reds exceeding 36 inches! But here’s where many anglers go wrong. They spend all their time fishing docks, mangrove shorelines, and other obvious structure. Luke admits he made this same mistake for years. He was consistently fishing the shoreline while some of the biggest redfish were roaming the open flats behind him! Where to Find These Schools During the fall, Luke focuses on large, expansive grass flats located near major current flows. These areas can hold tremendous amounts of bait, including: Mullet Pinfish Shrimp Other small baitfish And when the bait concentrates, those big schools of redfish aren’t usually far behind. Luke particularly likes searching these areas early in the morning. Look for signs of life, including mullet schools, tailing redfish, or fish pushing water across the flats. The important thing to remember is that these fish MOVE! A school might be holding in one section of a grass flat today and roaming another section tomorrow. That’s why covering water is so important. Rather than spending your entire trip casting at shoreline structure, get out onto those expansive flats and actively search for feeding fish. You might be surprised at what you’ve been missing! The Right Lure Can Help You Find More Fish There’s another important difference between Luke’s tripletail and bull redfish strategies. For tripletail, he’s making accurate presentations to individual fish. But for schooling bull redfish, he’s trying to cover as much productive water as possible. That means switching to larger lures capable of making LONG casts. Two of his favorite options are: Skinny Lipper XL: A larger, shallow-running plug that casts extremely far and allows anglers to cover expansive flats. Mulligan 5″ Bomber: A larger paddletail that can help cover water while presenting a substantial baitfish profile. The advantage? These lures allow you to search water efficiently without constantly repositioning your boat. And when you finally locate a school of feeding redfish, things can get exciting FAST! With so many fish competing for food, one fish committing to your lure can trigger an incredible reaction from the rest of the school. Of course, the same grass flats can also hold excellent numbers of snook and speckled trout. Luke generally looks for snook closer to prominent shoreline points, oyster bars, and mangrove edges, while the larger redfish schools tend to roam more freely across the open flats. Find the food, and you’ll dramatically improve your chances of finding the fish! Final Thoughts There’s a reason Luke considers fall his FAVORITE time of year for inshore fishing. Between tripletail gathering around crab trap buoys, schools of bull redfish moving onto expansive flats, and excellent opportunities for snook and trout, there’s a LOT to get excited about! And in many areas, there’s another major advantage. LESS fishing pressure! With hunting season, football, and other fall activities keeping anglers off the water, you might find yourself enjoying some incredible fishing without the summer crowds. So if you’ve got a few extra hours to get on the water, TAKE ADVANTAGE! Have you been seeing tripletail around crab trap buoys or big schools of redfish in your area? Let us know where you’re fishing and what you’re catching in the comments below! Frequently Asked Questions When is the best time to catch tripletail? Fall is one of the best times to target tripletail, particularly as crab traps are deployed along the coast. Luke considers fall his favorite season for tripletail fishing, followed by spring. Where can you find tripletail in the fall? Tripletail frequently gather around crab trap buoys, channel markers, and floating debris. They can be found in bays, along beaches, and in nearshore waters at varying depths. What is the best artificial lure for tripletail? Luke recommends the Prawn XT Jr. rigged on a jighead. The realistic shrimp profile and controlled sink rate make it effective for presenting a lure directly in front of tripletail holding near floating structures. Where do big redfish schools go in the fall? Large schools of bull redfish frequently move onto expansive grass flats near major current flows and abundant baitfish populations. Look for mullet, surface disturbances, and other signs of feeding activity. What are the best lures for big redfish in the fall? Long-casting, shallow-running lures are excellent options for covering large grass flats. Luke recommends larger presentations such as the Skinny Lipper XL and Mulligan 5″ Bomber.

items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Most anglers think they need a cast net to catch quality baitfish. But over the years, I’ve found that some of the best bait for snook, redfish, trout, and tarpon can be caught with nothing more than a simple hook-and-line rig. Not only is this metho
items.search_text: Most anglers think they need a cast net to catch quality baitfish. But over the years, I’ve found that some of the best bait for snook, redfish, trout, and tarpon can be caught with nothing more than a simple hook-and-line rig. Not only is this method easy to use, but it also allows me to target specific baitfish around docks, seawalls, bridges, jetties, and other productive structure. In this video, I’ll show you the exact rig I use, how to tie it, and where to fish it to catch top-quality baitfish without ever throwing a cast net. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. The Easy Rig I Use To Catch Baitfish The setup is simple. I use a dropper-style rig with a sinker tied at the bottom and a small hook positioned above the weight. One reason I like this setup is because the sinker isn’t absorbing the bite. Since the hook is tied above the weight, I can feel those subtle taps from smaller baitfish much more clearly through the rod tip. That makes it easier to detect bites and quickly catch bait. What You’ll Need The great thing about this rig is that you probably already have everything needed to tie it. Leader Material I typically use 15-20 lb monofilament. Hooks For most baitfish, I use small hooks ranging from a #6 up to a #2 depending on the size of the bait I’m targeting. As a general rule, smaller baitfish require smaller hooks. Sinkers Any basic sinker will work. I commonly use: Egg sinkers Bank sinkers Pyramid sinkers The weight you choose will depend on the depth and current where you’re fishing. Why This Rig Works So Well For Catching Quality Baitfish One of the biggest advantages of this rig is simplicity. There’s no cast net to throw. No expensive equipment. And no need to chase schools of bait around. Instead, you can present a small piece of shrimp directly around structure where baitfish naturally gather. This allows you to target healthy croakers, pinfish, pigfish, and other baitfish that make excellent offerings for larger gamefish. The Best Bait For This Rig Fresh shrimp is tough to beat. I simply cut the shrimp into small pieces and thread a chunk onto the hook. The smaller pieces work extremely well for croakers, pinfish, pigfish, and other baitfish commonly found around inshore structure. Where To Catch Baitfish When I’m looking for baitfish, I’m focused on structure. Some of my favorite places to fish this rig include: Boat ramps Docks Seawalls Bridge pilings Rocky shorelines Jetties Channel markers If I don’t get bites right away, I’ll simply move a few feet and try another spot. Most of the time, once I locate the baitfish, the action can be pretty steady. How To Fish The Rig Fishing this rig couldn’t be much easier. Simply drop it straight down beside structure or cast it close to your target area and keep a tight line. When you feel a tap, there’s no need for a big hookset. Just lift the rod and start reeling. Many times you’ll quickly find yourself catching croakers, pinfish, pigfish, and other baitfish that make excellent offerings for larger gamefish. Featured Gear Leader Material 15-20 lb monofilament Hooks Size #2 to #6 bait hooks Sinkers Egg sinkers Bank sinkers Pyramid sinkers Bait Fresh shrimp Final Thoughts If you’re looking for an easy way to catch top-quality baitfish without carrying a cast net, this rig is hard to beat. It’s inexpensive, easy to tie, and can be fished from virtually anywhere. Give it a try the next time you need bait, and let me know how it works for you in the comments below.

items.title: EASIEST Way to Catch Mangrove Snapper (No Live Bait!)
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Learn how to catch mangrove snapper without live bait using one simple shrimp lure, shallow grass flats, and the right retrieve.
items.search_text: Who says you need live bait to load up on mangrove snapper? On a recent trip to the Florida Keys, I decided to keep things simple. One shrimp lure, a basic inshore setup, and a few promising spots on the map. The result? I caught my limit of mangrove snapper before 9 AM! And here’s the really cool part… You don’t need to be in the Keys to put this strategy to work! In this video, I’ll show you exactly where I found the fish, how I worked my lure to get consistent bites, and a few simple tricks you can use to catch more fish on your next trip! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slot Machine 7’6″ Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Line: 10 lb J-Braid 8 Grand Leader: 20 Ib Ande Mono Lure: Prawn XT Jr Rigging Low Current: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye 1/4 oz Rigging High Current: 3/0 Hoss Weedless Round Eye 1/2 oz 1. Find the Potholes on Shallow Grass Flats When most anglers think about mangrove snapper, they picture fishing around bridges, docks, and deeper structure. But don’t overlook shallow grass flats! For this trip, I focused on sandy potholes surrounded by seagrass , especially areas with good current flow. These potholes create natural feeding opportunities where snapper and other predators can hang out and ambush prey. My strategy was simple: Find a productive stretch of grass flats with scattered potholes. Position up-current when possible. Cast into the potholes and work the lure along the bottom. Make a few casts before moving to the next one. When you find fish, slow down and thoroughly cover that area. And once I found one snapper, there were often more nearby! 2. One Shrimp Lure Was All I Needed I kept my setup about as simple as possible. My lure of choice was the Prawn XT Jr. rigged weedless on a 1/4 oz Hoss Round Eye Jighead. This combination allowed me to fish through the grass without constantly getting snagged while still dropping the lure into potholes several feet deep. The retrieve wasn’t complicated, either. I simply cast into the target area, let the shrimp sink toward the bottom, and worked it back with small hops and bumps. The key was keeping the lure near the bottom where the snapper were feeding. As the current picked up and I moved into a deeper channel, I switched to a 1/2 oz jighead to maintain better bottom contact. That small adjustment helped keep the bites coming! And the Prawn XT Jr. didn’t just catch mangrove snapper. I also hooked into mutton snapper and several other species throughout the trip. 3. Let the Current Help You Catch More Fish One of the biggest factors in this trip was how I positioned the boat relative to the current. Rather than randomly casting around the flat, I used the current and wind to quietly drift through productive areas. Whenever possible, I cast up-current and retrieved the shrimp back with the flow, letting it naturally bounce along the bottom. When I hooked a fish, I’d also make additional fan casts to see if more snapper were holding nearby. And when the current became too strong for the lighter jighead, adding weight allowed me to keep fishing effectively. The takeaway? Pay attention to current direction, keep your lure in the strike zone, and don’t be afraid to adjust your presentation. Those little details can make a BIG difference! Final Thoughts What I loved most about this trip was how simple everything was. No live bait. No complicated tackle. Just a shrimp lure, a basic inshore spinning combo, and some productive shallow-water structure. I even managed to catch my limit of mangrove snapper before 9 AM! And this isn’t just a Florida Keys strategy. The same approach to finding potholes, working current, and fishing a shrimp lure can be effective in shallow-water fisheries throughout the Southeast and Gulf Coast. Have you ever targeted mangrove snapper with artificial lures, or do you normally stick with live bait? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Can you catch mangrove snapper without live bait? Absolutely! Artificial shrimp lures like the Prawn XT Jr. can be very effective, especially when worked near the bottom around productive structure and current. Where should I look for mangrove snapper on shallow flats? Look for sandy potholes surrounded by grass, particularly where there’s good current flow. These areas can hold surprising numbers of fish. What jighead weight works best for mangrove snapper? On this trip, I started with a 1/4 oz weedless jighead in shallow water and switched to a 1/2 oz jighead when stronger current made it difficult to maintain bottom contact. What’s the best retrieve for a shrimp lure? Start by allowing the lure to sink near the bottom, then work it back using small hops and bumps. Adjust your retrieve and weight based on current, depth, and where the fish are holding.

items.title: Best & Worst Rigging Options for TPE & Plastisol Lures
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Learn which hooks and jigheads work best for TPE vs. plastisol soft plastic lures so you can rig them correctly and fish with confidence.
items.search_text: Give me 2 minutes, and I’ll make choosing the right jighead or weighted hook for your soft plastics a whole lot easier. I’ve tested more hook and jighead styles than I care to admit, and this quick breakdown covers the biggest lessons I learned through trial and error. By the end, you’ll know which keeper styles work best with different soft plastic materials so you can rig with more confidence, avoid bad combinations, and know exactly what to reach for next time. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Lures (Top to Bottom): Prawn Junior (original) Prawn XT Junior Featured Terminal Tackle (Top to Bottom): Hoss Helix Hook Hoss Screw Lock Jighead (coming soon) Hoss Round Eye Jighead Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead Hoss Prawn XT Jighead (coming soon) Z-Man Pro ShroomZ Jighead Z-Man Texas Eye Jighead TPE vs. Plastisol: Why Rigging Changes Most traditional soft plastic lures are made from plastisol. It’s soft, easy to work with, and usually rigs extremely well on corkscrew-style keepers. That’s why corkscrew weighted hooks and jigheads are some of my favorite options for plastisol lures. You can twist the lure onto the keeper, line everything up, and get a clean, secure presentation without much effort. TPE is a different story. TPE lures are MUCH tougher and stretchier. That durability is a huge advantage on the water. I fished the exact same Prawn XT for three days on a Louisiana trip and caught more than 60 fish on it. That same lure was still in great shape afterward, including both eyes. That’s pretty wild. But that same toughness can make TPE harder to rig on traditional corkscrew-style keepers. For TPE lures, I generally prefer a smaller hook-style keeper or a simpler keeper design that grabs the material without making you fight to twist or force it into place. The Simple Rule If you’re fishing plastisol , corkscrew-style keepers are usually an excellent choice. If you’re fishing TPE , smaller hook-style keepers are typically much easier to rig. There are exceptions, and most of these hooks can technically work with either material. But “can work” and “works well” are two different things. One Keeper Style I’d Be Careful With There’s also a popular keeper style that uses a larger horn or spike to hold the lure in place. That can work really well with certain materials, especially ElaZtech. But it’s not automatically a great fit for every soft plastic. On softer plastisol, that larger keeper can tear up the material. And on very tough TPE, getting the lure over a large keeper can be a pain. So the biggest takeaway is simple: Match your hook keeper to the MATERIAL of the lure, not just the lure size. Doing that makes rigging easier, helps the lure sit straighter, and can save you from wasting soft plastics or buying hook styles that don’t match what you fish. Final Thoughts The good news is that most weighted hooks and jigheads are still pretty interchangeable. You’re not totally locked into one style. But choosing the right keeper for the material makes a BIG difference. For plastisol, I generally like corkscrew-style keepers. For tough TPE lures, I’d lean toward smaller hook-style keepers that are easier to rig. That one little adjustment can save you a lot of frustration. What soft plastic and hook combination are you using right now? Let me know in the comments! FAQs What is the difference between TPE and plastisol soft plastic lures? Plastisol is the traditional soft plastic material used in many fishing lures. It’s soft, flexible, and easy to rig, but it can tear after repeated fish catches. TPE is much stretchier and more durable, which can help a lure last through a lot more fish. The tradeoff is that its toughness can make some hook keepers harder to rig. What hooks work best with TPE soft plastics? Hooks and jigheads with smaller, simpler keeper designs are usually easier to rig with TPE. Large corkscrews or keeper horns can be more difficult to twist or push into the tougher material. Are corkscrew hooks good for soft plastic lures? Yes. Corkscrew-style keepers work especially well with traditional plastisol soft plastics because the softer material twists onto the keeper easily and stays secure. Can you use the same jigheads for TPE and plastisol lures? In many cases, yes. But the keeper design can make one hook much easier to use with one material than another. Matching the keeper to the lure material will usually give you a cleaner rig and easier setup. Why are TPE fishing lures so durable? TPE is extremely elastic and resistant to tearing. That makes it much tougher than traditional plastisol and allows one lure to potentially survive dozens of fish catches.

items.title: Before You Fish the 2.0 Paddletail, Watch This
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Simplify your tackle with the Slam Shady 2.0 paddletail. See my favorite rigs and a simple trick to fish more situations with confidence.
items.search_text: Ever look at a tackle box FULL of lures… and still wonder what to throw? Let’s make that decision a little easier. The 2.0 paddletail is one of the few lures I trust all year long. Shallow water, deeper water, even those times when the bait suddenly looks too small for what you’re throwing. And there’s a simple adjustment that makes this little lure even MORE versatile. Watch the video below to see how I choose my rigs and adapt this lure to different situations, so you can carry less tackle and feel confident putting it to work on your next trip. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Lure: The 2.0 Paddletail – The 3.5-inch lure featured in the video, shown in Slam Shady. Rigging 1: Hoss Helix Hooks – My favorite shallow-water option. A 3/0 hook is the perfect size for this lure. Rigging 2: Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jigheads – My go-to for getting deeper while staying weedless, also with a 3/0 hook. Match Your Rig to the Water You’re Fishing One of the biggest advantages of the 2.0 is how many ways you can rig it. For shallow water, I love the Hoss Helix weighted hook . When I need to get deeper, I reach for a Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead . Those two options cover about 95% of my fishing with this lure. They also let me fish tight to structure, where snook, trout, and flounder often hold, with fewer snags. Traditional exposed-hook jigheads have their place, too. I’ll use them when there’s little to snag on, such as fishing an open beach or trolling above a reef without contacting the bottom. Start with the depth and structure in front of you, then choose the rig that lets you fish it effectively. Small Bait Everywhere? Try the “Nub” Here’s one of my favorite things about this lure. When the fish are feeding on tiny baitfish, you can cut or pull off the paddle tail to create what we call the “nub.” Yep. Pull the tail OFF. That gives you a smaller baitfish profile without digging around for another lure. You can still rig it on the weighted hooks and jigheads shown above. It’s especially handy when small fry bait is abundant in spring. The full 3.5-inch paddletail gives me a versatile starting point. The nub gives me another option when I need to downsize. Know the Tradeoff Before You Tie One On The 2.0 is easy to rig and has great action, but it isn’t indestructible. Pufferfish and mangrove snapper can bite or pull the tail off. Strong fish can also tear the body around a traditional jighead as they shake their heads. That’s another reason I prefer the weedless rigs shown in the video. In my experience, they help this material last longer. And if you lose the tail but the body is still usable? You’ve already got a nub ready to go. For color, Slam Shady is my personal starting point. I’ve tested it across different water clarities, and it’s the one I reach for when I want to keep things simple. Final Thoughts You don’t need to make lure selection complicated. With the 2.0, a couple of rigging options and one simple adjustment give you plenty of ways to respond to what’s happening in front of you. That means less second-guessing your tackle and more time fishing with confidence. Have you tried the 2.0 with the tail removed, or do you always fish it as a paddletail? Let me know what’s worked for you in the comments! Check Out the 2.0 Paddletail Here Frequently Asked Questions What size is the 2.0 paddletail? The full lure measures 3.5 inches. Removing the paddle tail creates a smaller presentation for mimicking tiny baitfish. What hook size do you recommend for the 2.0? I prefer a 3/0 hook on both the Hoss Helix and Hoss Weedless Round Eye Jighead. A 4/0 Helix can work, but 3/0 is my ideal fit. Can you fish the 2.0 in both shallow and deep water? Yes. I use weighted hooks for shallow water and weedless jigheads when I need to get deeper. Match the rig and weight to the conditions you’re fishing. Will the 2.0 still catch fish without its tail? Yes. The tail-free “nub” presentation is useful when fish are feeding on smaller bait. If a fish bites the tail off, you may be able to keep using the remaining body. Where can I learn how to rig the 2.0? You can find detailed rigging lessons in the Slam Shady paddletail tutorial .
