items.title: Back to My Best Fishing Spot After 10 Years. Would It Still Produce?
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: Fishing an old favorite spot after 10 years? See what Luke changed to turn a slow start into a strong redfish and snook bite.
items.search_text: Ever wonder what would happen if you went back to your BEST fishing spot from 10 years ago? I just did. This was a stretch of the Indian River where we used to catch big trout consistently. But after the seagrass disappeared, it was tough to even look at the place. Then I heard some encouraging reports and decided to make the trip. I showed up expecting a big trout bite. What actually happened? Let’s just say the fish had OTHER plans. You’ll see how to adjust when a promising spot isn’t producing, so you can spend less time running around and more time getting bites. Watch the video below to find out what happened when I went back. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Lure 1: Polk County Tweaker Lure 2: Skinny Lipper Rod: Slot Machine Reel: Otis 2500 Line setup: 8-pound braid , a 12-pound mono leader, and a short 20-pound mono bite tippet. Look for Life Before Giving Up on a Spot Years ago, this area had beautiful grass flats and some incredible trout fishing. On a previous visit, those flats had turned into mud, and the water was murky. It was a pretty sad sight. This time, the section I fished had grass growing again. It wasn’t all the way back, but there were mullet everywhere and pinfish flashing below. That gave me a reason to stay, even when the first drift produced nothing but a few weak topwater strikes. I knew there was life in the area. I needed to figure out what the fish would eat. A slow first pass doesn’t automatically mean you picked the wrong spot. Try LESS Action When Fish Are Spooky Once the sun came up, the wind was light and the water was calm. I switched to a Black Ice Tweaker and did something I rarely did back when I fished this area regularly. I stopped twitching it. Instead, I slowly dragged the lure just above the grass in roughly 12 to 18 inches of water. When I spotted a redfish cruising, I cast ahead of it and brought the lure across its path. And those reds were pouncing on it. In those calm conditions, I suspect the extra disturbance from my earlier presentations was putting fish off. That quiet, steady retrieve made a big difference. But that doesn’t mean you should NEVER twitch a jerk shad. Later, the wind picked up and disturbed the surface. Adding twitches helped get their attention, and that’s how I caught my biggest snook of the trip. Let the conditions and the fish’s response guide how much action you give your lure. Rethink Your Color and Leader Choices Ten years ago, I wasn’t throwing black lures in bright, clear conditions. Now, black has become one of my first choices when it’s sunny, calm, and the fish are finicky. That change came from comparing light and dark lures on the water. In those comparisons, dark colors have often done better in conditions where I used to automatically reach for white. On this trip, Black Ice earned its place. I also went lighter with my line: 8-pound braid and a 12-pound mono leader, with a short 20-pound mono bite tippet. The idea was to keep the presentation subtle while adding abrasion protection near the lure. My own abrasion tests are why I now prefer mono leaders. In the comparisons I’ve done, mono outperformed the fluorocarbon I tested, including when I compared similar diameters. That setup helped me land an unexpected big snook. Although I normally use a heavier bite tippet when expecting snook, I had rigged this one with trout and redfish in mind. Fish the Same Water With a Different Approach I drifted through the same stretch THREE times. Each pass got better. In the past, I might have left after the first drift and run several miles to another spot. This time, the bait and activity convinced me to give those fish another look. The second pass produced redfish and snook. The third brought more snook, including the biggest one. The big trout I came for? I saw one follow the lure, watched its mouth open, and set the hook before I felt the bite. Yep. Pulled it right out of its mouth. Still thinking about that one. But I caught more redfish and snook in that zone than I ever had before. Returning to familiar water with a different approach made for a very different trip. Final Thoughts Your old favorite spot might still have plenty to offer. Start with what’s in front of you today: the habitat, the bait, the conditions, and how the fish respond. If those signs look good, try changing your presentation before firing up the motor. Sometimes the next productive spot is the one you’re already fishing. Have you returned to a favorite fishing spot after years away? Did your old approach still work, or did you have to change things up? Let me know in the comments! Check Out the Polk County Tweaker Here Frequently Asked Questions How did you retrieve the Tweaker on this trip? In the calm water, I used a slow, steady retrieve with no twitches. I moved it just fast enough to skim above the grass. When the wind picked up, I added twitches. What lure color worked best for you? Black Ice was the productive Tweaker color on this trip. Black has also become one of my go-to options for bright, calm conditions based on my recent lure comparisons. What line setup were you using? I used 8-pound braid, a 12-pound mono leader, and a short 20-pound mono bite tippet. When I’m specifically expecting snook, I typically use a 30-pound bite tippet. Why did you keep fishing the same spot? There was returning seagrass, plenty of mullet, pinfish, and some strikes. Those signs gave me a reason to change my approach before changing locations. Is the seagrass back throughout the Indian River? I can only speak to the section I visited. That area looked better than I expected, but it wasn’t back to what I remembered from its best years. More exploring is needed to see how other areas are doing.

items.title: 6 Fishing Tackle Purchases We Regret Buying
items.author: Salt Strong
items.excerpt: Avoid fishing tackle purchases you’ll regret. We share six mistakes, what’s worth your money, and when cheaper gear is the better choice.
items.search_text: I spent $900 on a fishing reel… and I wish I could take it back. And Luke’s biggest regret? Something we STILL SELL. In this podcast, we’re sharing six tackle purchases we regret, so you know what to skip, what’s actually worth your money, and when the CHEAPER option is better. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Reel: Otis 2500 Lure 1: Mulligan 5-Inch Bomber Lure 2: Prawn Original Rod: Slot Machine I’ve owned a reel that cost around $900. It’s incredibly smooth, lightweight, and fun to fish with. But I started worrying about it so much that I didn’t want to travel with it or let my kids use it. That’s a lot of money tied up in something I’m sometimes afraid to enjoy. Luke made a different version of the same mistake: spending most of his budget on the reel, then buying a rod with whatever was left. For fishing with artificial lures, his priorities now are: Choose a rod suited to the fishing you’ll be doing. Pair it with quality line. Choose a reel that fits the rod and line. The rod affects your casting, your ability to feel a bite, and your hookset. It deserves more attention than the leftover budget. Luke now often spends at least twice as much on his rod as his reel. You don’t have to follow an exact ratio, but the point is worth remembering before you spend big on a reel. That’s also why we wanted the Otis 2500 to deliver the performance we need at a price that lets us enjoy using it. Buy Gear for the Fishing You Actually Do Years ago, I bought an expensive setup for a beach tarpon trip. I had one very specific situation in mind, went all in, and barely used that setup afterward. Then I made a similar mistake buying a dedicated live bait combo for an outing. The guide had gear available, and I could have used an inshore setup I already owned anyway. Before buying another rod and reel, ask yourself: How often will I actually use this? Can something I already own handle the job? Could I borrow the gear for this trip? Some situations call for specialized equipment. But buying a whole new setup for a single outing can leave you with an expensive reminder sitting in the corner. Be careful with combos that make the rod feel like a free bonus, too. A bargain loses its appeal when the rod doesn’t perform the way you need it to. Buy for the fishing you regularly do, and make sure the rod is right for the job. Choose Versatile Lures Before Fancy Colors It’s easy to look at a realistic paint job and think, “That HAS to catch fish.” Luke used to put a lot more value on those details. After years of testing, he cares much more about what a lure lets him do. Can he rig it weedless? Fish it shallow? Put it on a jighead and reach deeper water? That’s why he brought up the Prawn and Mulligan Bomber. With different rigging options, he can use those profiles across a range of depths and conditions without carrying a tackle bag full of specialized lures. Color can be part of the decision, but it shouldn’t distract you from getting your lure to the fish and presenting it effectively. Being good with a few versatile lures is more useful than owning every color of a lure you barely know how to fish. Focus on depth coverage, rigging, and learning how your lures work. A fancy paint job won’t do those things for you. Make Your Leader Earn the Extra Cost One of Luke’s biggest regrets was spending so much money on fluorocarbon leader. He believed the claims about its advantages. In fact, he started testing it because he expected to prove how good it was. His results changed his mind. In the comparisons he describes in this episode, regular monofilament performed better in abrasion testing, and he didn’t see a strike advantage from fluorocarbon when matching line diameters. That last detail matters: matching the pound-test rating isn’t necessarily the same as matching the diameter. Luke now uses mono for his inshore leaders based on those results and his experience landing fish. We sell both, but we’re going to share what we’ve found even when the less expensive option is the one we prefer. Before paying more for a leader, make sure the benefit you’re buying shows up in the fishing you do. Final Thoughts I’m all for buying good fishing gear. I just want it to earn its place on the boat. A rod that helps you fish better, a reel you enjoy using, and a few lures you know well can go a long way. The expensive setup collecting dust at home doesn’t help much. Now I want to hear yours. What’s a fishing purchase you regret, whether it didn’t work, wasn’t worth the money, or got used once and has been collecting dust ever since? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions Should I spend more on my rod or my reel? For the lure fishing we discuss here, Luke prioritizes the rod first, quality line second, and the reel third. Choose a rod suited to your fishing, then match the rest of the setup to it. Do I need a separate setup for live bait fishing? Not always. For the inshore live bait trip I describe, a setup I already owned would have handled the job. Consider the bait, target fish, and conditions before buying another combo. Does lure color matter more than depth? Luke puts more emphasis on depth coverage and presentation than exact color or realistic paint details. Start with a lure you can rig to reach the fish and work effectively. Which Mulligan lure does Luke mention? Luke discusses the 5-inch Mulligan Bomber . He highlights its versatility, including the ability to rig it weedless or use it on a jighead. Why does Luke prefer monofilament leader? In the testing and fishing experiences he describes, mono gave him better abrasion resistance without a noticeable reduction in strikes at comparable diameters. Those results led him to switch his inshore leaders to mono.

items.title: 5 Fishing Gear Checks That Could Save Your Next Fish
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: These 5 simple fishing gear checks can help prevent lost fish, broken knots, damaged hooks, and other frustrating mistakes on the water.
items.search_text: I just lost two really nice fish back-to-back. And the frustrating part? I had already done the hard work. I found the fish, made the right presentation, got the strikes… and still watched both of them get away. The problem ended up being something embarrassingly simple that I should have caught before I ever made another cast. That got me thinking about all the little gear checks we tend to overlook while fishing. So here are 5 simple fishing gear checks you can knock out in about five minutes that could save your next big fish. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear: A few pieces of gear I use regularly for inshore fishing: Rod 1: Slot Machine Medium Rod 2: Slam Stick Medium Reel 1: Otis 2500 Reel 2: BG MQ 2500 Lure 1: Prawn XT OG (4.3″) Lure 2: Wake Mullet Lure 3: Moonwalker Insiders can save 20% on eligible tackle at Fish Strong . 1. Check Your Leader And Knots Your leader takes a beating throughout a fishing trip. Snook can rough it up. Rocks, oysters, docks, and other structure can damage it. Even a small rough spot can create a weak point that eventually costs you a fish. Run your fingers along the leader and feel for: Fraying Rough spots Nicks Abrasion If anything feels questionable, cut that section off and retie. You should also inspect the knot connecting your lure to your leader. And don’t forget the connection between your braid and leader. If the knot starts looking different, the tag end begins getting longer, or the nearby braid feels damaged, stop and retie it. It takes a minute. But losing a big fish over a bad knot will stick with you a lot longer. 2. Inspect Your Split Rings And Hardbait Hardware Hardbaits have several small pieces of hardware that can fail if you never check them. Start with the split rings . Make sure they’re still round and haven’t started spreading apart or becoming misshapen. If one looks damaged, replace it. I’d rather put a lure away than keep fishing something I don’t trust. While you’re checking the split rings, inspect the hook hangers too. Give them a little wiggle and make sure nothing feels loose. You don’t need to inspect this stuff every 15 minutes, but checking it before a trip, while tying on a lure, or while cleaning your gear afterward is a great habit. 3. Reset Your Drag Before Your Next Cast Some anglers like adjusting their drag while fighting a fish. I’m more of a set-it-and-forget-it guy. But if you DO adjust yours during the fight, make sure you reset it before making another cast. A drag that’s too loose can make it harder to drive the hook home. Too tight and you can: Straighten hooks Break your leader Break your knot Snap your line It only takes a second to check, especially after catching or losing a fish. 4. Inspect The First Few Feet Of Your Braid Your leader isn’t the only thing that can get damaged. Check the first few feet of braid above your leader connection. Look and feel for: Rough sections Burrs Fraying Damage from structure If anything looks questionable, cut that section off and retie your leader. This is especially important if you’ve been fishing around docks, rocks, oysters, or other abrasive structure. 5. Check Your Hook Point This is the one that got me. A lot of anglers check whether their hook is sharp. But there’s another problem to watch for. The actual hook point can roll over or bend slightly. That means your hook might still LOOK okay, but it won’t penetrate nearly as well. I check mine by carefully running my finger along the hook point from different directions. If I feel a burr, catch, or bent section, that hook needs attention. That tiny rolled point was enough to cost me two good fish. And I should have caught it sooner. Final Thoughts None of these checks are complicated. And you definitely don’t need to inspect every single piece of gear after every cast. But getting into the habit of checking your leader, knots, braid, drag, lure hardware, and hook points throughout the day can prevent a lot of unnecessary heartbreak. Because once you’ve found the fish, made the right cast, and finally gotten that bite… The last thing you want is a tiny gear problem ruining all that work. What’s something you always check while you’re fishing that I missed? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions How often should I check my fishing leader? Check it regularly throughout the trip, especially after catching fish or fishing around docks, rocks, oysters, and other abrasive structure. If you feel roughness or see damage, cut the damaged section off and retie. How often should I check split rings on fishing lures? Split rings and lure hardware generally don’t need constant inspection. Checking them before a trip, when tying on the lure, or while cleaning your tackle afterward is usually enough. Why do I keep losing fish on the hook set? There are several possible reasons, including a dull or rolled hook point, improperly set drag, damaged knots, or weakened line or leader. Inspecting your gear can help eliminate those problems. How can I tell if a fishing hook is damaged? Check both the sharpness and the actual shape of the hook point. A hook point can roll or bend slightly and become much less effective even if the hook doesn’t look obviously damaged. Should I retie my fishing knots every trip? It’s a good habit. Knots and leader material can weaken from fish, structure, casting, and general wear. If anything looks or feels questionable, retie it before it costs you a fish.

Inspect The First Few Feet Of Your Braid 5. Check Your Hook Point Final Thoughts Frequently Asked Questions How often should I check my fishing leader? items.title: 4 Ways to Beat the Summer Fishing Slump
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Ever hit that point in the summer where it feels like the fish just STOP biting? You were catching them consistently a few weeks ago… Then the water temperatures climbed into the upper 80s and 90s, and suddenly those same spots and tactics stopped pr
items.search_text: Ever hit that point in the summer where it feels like the fish just STOP biting? You were catching them consistently a few weeks ago… Then the water temperatures climbed into the upper 80s and 90s, and suddenly those same spots and tactics stopped producing. Welcome to the summer slump! The good news is the fish haven’t disappeared. You may just need to change WHEN and WHERE you’re fishing. Here are four things you can do to find more redfish, snook, trout, and flounder during the dog days of summer. Check it all out below! Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Should You Start Fishing Earlier In The Summer? Absolutely. And we’re not just talking about getting on the water at sunrise. During the hottest part of the summer, many fish shift their feeding windows to the coolest part of the day. That can mean 2, 3, 4, or 5 o’clock in the morning. By that point, the water has had all night to cool down, and fish may become more active before the sun comes up and starts heating everything back up. So if you normally arrive at your fishing spot around first light, try getting there BEFORE first light. You may discover that the best feeding window is already happening while you’re normally still driving to the ramp. Just remember that fishing and boating in the dark comes with additional risks. If you’re not experienced fishing before sunrise, go with someone who knows the area and is comfortable navigating in the dark. Why Are Grass Flats So Good During The Summer? One of the biggest problems with extremely hot water is lower dissolved oxygen. And fish need oxygen! Healthy green grass can help create better conditions for fish because it produces oxygen. So if your area has healthy grass flats, they can be excellent places to start looking during the summer. But not every grass flat is created equal. One of the best things to look for is a broken bottom . These are areas where grass is mixed with patches of exposed sand, creating a camouflage-like appearance. Those sandy potholes create ambush points where predators can wait for baitfish and other prey. Another major factor is nearby deeper water. Look for grass flats next to: Channels Drop-offs Deeper holes Other significant depth changes Fish can move onto the grass when conditions are comfortable and then slide into deeper water as the sun gets higher and the shallows heat up. A healthy grass flat with broken bottom AND quick access to deeper water can be a great combination during the summer. Why Should You Fish Closer To Inlets And Passes? No grass flats in your area? Start looking toward inlets and passes. An incoming tide can bring cooler, oxygen-rich water from the Gulf or Atlantic into warmer bays and estuaries. That moving water can also bring bait with it. And the fish know it! This doesn’t mean you have to fish directly inside a pass or inlet. Nearby marshes, structure, flats, and other areas influenced by that incoming water can all hold fish. This can be especially important if you’ve been fishing way back inside creeks and only finding smaller fish. Juvenile fish may remain in those backwaters, but larger fish can shift toward areas closer to inlets, passes, and better water during the hottest part of the year. Don’t Forget About The Surf! The surf can be another excellent option during the dog days of summer. Redfish, snook, trout, and flounder can all move along the coastline this time of year. And you don’t necessarily need to make a 100-yard cast to reach them. During higher tides, fish can move into the first trough right along the beach. In some situations, that means casting almost parallel to the shoreline rather than bombing your lure as far offshore as possible. If your usual spots inside the bay aren’t producing, the beach may be worth checking out. Can Fishing A New Area Help Break A Slump? Sometimes the best thing you can do is leave your favorite spot behind. When we fish the same areas over and over, we develop expectations. We know where we caught fish last week. We know which point usually holds redfish. We know which shoreline “should” have trout. And when those patterns stop working, it can be difficult to abandon them. Fishing completely new water forces you to start thinking again. Instead of relying on old waypoints and previous catches, you have to look at the conditions and figure out where the fish SHOULD be right now. Try driving an hour north or south. Fish another bay. Try the opposite coast if that’s an option. Worst-case scenario, you explore some new fishing grounds. Best-case scenario, you break out of that summer slump and discover a completely new fishery! Final Thoughts You don’t have to stop fishing just because the water gets HOT. But you may have to stop fishing the same way you did earlier in the year. Start earlier, find healthy grass near deeper water, move closer to inlets and passes, check out the surf, or explore completely new water. The fish are still out there. You just have to adjust to what they’re doing NOW. What’s your favorite way to find fish during the dog days of summer? Let us know down in the comments!

items.title: 4 Fall Fishing Lures I Trust for Bigger Inshore Fish
items.author: Luke Simonds
items.excerpt: These four fall fishing lures help you adjust when the bite changes. See when I switch so you can target bigger inshore fish with confidence.
items.search_text: Which fall fishing lures deserve a spot in your tackle box? I’ve narrowed my lineup down to four favorites for targeting BIG redfish, trout, snook, and flounder. But having these lures is only part of it. Knowing when to put one down and pick up another is what makes this lineup so useful. Watch the video below to see how I make that call, so you can spend less time second-guessing your lure and more time making casts that count. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Ready to put these lures to work? Grab the Ultimate Fall Lure Bundle to save on the full lineup plus rigging, and get the Skinny Lipper XL FREE! Grab Your Ultimate Fall Lure Bundle Here. Featured Gear: Moonwalker : My go-to 4-inch topwater in the mullet pattern. Skinny Lipper XL : A long-casting plug for searching big flats. Mulligan Bomber : A 5-inch paddletail, also shown in the mullet pattern. Prawn Original : A 4.3-inch shrimp imitation for a quieter presentation. Hoss Helix Hooks : Weighted, weedless hooks for fishing the Mulligan Bomber and Prawn Original in shallow water and around grass or cover. Hoss Round Eye Jigheads: Traditional exposed-hook jigheads for getting your soft plastics deeper when snagging isn’t a concern. Ultimate Fall Lure Bundle: Save on all four lures above, plus the rigging to go with them, and get the Skinny Lipper XL FREE with the bundle! Moonwalker: Take Advantage of the Topwater Bite When fish are aggressive, especially in the morning, the Moonwalker is tough to beat. I love the mullet pattern for fall because there’s so much mullet around. And for targeting bigger fish, I’m a big fan of the single inline hooks. Here’s why. If I’m trying to catch a 30-inch trout, the last thing I want is to hook a little 14-incher and spook the bigger fish nearby. Smaller fish can peck at this lure without getting hooked as easily as they would on trebles. That gives the bigger fish a chance to come over and grab it. When the surface bite slows, I reach for the next lure in the lineup. Skinny Lipper XL: Reach More Fish on the Flats If I’m searching a big grass flat for schools of redfish, casting distance matters. The Skinny Lipper XL casts an absolute mile. Its weight shifts toward the back during the cast, helping it carry through the wind and reach water farther from the boat. That means I can search more water with each cast. It also gives me options once it lands. I can use a straight retrieve, work it like a slashbait, or dip it below the surface and let it float back up. This is one of my favorite fall fishing lures when the topwater bite fades but fish are still willing to respond to a plug. If they’re turning down the plugs, I’m quick to switch to soft plastics. Mulligan Bomber: Make the Switch to Soft Plastics The Mulligan Bomber gives me a big baitfish profile with a softer presentation. Its paddle tail puts out vibration without being too noisy, and the mullet pattern looks great swimming through the water. It also casts well, which helps when those fall redfish schools are moving around and I need to find them. For shallow water, I rig it on a Hoss Helix weighted hook. When I need to get deeper, I switch to a jig head. That flexibility lets me keep fishing the same lure as the depth changes. And if I need to skip it under a dock or mangroves, it can handle that, too. Prawn Original: Have an Answer for Spooky Fish When fish get really spooky, the Prawn Original is one of my favorite options. Sometimes, extra noise and vibration work against you. That’s when I want the quiet, natural presentation of a shrimp imitation. I’ve caught some of my biggest fish across several species on this lure. It works throughout the year, but it’s especially valuable when fish won’t respond to the more aggressive options. Like the Mulligan Bomber, I can rig it on a weighted hook for shallow water or a jig head when I need to fish deeper. It’s the lure I want ready when the fish make me work for a bite. Final Thoughts These four lures make it easier to adjust throughout a fall fishing trip. I can cover water, take advantage of an aggressive bite, and go subtle when the fish get wary, all without digging through a pile of different options. Pay attention to how the fish respond. If one presentation isn’t getting it done, make an adjustment. Which of these four would you tie on first for a fall trip? Let me know in the comments! Check out the featured lures at Fish Strong here. Frequently Asked Questions What are your favorite fall fishing lures? My lineup is the Moonwalker, Skinny Lipper XL, Mulligan Bomber, and Prawn Original. Together, they give me options for aggressive fish, searching open flats, and getting bites from spooky fish. What do you throw when the topwater bite stops? The Skinny Lipper XL is my next option when fish stop feeding on the surface. If they aren’t responding to plugs, I switch to soft plastics. What lure do you use for spooky redfish? The Prawn Original is one of my favorites. Its subtle shrimp presentation is useful when fish shy away from more noise or vibration. Can you use these soft plastics in deeper water? Yes. I use weighted hooks for shallow presentations and switch to jig heads when I need to fish the Mulligan Bomber or Prawn Original deeper.

items.title: 3 Things That Determine Your Tailing Redfish Lure
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Seeing a redfish tail sticking out of the water is about as exciting as it gets. You found a fish. It’s actively feeding. Now you just have to convince it to eat YOUR lure. And that last part isn’t always as easy as it sounds. Tailing redfish can be
items.search_text: Seeing a redfish tail sticking out of the water is about as exciting as it gets. You found a fish. It’s actively feeding. Now you just have to convince it to eat YOUR lure. And that last part isn’t always as easy as it sounds. Tailing redfish can be surprisingly picky, especially in clear water or heavily pressured areas. So instead of reaching for one “magic” lure every time, there are 3 things you should look at before making your first cast. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots Featured Gear: Prawn XT JR What Is A Tailing Redfish? A tailing redfish is simply a redfish feeding with its nose down toward the bottom. As it roots through grass, mud, or shell looking for food, its body tips forward and its tail can break the surface. Sometimes you’ll only see the very tip of the tail. Other times, nearly the entire tail is sticking straight out of the water. Either way, there’s one important thing you already know: That fish is feeding. But feeding doesn’t necessarily mean easy to catch. The lure you choose and how you present it should depend on what that particular fish is telling you. The 3 Things That Determine Your Lure Before picking a lure, Pat looks at three variables: 1. How Spooky Are The Fish? This is one of the biggest factors. Tailing redfish in heavily pressured areas may have boats, anglers, birds, dolphins, and lures around them all day long. Those fish can get VERY skittish. In that situation, Pat prefers a natural, subtle presentation that isn’t going to create a bunch of flash, vibration, or splash. A small shrimp imitation like the Prawn XT JR is a great example. Another option is a simple “do nothing” style bait like the Polk County Tweaker . There doesn’t need to be anything flashy about the presentation. You’re simply trying to make an easy meal appear in front of a feeding fish without giving it a reason to spook. But if the redfish are aggressive and aren’t showing signs of being pressured, you can get away with more vibration. That’s when a paddletail like the Slam Shady 2.0 or 4-inch Mulligan can shine. The vibration helps the fish locate the lure, which can be especially important because a tailing redfish is often focused almost entirely on what’s directly underneath it. 2. What Are The Conditions? Conditions can completely change the amount of commotion you want from your lure. Think about it this way: Calm water = calm presentation. Windy or dirty water = more vibration can help. If the water is slick calm and clear, a loud lure landing near a redfish can send it running. A subtle shrimp or stickbait presentation is usually the safer choice. But if there’s wind, chop, dirty water, or slightly deeper water, the fish may need a little more help finding your lure. That’s where a paddletail can become much more effective. You also need to consider the bottom. Thick grass may require a weedless presentation, while cleaner bottom gives you more freedom with how you rig your lure. 3. What Are The Redfish Eating? Tailing redfish are commonly digging around for: Shrimp Crabs Marine worms Small baitfish Other crustaceans But don’t assume. Look around you. If you see shrimp spraying across the surface as the fish feed, throw something that resembles a shrimp. If you see small baitfish or mud minnows scattering, switch to a baitfish profile. The fish will often tell you exactly what they’re eating if you pay attention. Lure Placement May Be More Important Than Lure Choice You can have the perfect lure tied on and still ruin your shot with one bad cast. This is especially true with spooky redfish. If a fish is moving in a particular direction, resist the temptation to drop your lure right on its head. Instead, lead the fish. For pressured fish in clear water, Pat likes to place the lure at least a couple of feet ahead of the redfish and let the fish swim toward it. That gives the lure time to settle naturally without startling the fish. If the fish doesn’t notice it, you can gradually make your next cast a little closer. It’s much easier to move your presentation closer than it is to bring back a redfish you just scared halfway across the flat. The Tailing Redfish Tip Most Anglers Miss Not every tailing redfish gives you the same opportunity. Pay attention to the angle of the fish. If the tail is sticking almost straight up at a 90-degree angle, the fish is basically vertical with its nose buried toward the bottom. That fish is extremely focused on what’s directly underneath it. Your lure may need to land very close for the fish to even notice it, which makes the cast much more difficult. But if the tail is sitting at a lower, more horizontal angle, the fish itself is also more horizontal. That means it can see farther ahead. You can place the lure farther away, give the fish time to find it, and often watch the redfish swim over and crush it. The more horizontal the fish is, the higher-percentage opportunity it usually becomes. That doesn’t mean you shouldn’t cast at the vertical fish. Just know which fish gives you the better odds. Final Thoughts There isn’t one lure that wins every time you see a tail sticking out of the water. Instead, ask yourself three questions: How spooky are these fish? What are the conditions? What are they eating? Then adjust your lure and presentation accordingly. Start subtle when you can. Add vibration when the conditions or fish behavior call for it. And most importantly, pay attention to where you place that first cast. Because when you’ve already found an actively feeding redfish, the last thing you want to do is scare it before it ever sees your lure. Have you noticed certain lures or presentations working better on tailing redfish in your area? Let us know in the comments!

What Are The Redfish Eating? Lure Placement May Be More Important Than Lure Choice The Tailing Redfish Tip Most Anglers Miss Final Thoughts

items.title: 3 Simple Retrieves to Bring Your Suspending Hard Bait to Life!
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: Ever watch a fish follow your lure all the way to the boat… and then turn away at the last second? That’s usually a sign the fish WAS interested, but never got the trigger it was looking for. One of the biggest advantages of a suspending twitchbait i
items.search_text: Ever watch a fish follow your lure all the way to the boat… and then turn away at the last second? That’s usually a sign the fish WAS interested, but never got the trigger it was looking for. One of the biggest advantages of a suspending twitchbait is the control it gives you over that trigger. By changing your retrieve, pause length, and lure depth, you can match the way fish are feeding instead of forcing them to chase. In this video, I’ll show you three simple retrieves you can start using right away to get more bites with a suspending twitchbait. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Insider Exclusive: August’s Tackle Tester is the Flea Flicker , our suspending twitchbait, available for FREE exclusively to Salt Strong Insiders as part of their membership. 👉 Get yours here (Insiders Only). Featured Gear: Lure: Flea Flicker Why Fish a Suspending Twitchbait? Unlike a paddletail or jerk shad that continues sinking or rising, a suspending twitchbait pauses in the water column , often right in front of a fish. That pause is what makes these lures so effective. Many strikes happen while the lure is sitting nearly motionless after a twitch, not while it’s moving. This makes suspending twitchbaits especially effective when: Fish are feeding slowly. Water temperatures are cooler. Fish are suspended in the water column. You need to keep your lure in the strike zone longer. Retrieve #1: Twitch, Pause, Repeat This is the classic suspending twitchbait retrieve and one every angler should learn first. Here’s the basic sequence: Cast and let the lure settle. Reel in the slack. Give the lure 2–4 quick twitches. Pause. Repeat all the way back. The important part isn’t the twitches. It’s the pause. Some days fish want only a one-second pause. Other days they’ll wait five, six, or even seven seconds before committing. If you’re not getting bites, experiment with: Number of twitches Length of the pause Retrieve speed Let the fish tell you what they want. Control Your Depth with Your Rod Tip One of the easiest ways to fish a suspending twitchbait at different depths is simply by changing your rod position. Rod Tip Down Keeping your rod pointed toward the water helps keep the lure deeper during the retrieve. This works well when fish are holding lower in the water column. Rod Tip Up Holding your rod higher keeps the lure working closer to the surface. Just remember to extend your pauses slightly so the bait has time to suspend and settle instead of being pulled out of the water. This simple adjustment allows you to cover multiple depth zones without changing lures or jigheads. Retrieve #2: Slow, Steady Retrieve One of the biggest surprises for anglers new to suspending twitchbaits is how well they fish with almost no action at all. Simply: Cast. Let the lure sink briefly. Retrieve it at a slow, steady pace. The lure’s built-in action creates enough movement to attract fish without any extra rod work. This is an excellent retrieve for: New anglers Covering water Searching for active fish Fishing from boats or kayaks Many anglers also troll suspending twitchbaits behind the boat while moving between spots and end up catching fish they otherwise would have missed. Retrieve #3: Let the Current Do the Work If you’re fishing tidal creeks, river mouths, or any area with moving water, current can become your best retrieve. Cast upstream or across the current and allow the flow to carry the lure naturally. Instead of constantly working the bait, simply: Keep the slack out of your line. Stay in contact with the lure. Be ready when you feel the bite. This presentation shines around: Creek bends Oyster bars Current seams Winter trout areas Often the lure is doing almost all of the work while you simply maintain contact. Don’t Be Afraid to Experiment No single retrieve works every day. Sometimes fish want aggressive twitches. Other days they’ll only bite after a long pause. That’s why successful anglers constantly adjust: Pause length Number of twitches Retrieve speed Lure depth Small changes often make a big difference. Final Thoughts A suspending twitchbait is one of the most versatile artificial lures you can throw for inshore species. Whether you’re working shallow grass flats for redfish, targeting speckled trout in moving current, or covering water with a steady retrieve, these simple techniques will help you get more bites. The best retrieve is ultimately the one the fish tell you they want, so don’t be afraid to experiment until you find the pattern. Then repeat it until the bite changes. Frequently Asked Questions What is a suspending twitchbait? A suspending twitchbait is a hard or soft lure designed to remain nearly motionless in the water during pauses. This allows it to stay in the strike zone longer and trigger reaction bites from fish. What fish can you catch with a suspending twitchbait? Suspending twitchbaits are excellent for redfish, speckled trout, snook, flounder, and many other inshore saltwater species. What’s the best retrieve for a suspending twitchbait? A twitch-pause retrieve is usually the best place to start. Cast the lure, give it a few twitches, pause, then repeat while adjusting your cadence based on how the fish respond. How do I fish a suspending twitchbait deeper? Lower your rod tip during the retrieve to keep the lure deeper in the water column. Raising your rod tip keeps the lure working higher in the water. Can beginners fish a suspending twitchbait? Absolutely. A slow, steady retrieve is often incredibly effective and requires very little rod action, making suspending twitchbaits one of the easiest artificial lures for new anglers to fish.

items.title: 3 Essential Cut Bait Rigs for Shallow Water Inshore Fishing
items.author: Tony Acevedo
items.excerpt: Learn 3 essential cut bait rigs for shallow water fishing, when to use each one, and how to avoid wasting bait in the wrong conditions.
items.search_text: Most anglers make cut bait WAY harder than it needs to be. In fact, 3 simple rigs will cover just about any shallow-water situation you’ll run into. But the rig is only HALF the equation. There’s one other detail that can mean the difference between quality fish and feeding catfish all day. Check out this video and you’ll be ready to catch more fish on cut bait the next time you hit the water. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Gear Rod: Slam Stick Medium Reel: Otis 2500 Popping Cork Rig: Dr. Popper Freeline Rig: Gamakatsu Circle Hooks Leader: 20–30 lb Ande Mono Salt Strong Insiders can save 20% on eligible tackle at Fish Strong. 1. Freeline Rig: The Simple Go-To This is about as simple as cut bait fishing gets. Tie an inline circle hook to your leader, add your cut bait, and that’s it. No weight. This is the rig I use most often when fishing shallow, relatively clean water without a bunch of grass or structure along the bottom. Without a weight holding everything in place, your bait can naturally move with the wind and current. That’s a GOOD thing. Position yourself upwind or upcurrent from the area you want to target and let the bait slowly work toward it. Your bait moves naturally while its scent gets carried directly toward the fish. For most open-water situations, 20 lb monofilament leader is plenty. And make sure you’re using an inline circle hook , especially if you’re putting your rod in a rod holder and letting the fish hook itself. 2. Knocker Rig: When You Need More Control Take that same basic setup and add an egg sinker that can slide down your leader to the hook. Now you’ve got a knocker rig . This is the next rig I’ll reach for when the water gets a little deeper or the current gets strong enough that my bait won’t stay where I want it. For example, you might be fishing 3 to 4 feet of water and notice your freeline bait constantly rolling away from your target. That’s when some extra weight can help. The exact weight depends on the conditions. You don’t need to automatically grab the heaviest sinker in your tackle box. Use just enough weight to control your bait based on the depth and strength of the current. That keeps your bait in the strike zone without making the presentation unnecessarily heavy. 3. Popping Cork Rig: Grass, Structure & Dirty Water Sometimes you DON’T want your cut bait sitting on the bottom. Thick grass, oyster bars, and other structure can quickly bury your bait or leave you constantly snagged. A popping cork solves that problem by suspending your bait just above the structure. For this setup, I use a short section of 30 lb leader between my braid and the top of the cork. Below the cork, I’ll typically use 20 lb leader down to an inline circle hook. The length of that bottom leader depends on the depth and how high the grass or structure comes off the bottom. The goal is simple: Keep your bait right above it. There’s another advantage here, too. In dirty water, the popping cork creates additional sound as it moves around in the waves. That noise can get a fish’s attention before the scent of your cut bait helps close the deal. Where You Throw Cut Bait Matters MORE You can have the perfect cut bait rig and still waste an entire day. That’s because cut bait isn’t something you should randomly throw into the middle of a giant flat and hope a good fish eventually smells it. Instead, look for areas fish naturally use to travel and stage. One of my favorites is the edge of a flat where shallow water transitions into slightly deeper water. Those edges can act like highways for fish moving between feeding areas. Another great option is a deeper trough running alongside a shoreline. Pay attention to which direction the wind and current are moving. Position yourself so the scent from your bait travels through the area you’re trying to target. And don’t ignore points, oyster bars, and other staging areas connected to those travel routes. If a deeper trough leads toward a point, for example, fish can use that trough as a highway before stopping around the point to feed. Finally, look for life. Baitfish. Diving birds. Surface activity. Those clues can turn a massive stretch of water into a much smaller target zone. If you don’t get a bite after about 10 minutes, move down and try the next high-percentage area. You’re still covering water, just much slower than you would with artificial lures. Final Thoughts You don’t need a dozen complicated rigs to fish cut bait effectively. A freeline rig, knocker rig, and popping cork rig will cover the vast majority of shallow-water situations. The bigger key is knowing when to use each one and putting your bait somewhere quality fish are actually likely to travel or feed. That’s where planning your trip ahead of time can make a huge difference. If you need help identifying depth changes, points, structure, contours, and other high-percentage areas in your local waters, Smart Fishing Spots can help you narrow down where to start before you hit the water. Which of these three cut bait rigs do you use most often? Or do you have another way? Let me know in the comments! Frequently Asked Questions What is the best cut bait rig for shallow water? A freeline rig with an inline circle hook is a great starting point when fishing shallow water with relatively clean bottom and manageable current. It allows your bait to move naturally with the water. When should I add weight to a cut bait rig? Add weight when stronger current or deeper water causes your bait to move too far from your target area. A simple knocker rig allows you to add enough weight to keep the bait under control. Should I use a circle hook for cut bait? Inline circle hooks are ideal for this style of fishing, especially when you’re placing the rod in a rod holder and allowing the fish to hook itself. Avoid offset circle hooks if your goal is to reduce the chance of deeply hooked fish. When should I use a popping cork with cut bait? Use a popping cork when fishing over grass, oyster bars, or other structure where you want to keep the bait suspended off the bottom. It can also provide additional sound and attraction in dirty water. Where should I throw cut bait? Focus on areas fish use as travel routes or staging areas, including flat edges, deeper shoreline troughs, points, oyster bars, and depth changes. Visible baitfish, birds, and other signs of feeding activity can help you narrow down the best places to fish. What can I use for cut bait? Mullet, ladyfish, pinfish, shrimp, and blue crab can all be used as cut bait. The best choice will depend on the forage available and the species you’re targeting.

items.title: 10 Inshore Saltwater Fishing Terms Every Angler Needs To Know
items.author: Pat Ogletree
items.excerpt: If you’ve ever watched a fishing video and heard someone say, “Fish the point,” “Work the drop off,” or “Target the drain,” you might have wondered… What does that actually mean? The truth is, these aren’t just fishing buzzwords. They’re names for th
items.search_text: If you’ve ever watched a fishing video and heard someone say, “Fish the point,” “Work the drop off,” or “Target the drain,” you might have wondered… What does that actually mean? The truth is, these aren’t just fishing buzzwords. They’re names for the features that consistently hold fish. Once you understand what they are and why fish use them, you’ll start looking at the water completely differently and finding better spots before you even make your first cast. Ready To Finally Fish With Confidence? Then sign up for our FREE INTERACTIVE Saltwater Fishing School below. YES! Sign me up! NO. I hate fishing. Featured Software: Smart Fishing Spots The 10 Fishing Terms Every Angler Should Know In this video, Coach Pat breaks down ten of the most common terms you’ll hear inshore anglers use, including: Points that funnel bait into predictable feeding lanes. Drop offs that let fish move between shallow feeding areas and deeper water. Flats where fish feed during the right tides and conditions. Transition zones where different bottom types or depths meet. Potholes that create natural ambush points. Oyster bars that attract bait and predator fish year-round. Grass lines that define productive feeding edges. Drains where moving water carries bait directly to waiting fish. Pinch points that increase current and concentrate feeding activity. Current breaks where fish conserve energy while waiting for food to drift by. Each one plays a different role, but they all have one thing in common: They help concentrate fish. The Simple Formula For Finding Better Fishing Spots You don’t need to memorize every fishing term to become a better angler. Instead, look for areas that combine these three ingredients: A change in depth A change in bottom composition Moving water When multiple features overlap in one location, your odds of finding feeding fish increase dramatically. That’s why experienced anglers spend so much time looking at maps and reading the water before they ever make a cast. Final Thoughts Learning fishing terminology isn’t about sounding like an expert. It’s about understanding why fish position themselves where they do. Once you know what these features are, you’ll spend less time guessing and more time fishing productive water. Watch the video above, then let us know in the comments: What fishing term confused you the most when you first started?
